1021-the-congo-and-other-poems:
Vachel Lindsay, an American poet who read his verse aloud on the road, fills this book with chants meant to be heard, not just read on the page. Its best-known piece, "The Congo," beats out drums, chants, and crowd noise to tell of Africa as seen through American fancy. Other poems praise small towns, heroes, and the open road.

Lindsay wrote for plain folk and sang his lines with a performer's verve, which made him a popular voice in his day. The poems mix praise, satire, and gospel fire. Read now, the title poem also shows the limits of its age, and the book stands as a loud, odd, and vivid piece of early American verse.
10216-poems:
Marietta Holley, best known as Josiah Allen's Wife, gathered these poems in a volume dedicated to her mother's memory. Holley wrote many verses when young, and here she pairs humor and sentiment with tales of love, loss, and home. The book shows a side of her work apart from her famous comic prose.

Pieces range from summer and the sea to haunted castles, knights, deacons' daughters, and fisher wives, with titles like The Brothers, Little Nell, and A Dream of Spring. Some poems moralize, others simply sing. Readers get a varied, Victorian-era collection, warm, plain, and easy to enjoy in small doses.
1031-charmides-and-other-poems:
Oscar Wilde, still a young Oxford man, opens this early book with "Charmides," a lush retelling of a Greek myth, and follows it with lyrics on art, love, Rome, and the sea. The poems show a student drunk on beauty, keen to prove himself in the high style of Keats and the classics.

Gods, statues, flowers, and tombs crowd the lines, and the verse aims for rich sound and fine finish over plain sense. Some pieces already carry Wilde's wit and polish. The book marks the start of a career that would soon move from verse to plays and prose, and it pleases readers who love ornate late Victorian song.
10328-poems:
Walter R. Cassels published this poetry volume in London in 1856, gathering lyrics, sonnets, and narrative pieces. Titles range from Mabel and Hebe to Spring, The Eagle, and The Delectable Mountains, with songs on love, parting, and the sea. Cassels writes in a mid-Victorian romantic voice, fond of nature and myth.

Sonnets on the death of the Duke of Wellington, a poem on Guy of Warwick, and pieces on Orion and Vulcan show his wide taste. Some poems are short and musical, others more formal. Readers get a varied, period collection, pleasant for browsing and for students of minor Victorian verse.
1034-poems:
Wilfred Owen, a young English officer killed a week before the Armistice in 1918, left behind the fiercest poems of the First World War. His lines put readers in the trench: gas, mud, rotting feet, and boys sent to die for old lies about glory. The poems were gathered after his death by friends.

Owen's pity runs through every page, but so does his anger at generals, priests, and poets who praised war from afar. Images of blinded men and wasted youth still hit hard. The book made him the voice of his generation's loss, and it stands at the heart of English war poetry.
10367-poems:
Sir John Carr published this poetry volume in 1809, dedicating it to Lady Warren with modest, polite thanks. Carr, a traveler and writer, had written many verses in boyhood and later as relief from harder work. He offers them with diffidence, claiming no deep or solid power.

The poems mix light verse with graver pieces, joining jest to serious thought, as his Latin motto promises. Travel, society, and private feeling supply the subjects. Readers get a polite, early nineteenth-century collection, charming in parts, and useful for students of travel writers who also versified.
1042-a-reading-of-life-with-other-poems:
George Meredith, the Victorian novelist turned poet, reads human life as a choice between ease and effort in the title sequence of this 1901 book. Short lyrics weigh manhood, love, and fate, while a second part turns Homer's Iliad into English hexameters, with Achilles raging and armies massing.

Meredith's verse is dense and aphoristic, packed with nature images and hard-won maxims. He urges readers to face pain and grow, not to drift. The book shows his late style at full stretch, and it appeals to readers who like poetry that thinks as hard as it sings.
10457-the-lonely-dancer-and-other-poems:
Richard Le Gallienne published this poetry book in 1913, with a frontispiece portrait by Irma Le Gallienne, to whom it is dedicated. Le Gallienne opens with a sonnet on time as a bandit who locks fair women, friendships, and noble dreams in glimmering caverns of the past. Only love, he says, remains in the last shrine.

The lonely dancer gives the book its title, followed by lyrics on birds at dawn, Venus, and a faithful friend. Short, musical poems on love, loss, and faith fill the set. Readers get a lyrical, early twentieth-century collection, tender, romantic, and easy to read aloud.
10518-poems:
John Hay published this poetry volume, with a note to a revised edition explaining why he left the poems as they were. Hay wrote most of the pieces in the first half of 1870, while in Spain, then left Madrid in August as war broke over Paris and Sedan. He never returned to Spain, though he long dreamed of revisiting it.

Hay says the poems' merits and faults are those of youth, and cannot be fixed without tearing the book apart. He corrects only the plainest errors, leaving hot prejudices, lyric praise, and rapid judgments intact. Readers get a youthful, romantic collection, full of Spain, war, and early promise.
10578-a-hidden-life-and-other-poems:
George MacDonald, the Scottish novelist and poet, published A Hidden Life and Other Poems in 1864. The book opens with a dedication to his father and takes an epigraph from Dante, setting a tone of faith, gratitude, and sober thought. Its poems range from childhood memory to prayer, fatherhood, and the quiet work of conscience.

MacDonald writes in plain, musical verse, often turning a small scene into a thought about God and human life. The title poem and its companions reward slow reading, with feeling held in check rather than spilled out. Readers who know his novels will find the same moral warmth here, in shorter and more personal form.
10750-the-miracle-and-other-poems:
Virna Sheard published The Miracle and Other Poems in 1913, dedicating the book to her brother Eldridge Stanton, who died bravely at Niagara on February 4, 1912. Its contents range from "The Crow" and "When April Comes" to "A Song of Summer Days," "The Heart Courageous," "A Southern Lullaby," and "The Fairy Clock." Seasons, nature, and faith recur throughout.

Sheard writes in a gentle, musical voice, with feeling held in simple images of birds, flowers, and roads. The poems suit reading aloud and quiet reflection. Readers get a tender early twentieth-century collection, marked by grief for a brother and by hope beyond it.
10814-legends-tales-and-poems:
Gustavo Adolfo Becquer, the Spanish Romantic poet, appears in Legends, Tales and Poems, edited with introduction, notes, and vocabulary by Everett Ward Olmsted of Cornell University. The book opens with a life of Becquer. Its first legend is set in Seville, along the Guadalquivir near the convent of San Jeronimo, where a lagoon feeds a small valley under white poplars.

Olmsted's edition was made for students of Spanish, with help for reading Becquer's prose and verse in the original. The legends mix the supernatural with Andalusian scenery, in the author's haunting manner. Readers get a scholarly doorway into a poet Spaniards rank among their finest Romantics.
109-renascence-and-other-poems:
Edna St. Vincent Millay's first book announces a voice both tender and defiant. Renascence and Other Poems opens with the title poem, in which the speaker's soul swells beyond the world and returns chastened. Short lyrics on love, sorrow, and the hills follow.

Poems like Interim, The Suicide, God's World, and Afternoon on a Hill show Millay's range in few lines. Sonnets close the volume with formal control and feeling. The book made the young poet famous before she turned twenty-five. It remains a bright entry point to her work.
10910-robert-louis-stevenson-an-elegy-an:
Richard Le Gallienne honoured Robert Louis Stevenson with this 1895 book of poems, opening with a long elegy for the Scottish writer who died in the South Seas. The elegy pictures Stevenson asleep on his Pacific island, a northern dreamer under strange stars, and praises his roaming life and Scottish pride. Other poems follow, mainly personal in theme.

Spring odes, a ballad of London, verses on Tennyson, Gladstone, and Omar Khayyam, and love lyrics fill the collection. Le Gallienne writes in a musical, late-Victorian style, mixing grief for a friend with reflections on art, faith, and home. The book appeals to readers of Stevenson and to anyone who enjoys poetry of friendship and remembrance.
10913-english-poems:
Richard Le Gallienne published English Poems in 1895, in a fourth edition revised that April after editions in 1892 and 1894. The book opens with an epistle dedicatory to his sister Sissie, teasing her for dreaming, loving, and aspiring only to hive little lyrics and sell them to a publisher. A bee-farm reminds him of a publisher's trade, where stolen kisses become comb sold by weight.

The lyrics that follow are musical, romantic, and lightly ironic, in the manner of the nineties. Le Gallienne writes of love, art, and youth with grace. Readers get a representative collection from a poet of the Bodley Head circle, in its revised form.
10945-lays-of-the-scottish-cavaliers-and:
W. E. Aytoun gathered his Scottish ballads in this volume, first published in 1849 and reprinted from that edition. The lays retell episodes of Scottish history in stirring verse: Edinburgh after Flodden in 1513, the execution of Montrose, the heart of Bruce, the burial march of Dundee. Notes explain the history behind each poem.

Miscellaneous poems follow, including pieces on Milton, the Danube, and the sheik of Sinai. Aytoun writes as a patriot storyteller, praising loyalty and courage while mourning defeat. The collection helped shape how Victorian readers imagined Scotland's past, and its best-known ballads are still recited for their marching rhythm and vivid battle scenes.
11059-the-sylphs-of-the-season-with-othe:
Washington Allston, American painter and poet, wrote these poems, opening with The Sylphs of the Seasons, a poet's dream. Allston assigns images to seasons by their strongest impression: the running brook to spring, for its spirit of renewal, and the placid lake to summer. A prefatory note explains his choices.

Other poems include tales, sonnets on artworks by Michelangelo, Raphael, and Rembrandt, ballads such as First Love and Will the Maniac, and satirical verses on fashion and taste. Allston writes as a painter-poet, attentive to pictures and to nature. The collection suits readers of early American poetry and of the romantic imagination in verse.
11064-andromeda-and-other-poems:
Charles Kingsley collected poems in this volume, opening with Andromeda, a classical tale in verse. Over the sea past Crete, on the Syrian shore, a dark-haired Ethiopian people, skilled with needle, loom, and dye, fear the stars, the sea, and the gods of Olympus. Andromeda's story unfolds from that fearful world.

Other poems include The Sands of Dee, The Three Fishers, The Last Buccaneer, Songs from The Water-Babies, and ballads of knights, outlaws, and saints, with sonnets and songs of the seasons. Kingsley writes in a musical, narrative style, fond of legend and moral reflection. The collection suits readers of Victorian poetry who enjoy myth retold with earnest feeling.
11091-poems:
John L. Stoddard published this 1913 volume of poems, opening with a proem about an old man playing a silent violin, a dreamer whose songs may never touch the human heart. The contents range widely: a promenade solitaire, reincarnation, the Ring Nebula, the Sphinx, youth and age, sunset at Interlaken, Corsica, the Venus of Melos, and a story of the sea.

Later poems visit Rome, Fontainebleau, Japan old and new, Meran in the Tyrol, and Lake Como, with verses on friendship, a dead dog, sleep, gratitude, and weariness. Stoddard writes in a traditional, musical style, fond of travel, nature, and reflection. The collection suits readers of late romantic verse, offering quiet poems of place, memory, and the passage of time.
11096-tales-of-ind-and-other-poems:
T. Ramakrishna published this 1896 volume of verse, dedicated to the memory of his daughter Kamala. The opening poem to his daughter calls her the star that rose to cheer a humble life, and a poem to Lord Tennyson mourns the master whose songs purified and ennobled men.

Longer tales follow Seeta and Rama, a tale of the Indian famine set in a deep sunk lonely vale between verdant hills. Others tell of Prince Désing, Rudra, the royal huntress, Chandra at Tellikóta, and the Korathy's lullaby. In one tale, Timma on horseback hurls javelins at a charging elephant, six in succession, until the beast flees toward Vijiapore. The poems blend Indian legend with Victorian verse forms.
11101-coleridge-s-ancient-mariner-and-se:
Frederick H. Sykes edited this 1908 school edition of Coleridge's poems for the Scribner English Classics, using J. Dykes Campbell's Globe text. An introduction traces Coleridge's life, from his birth into a momentous age to his friendships and failures, drawing on Campbell's memoir and the poet's letters. Notes by the editor and Lane Cooper explain hard passages.

The poems include The Ancient Mariner, Christabel, Kubla Khan, Love, France: An Ode, Dejection: An Ode, Youth and Age, and Work Without Hope. In the Mariner, two voices debate the sailor who shot the harmless albatross and must do penance long and heavy. The volume suits students meeting Coleridge for the first time, with text, life, and notes together.
11193-elegies-and-other-small-poems:
Matilda Betham's early poems, dedicated to Lady Jerningham in November 1797, gather elegies and short miscellanies written in the author's youth. The dedication and preface apologize for their slightness while hoping they hold some merit, and Betham candidly notes she has altered or acknowledged any borrowed passage she could recall. Grief, friendship, and rural scenes supply most subjects.

The volume is valuable less for single famous poems than for what it reveals about a young woman entering print in the 1790s. Patronage, modesty, and careful self-presentation frame the verse. Readers of Romantic-era women's writing will find here a starting point, modest in claim and revealing in tone.
11398-a-further-contribution-to-the-stud:
This Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology study, a further contribution to mortuary customs, catalogs how peoples dispose of their dead, with illustrations of dead houses, Pima burial, towers of silence, Alaskan mummies. burial urns, grave pens, Tolkotin cremation, Eskimo lodge burial, Innuit and Ingalik graves, Dakota scaffold burial, tree burial, Chippewa scaffold burial, canoe burial, and offerings of food to the dead. A transcriber's note explains macrons, Greek words, and three forms of the text.

The article quotes extensively from published sources, with inconsistencies preserved and errors listed at the end. Its comparative scope, from North America to Australia, reflects early anthropology's collecting impulse. For readers of ethnology, it remains a detailed, if dated, survey of burial practice.
11558-poems:
S G Goodrich's Poems appeared in New York in 1851, from G P Putnam. The book opens with forest oaks over graves. A tumbling cliff sounds like a rough note in the song of centuries. Billings and other artists drew the pictures.

Titles run from the departure and voyage of the fairies to Lake Superior. The leaf and the bubble chase follow. The sea bird and the first frost of autumn appear too. Burial at sea closes part of the list. The poems mix nature, fancy, and American scenes, with Indian lovers and the Mississippi among the subjects.
1186-poems:
Alice Meynell, a Victorian poet of fine and Catholic sensibility, gathers lyrics on love, loss, nature, and faith in this 1903 volume. Sonnets to the beloved, songs of spring, and laments for the dead show her craft: short lines, clear images, and a grave, musical tone.

Meynell writes with restraint, letting a single image carry a poem's feeling. Her work won praise from poets who prized finish over noise. The book gives a compact view of a respected minor poet, and it suits readers who like quiet, polished verse. Meynell's restraint and clear images give the volume its lasting charm.
11939-life-s-enthusiasms:
David Starr Jordan, president of Leland Stanford Junior University, published Life's Enthusiasms in 1906 with the American Unitarian Association. The book opens with a reflection on poetry: truth expressed in the fewest possible words, in words that could not be changed without weakening meaning or melody.

Jordan argues for cheerfulness as a discipline. He notes that humor is necessary to the salvation of the serious man, and that Americans have a gift for seeing droll things and expressing them drolly. Verses about a campfire, minarets of snow, and a hoarded volume drawn from a pack give the essays a lyrical close. They link enthusiasm to both work and wonder.
12037-the-wild-knight-and-other-poems:
G. K. Chesterton's Wild Knight and Other Poems, published in 1900, thanks the editors of the Outlook and the Speaker for permission to reprint a considerable number of the poems. Chesterton notes that they were selected and arranged with a view to unity of spirit rather than unity of time or value, many of them being juvenile.

Contents open with By the Babe Unborn and The World's Lover, poems of chivalry, faith. Wonder that show Chesterton's early voice: paradoxical, musical, and earnestly romantic. The Wild Knight, as a figure, stands for the young poet's ideal, a champion of lost causes and unseen things, before Chesterton became famous as a journalist and novelist.
12217-economics-volume-ii-modern-economi:
Frank A. Fetter, professor of economics at Princeton, published this second volume of his Economics in 1916, devoted to modern economic problems. Fetter dedicated the book to his mother, with a youthful heart and sympathetic interest in all things human.

Part one covers resources and economic organization, part two money and prices, with chapters on coinage, fiduciary money, and the standard of deferred payments. Later parts treat tariffs, excises, and wartime revenues, noting how internal taxes spread in war to a multitude of articles. Fetter writes as a teacher, defining terms before arguing. The volume shows American economics just before the war economy remade its subject.
12391-poems:
Elizabeth Stoddard's 1895 poems gather lyrics on seasons, houses and married life, with a few longer narrative pieces. Contents move from November and March to August and October, and from a house by the sea to a house of youth. A baby song sits beside a wife speaking and a husband answering.

Stoddard writes in a plain, watchful voice, noting pain, memory and the small shocks of daily life. Longer items such as The Wolf-Tamer, The Abbot of Unreason and a bull-fight scene widen the range beyond domestic lyric. The collection shows a nineteenth-century American poet working at both intimate and dramatic registers, with feeling held close rather than declaimed.
12413-among-the-millet-and-other-poems:
Archibald Lampman's 1888 Ottawa volume, dedicated to his wife, gathers poems of Canadian fields and seasons. Contents run from Among the Millet and April through An October Sunset, The Frogs, Spring on the River and Heat, with a second section of further lyrics. Lampman thanks his wife in verse for hours spent musing, now brought back to her feet in print.

Nature is the centre: millet, rivers, frogs and autumn light, watched closely and rendered in musical, unforced lines. Lampman, later counted among Canada's Confederation poets, writes with a quiet eye for rural Ontario. The book offers an early, charming sample of a poet who found his subject close to home, in fields and weather.
12622-poems:
Denis Florence MacCarthy's Poems, Dublin 1882, published by M. H. Gill and Son, appear with a memorial appeal for the late Irish poet. Friends and admirers formed a committee to perpetuate his memory fittingly, with contributors including Cardinal Newman, Cardinal MacCabe, Cardinal MacClosky and Archbishop Trench. Lord O'Hagan, the Marquis of Ripon, Aubrey de Vere, Sir Samuel Ferguson and Ingram also gave.

Subscriptions were received by the Lord Mayor at the Mansion House and by friends in Dublin. MacCarthy's verse, Irish in subject and feeling, ranges from lyric to translation and national song. The volume offers a late nineteenth-century Irish poet in his own book, framed by the affection of a nation that mourned him.
12841-john-marr-and-other-poems:
Herman Melville's John Marr and Other Poems, published in 1922 with a note by Henry Chapin, gathers late sea poems and pieces from Timoleon. John Marr, Bridegroom Dick, Tom Deadlight, and Jack Roy lead the sailor poems, followed by sea pieces like The Haglets, The Maldive Shark, and The Berg. Battle Pieces poems form a supplement.

A poem on the good craft Snow Bird praises a brig that cares not for slanting snows or foul winds. Old Counsel warns a young master of a wrecked clipper not to grow over-elate. The book shows Melville's late, spare voice. It suits readers who know Moby-Dick and want the poet's final harbour.
12864-a-collection-of-college-words-and-:
B. H. Hall compiled this dictionary of college slang and customs, revised and enlarged in 1856, from his own senior year at college and friends' notes. It began as a foolscap list of twenty or thirty phrases. Explanations gathered in blue-covered exercise books grew it into a full record of student speech and habits at Yale, Harvard, and other colleges.

Entries cover dress fads, like white-topped boots mocked by a practical satire, societies, pranks, and classroom terms, with notes on what checked extravagance. Hall's friends dubbed him Antiquarian for the hunt. The book is a gold mine for readers curious about nineteenth-century student life.
13037-the-rowley-poems:
The Rowley Poems, edited by Maurice Evan Hare in 1911 from Tyrwhitt's third edition, presents Thomas Chatterton's famous medieval poems. Chatterton, born in Bristol on November 20, 1752, was the son of a cathedral subchanter who died before his birth, and grandson of sextons at St. Mary Redcliffe. The poems pretend to be the work of a fifteenth-century monk named Rowley.

Hare's introduction traces Chatterton's short life and the genesis of the poems, then weighs their value and the long Rowley controversy. Inside, pseudo-medieval spelling carries tournament scenes, with heralds, gauntlets, and knights like Nevylle and Bourtonne tilting before a king. The book remains a key text for the forgery that made a boy poet famous.
13045-war-time-financial-problems:
War-Time Financial Problems, by Hartley Withers, takes up how Britain should pay for war and run its money in wartime. Withers, already known for books on finance and the meaning of money, writes for readers who find the money market thorny. He treats war finance mainly as it touches industry, trade, and the daily work of the City.

Chapters warn against rash state control, such as seizing all profits above a set level or barring foreign issues, while admitting that some control must come. The book stands as a clear, plain-spoken wartime guide to credit, taxation, and the limits of government power over money.
13051-sketches-of-japanese-manners-and-c:
Sketches of Japanese Manners and Customs, by J. M. W. Silver, a lieutenant of Royal Marines, appeared in London in 1867. Silver gathered the sketches in 1864 and 1865 while attached to the Royal Marine battalion serving in Japan, and he dedicates them to Sir Edmund Prideaux. Native drawings, copied by chromo-lithography, illustrate the text.

A sham fight shows the book's eye for ceremony, as crested horsemen in gilt armor wheel in zigzag lines, spears flourished high and low like bayonet drill. The sketches give English readers one of their first close looks at Japanese dress, drill, and daily life.
13137-the-secret-of-dreams:
Yacki Raizizun's fifty-cent booklet The Secret of Dreams, with chapters on the dreamer, varieties of dreams, and the large consciousness, teaches that dreams reveal the inner man. Raizizun holds that the physical man is only a coat for the soul, and that material theories of dreams fail because they miss spirit. Everybody dreams, he says, but few weigh what dreams mean.

He claims past lives are stored in the subconscious, and that memory is their waking in dreams, strong in illness or low vitality. Newspaper tales close the book: a woman told in a dream to write songs, and a painter guided by Whistler's ghost. The booklet is a small, earnest work of popular mysticism from the 1920s.
13267-the-threshold-grace-meditations-in:
Percy C. Ainsworth's Threshold Grace, meditations in the Psalms, reprints pieces first published in the Methodist Times during his brief ministry. Contents run from the threshold grace and the habit of faith to eyes and feet, the safeguarded soul, a plea for tears, deliverance with honour, and the wings of the dove. Ainsworth writes quiet, pastoral devotion.

He holds that in the house of the Lord a man learns what beauty is, while out in the world beauty seems a sporadic flower where none expected a blossom. Later, he promises deliverance with light and glory in it, so that a man comes forth from trouble more noble, tender, and self-possessed. The book suits readers who seek a short, thoughtful pause in the Psalms.
13322-the-tongues-of-toil-and-other-poem:
William Francis Barnard's short book of poems speaks for working people in plain, rousing verse. The title poem calls labourers from many lands to hear their own strength, warning lords whose power rests on other men's hands. Other poems turn to child labour, broken homes, and women worn down by want.

Published in Pittsburgh by the Justice Publishing Company, the collection reads as protest poetry of its time: short lines, direct address, and anger at wealth drawn from infant blood and tired mothers. Barnard asks readers to see the human cost behind wages and goods, and to hear work itself as a voice demanding a fairer share.
13364-matthew-arnold-s-sohrab-and-rustum:
Matthew Arnold's Sohrab and Rustum and Other Poems, edited with introduction and notes by Justus Collins Castleman, head of English at South Division High School, Milwaukee, appeared in 1905. Contents gather narrative poems, Sohrab and Rustum, Saint Brandan, The Forsaken Merman, and Tristram and Iseult, with lyrics from Dover Beach and The Scholar-Gipsy to Thyrsis and Rugby Chapel. The volume is a school edition, with notes and questions.

In Sohrab and Rustum, Rustum wishes all he ever slew might live again. He wishes he himself lay on bloody sand by an ignorant stroke of his son, so Zal might weep above his grave, not his son's. Later, a scholar-gipsy passage tells of a shepherd who loved simple joys yet could not rest, since a shadow lowered on the fields. The book is a fine introduction to Arnold's verse.
13586-poems:
Samuel Rogers publishes his poems in London in 1814, opening with a wish that his mind, unfolded in his page, might enlighten climes and mould a future age. He hopes his verse, his leisure's best resource, might revive a generous wish, chase a sigh, or flush a faded cheek with honest joy, even if it does no more.

Memory appears as a herald of misery, telling of time misspent, comfort lost, and hopes too fondly nursed and rudely crossed. A boatman tells of Rob Roy, arm below knee, cattle ford, and mountain hold, as Rogers climbs Tarbat's shore and looks on another flood, the great ocean itself. The poems blend polite reflection, travel memory, and the quiet melancholy of a man of letters.
13759-secret-societies-a-discussion-of-t:
Three American clergymen argue against secret societies in this nineteenth-century volume. David MacDill opens with a treatise on their antiquity, secrecy, oaths, profanity, exclusiveness, and false claims. Jonathan Blanchard asks whether Christians should join such orders at all. Edward Beecher adds a report to a Congregational association in Illinois.

The writers hold that habitual secrecy breeds distrust and weakens open civic life. Oaths, they say, bind conscience in ways no private club should demand. Lodges are charged with claiming ancient roots they cannot prove. The book speaks from a Protestant reform stance of its time. It remains useful for the history of fraternal orders and their critics.
13809-mountain-idylls-and-other-poems:
Alfred Castner King published Mountain Idylls and Other Poems in 1901, after blindness ended his hope of arranging manuscripts himself. Friends helped prepare the volume, which he dedicates to them with affection. Poems picture Mount Wilson, the San Juan mountains, Ouray, and Uncompahgre Cañon. Pines sing sad music through the woods in one lyric.

King writes of grandeur in nature and of man's small place within it. Mountain views, streams, and forests fill the pages. His verse is earnest and devotional, shaped by loss and faith. The book preserves a little-known American poet of the Rockies. Readers of regional verse will find sincere, musical work here.
14315-old-english-sports-pastimes-and-cu:
P. H. Ditchfield, rector of Barkham and fellow of the Royal Historical Society, gathered Parish Magazine articles into Old English Sports in 1891. A preface thanks readers of his earlier Our English Villages and Canon Erskine for help. Sports follow the calendar, from spring May games through summer pastimes to October tournaments, with customs of village, church, and manor house throughout.

May Day opens in color. Men blow cow-horns to usher spring, maids carry garlands to churches, and Magdalen College choristers sing from Oxford's tower at dawn, a custom still kept each May first. Twenty or thirty yoke of oxen, horns decked with flowers, haul the May-pole to the green for raising with shouts and song. Cruel sports close in condemnation: bear-baiting, cock-fighting, and throwing at cocks ended when conscience and law intervened, and the new Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals marks the change.
1439-dreams:
Olive Schreiner's Dreams is a small book of allegories, printed in the order she wrote them. Each dream is a short parable. A hunter seeks truth, a woman stands at a gate, and a soul walks a road, all told in plain, biblical language that lets the image carry the meaning.

The pieces speak for women's freedom, for labour, and for a faith that must be lived rather than recited. Schreiner dedicated the book to a small girl-child who might one day grasp what her age could only glimpse. It is a brief, earnest work of vision, still fresh in its hope.
14638-the-lutherans-of-new-york-their-st:
George U. Wenner, pastor of Christ Church in New York, wrote The Lutherans of New York in 1918, covering their story and their problems. The Petersfield Press published it for the Lutherans of New York in the twentieth century.

Wenner traces German immigrant congregations, their churches, schools, and social work, and looks abroad as well, visiting Cologne and finding Protestant churches there newly strong through American methods. An epilogue, an appendix, and a bibliography close the book. It is a useful record of an immigrant church coming of age in a great city.
1469-poems:
Francis Thompson's Poems, in the 1909 Burns and Oates edition, gather the lyrics that made his name, including the love lyrics grouped as Love in Dian's Lap. Before Her Portrait in Youth and A Carrier-Song show his musical, image-rich manner, and later pieces turn from earthly beauty toward faith.

Thompson, a Catholic poet of the late Victorian age, writes of love, faith, and the divine pursued through earthly beauty. His diction is lush and his rhythms are bold. The volume is a good introduction to a poet once ranked among the finest lyric voices of his generation.
1471-new-poems:
Francis Thompson's New Poems, in its third English edition of 1907, gathers later lyrics headed by Sight and Insight, including The Mistress of Vision, Contemplation, and The Dread of Height. A dedication opens the book, and the poems that follow pursue vision, law, and the soul's ascent with Thompson's characteristic music.

The verse is dense with image and Catholic feeling, and its rhythms carry readers through long, meditative lines. Thompson's health was failing, and the book has a valedictory air. It is a rewarding volume for readers who already love his earlier lyrics and want his mature voice.
14871-poems:
Mary Alice Walton's 1910 booklet of poems, dedicated to the memory of her father, was composed when she was ill and either blind or nearly so. Its preface says the poems are offered to strengthen faith in God, and that a life filled by discipline and sorrow can still yield revelation and answers to prayer.

Walton writes of heavy crosses borne, of being brought through fire with faith unshaken in Christ, and of victory that leads to greater joy and fellowship with Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Life's battles, well waged, become a theme of endurance rather than complaint. Short and devotional, the poems speak as testimony: suffering remembered, faith kept, and gratitude for survival.
14906-songs-sonnets-miscellaneous-poems:
Thomas Runciman, born in Northumberland in 1841 and dead in London in 1909, left songs, sonnets and miscellaneous poems privately printed in 1922. Second son of Walter Runciman of Dunbar, he left the coast where his father was stationed to school and work in Newcastle.

Allowed for a time to study under William Bell Scott, on the fringe of the Pre-Raphaelite movement, Runciman painted portraits and landscapes through his life, loving landscapes most. His work was little known, for a nervous contempt for exhibitions kept his watercolours and oils from show. The poems, like the paintings, show a strong feeling for colour, place and quiet observation.
14953-oklahoma-and-other-poems:
Freeman E. Miller taught English at the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Oklahoma Territory. He publishes Oklahoma and Other Poems in Buffalo in 1895, dedicated to James Whitcomb Riley in affectionate memory of other days. Verses on joys flowing from fountains of long ago open the book.

To open each cage where a heartless age has chained a heart follows, in a poet's plea for feeling against a hard time. Miller writes of Oklahoma, of memory and of the prairie state taking shape, with the plain diction of a teacher poet. The volume is a period collection, local in subject and sentimental in tone, and it shows a territory finding its voice in verse.
14955-the-kings-and-queens-of-england-wi:
Mary Ann H. T. Bigelow's 1853 poems, published for the author and dedicated to the companion of her youth, middle age and declining years, begin with kings and queens of England. An inscription apologises for their careless, familiar style: they were hastily written from impulse for her own entertainment and that of her youngest granddaughter.

At her children's request she printed them, though failing eyes made revision hazardous, trusting friends to excuse the homely garb. Other poems follow the royal verses. Bigelow writes as a grandmother and amateur, warm and unpretentious, and the volume charms as a private family book made public by affection.
15079-green-fields-and-running-brooks-an:
James Whitcomb Riley's 1893 poetry book gathers Hoosier verse on farm life, seasons, and small-town folk. Titles run from August and autumn to the old retired sea captain, the iron horse, and a monument for soldiers. Riley dedicates the book to his sisters Elva and Mary.

His poems mix dialect speech with plain lyric feeling, praising home, harvest, and memory without high-flown artifice. Pieces on John Brown, Longfellow, and country pathways sit beside lighter ditties. Readers who like American regional verse will find Riley warm, homely, and easy to read aloud.
15101-the-mountain-spring-and-other-poem:
Nannie Glass's 1913 poetry book, dedicated to her parents, opens with a walk down a mountain road past flowers, rocks, and the Capon River in Hampshire. The title poem finds a silvery spring and takes its text from Revelation on the water of life. Other poems follow through seasons, Bible scenes, and nature lessons.

Titles include Go Wander, The Lilies, The Desert Spring, and pieces on Bartimaeus, Zacchaeus, and Bethlehem. Glass writes in a devout, lyrical voice, with simple rhymes and clear images. Readers who like gentle religious verse will find the book sincere, musical, and rooted in mountain country.
15205-the-feast-of-the-virgins-and-other:
H. L. Gordon's 1891 poetry book takes its title from the Feast of the Virgins, with other poems on flag, war, and home. Contents include an address to the flag, Gettysburg and the charge of the First Minnesota, Christmas Eve, and lines on Lincoln's letter. Minnetonka and the Black-Horse charge add Western and Civil War color.

Gordon writes in a patriotic, sentimental voice, with a motto preferring one word carved on rock to ten thousand in sand. His poems mix public occasions with private grief and hope. Readers of nineteenth-century American verse will find the book earnest, musical, and rooted in its time.
1567-poems:
T. S. Eliot's Poems of 1920, published by Alfred A. Knopf and dedicated to Jean Verdenal, gather his early lyrics after Prufrock. Gerontion opens the book, and Sweeney, Burbank with a Baedeker, A Cooking Egg, and The Hippopotamus follow, with whispers of immortality and Lune de Miel among them.

The poems are sharp, allusive, and often ironic, sketching a Europe of tourists, bankers, and weary talkers between the wars. Eliot's voice here is already distinct: cool, learned, and musical. The volume is a key early shelf for readers tracing the road to The Waste Land.
1568-poems:
William Ernest Henley's Poems, in the 1907 David Nutt edition, gather the verse of the poet best known for Invictus. A bust of Henley as frontispiece and a Shakespeare motto on love and summer flowers. The poems range from hospital sketches to London impressions and lyrics of courage under pain.

Henley, who knew suffering at first hand, writes with grit and music, and his short, strong lines carry a stoic temper. The tenth impression shows a book that found its readers. The volume is a good introduction to a Victorian poet of will, humour, and unflinching honesty.
16108-debris-selections-from-poems:
Madge Morris gathered her lyric poems under the title Debris, printed at Sacramento in 1881 by H. S. Crocker and Company. She dedicates the book to any reader who might find a grain of gold in its driftings, a modest image for a modest collection. Nearly forty poems follow, from Mystery of Carmel and Rocking the Baby to Uncle Sam's Soliloquy and A Neglected Woman's Right.

Home, love, loss, and faith run through the verses, with mothers, babies, old aunts, tramps, and ghosts of the heart taking their turn. The poems are short, plain, and musical, meant to be read aloud in a parlor rather than studied in a classroom. Readers of nineteenth-century verse will find a warm, personal voice from California's early literary scene.
16376-browning-s-shorter-poems:
Franklin T. Baker, professor of English at Teachers College, Columbia University, selected and edited Browning's Shorter Poems for Macmillan, in a fourth revised edition of 1917. First set up in 1899 and reprinted many times through 1917, the volume opens with a life of Browning. An essay on Browning as poet, appreciations, and a chronological list of works follow. A bibliography closes the front matter. The poems themselves follow in a generous selection.

Contents include The Pied Piper of Hamelin, Tray, Incident of the French Camp, and How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix. Herve Riel, Pheidippides, My Star, and Evelyn Hope follow. Love Among the Ruins closes the selection. Baker's school edition made Browning accessible to students. Readers will find a solid introduction to a great Victorian poet.
16424-some-christian-convictions-a-pract:
Henry Sloane Coffin restates Christian belief in modern terms in this 1915 volume, first preached and taught in New York. Chapters move from religion and the Bible to Jesus Christ, God, the cross, the new life, the church, and life everlasting. An opening survey tracks how nineteenth-century thought reshaped faith.

Coffin writes for thoughtful churchgoers caught between old creeds and new science. His style is calm and clear, with short chapters that build one on the next. The book aims to show that faith can be held with a modern mind, and it remains a fine sample of liberal Protestant thought before the First World War.
16735-lays-of-ancient-virginia-and-other:
James Avis Bartley of Orange County, Virginia, wrote this 1855 book of poems, issued by J. W. Randolph in Richmond and dedicated to his father. A prefatory letter to the public says the poems were written with pleasure, and asks only to be read with pleasure. The guardian angel of the father of Virginia, gliding through green shade, sparked the title lays.

Bartley mixes Virginia history with nature pictures and verses of virtuous affection. His lays praise old Virginia in lofty, earnest lines, while minor pieces turn to home and heart. The book gives a sample of mid-1800s southern verse, useful for readers of regional poetry and for those who study how Virginia told its own past in rhyme.
16839-sixteen-poems:
William Butler Yeats picked these sixteen poems by William Allingham for the Dun Emer Press at Dundrum in 1905. The set runs from Let Me Sing of What I Know and The Winding Banks of Erne, through The Fairies and The Lepracaun, to The Abbot of Innisfallen and The Ruined Chapel. Allingham sings of a west coast town, tides, winds, and little folk.

Yeats chose poems that show Allingham at his most Irish and most musical: fairies, maids, weddings, ducks on a pond, and ruined chapels. The verse is short, clear, and full of place. Readers who love Irish lyric verse will find a small, choice book, best read aloud, with Yeats's taste as its guide.
16950-goblin-market-the-prince-s-progres:
Christina Rossetti's two early books sit together in this World's Classics volume, first joined in one book in 1913. Goblin Market leads the set with its tale of two sisters, strange fruit sellers, and a rescue paid for in love and grit. The Prince's Progress follows, with shorter lyrics, songs, and devout pieces beside it.

Poems such as Remember, Up-hill, Cousin Kate, and A Birthday show her range: plain speech, strong music, and sharp feeling in small frames. Love, loss, faith, and choice return again and again, never dressed up in vague praise. For new readers, the volume is the best single start on Rossetti, with her most loved work at its head.
16992-on-the-king-s-service-inward-glimp:
The Rev. Innes Logan wrote this 1917 book of inward glimpses of men at arms. He served as chaplain to the forces from September 1914 to May 1916. Hodder and Stoughton issued it in London, New York, and Toronto, and Logan dedicated it to his wife. Chapters move from mustering men and a reinforcements camp into a clearing station with nothing to report. The aftermath of Loos, with doubts, fears, and the flavor of victory, closes the set.

Logan writes as a chaplain who lived with soldiers for twenty months, in tribute to those he served. His glimpses mix humor, grief, and faith in short scenes. The book gives a moving, first-hand view of Great War chaplaincy, valued for its human warmth and its plain sense of men under fire.
17081-cottage-poems:
Patrick Bronte's Cottage Poems, in this 1893 Dent text, open with an epistle to a traveling friend, written in plain, rustic verse. The muse sings not of palaces and kings, but of poor folk in pool cots, hens, and humble homes, hoping to mend hearts and soothe cares with rhyming stories. Flatterers, critics, friends, and foes all meet the verse, yet its aim stays kind.

The poems speak for a parson's care for his poor parish, in simple lines meant to be read aloud. Their faith is plain and their feeling warm, without show or polish. Readers of the Bronte family will find here the father's own voice, modest and earnest, beside the fame of his children.
17754-gustavus-vasa-and-other-poems:
W. S. Walker published this book of verse in London in 1813, led by a long poem on Gustavus Vasa, the Swede who freed his land from Danish rule. The book is dedicated to the Baroness Howe, daughter of a famed sea lord, and Walker sings the patriot as a gift of thanks.

Book one hails the Swede ordained by Heaven to save his land, restore its laws, and fix its freedom on a firm base. Shorter poems follow, on love, fame, and the calm virtues of home life. The verse is high, old-style, and earnest, a fair sample of the patriotic poetry read in Britain during the wars with France.
17768-the-hundred-best-english-poems:
Adam L. Gowans chose this hundred-poem set, printed in New York in 1904 by Thomas Y. Crowell and Company. Gowans admits in his preface that no one man's taste could settle such a list, and that only a vote of true poem lovers could claim to do it beyond doubt.

The poems run from an old madrigal through Arnold, Barbauld, Browning, Burns, and on to Wordsworth's sonnet on a world too much with us. The set gives a quick tour of English verse, from short songs to grave meditations. It still works as a first shelf of English poetry, and as a look at what readers prized in 1904.
17884-fifty-years-other-poems:
James Weldon Johnson, best known for The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man, published this book of poems in Boston in 1917, with a preface by Brander Matthews. The title poem marks fifty years since emancipation, and the book speaks from and for Black America in the years just before the Harlem bloom.

Poems honor unknown Black bards, the Southland, soldiers, mothers, and Abraham Lincoln, while others sing of the sea, the night, and young love. Johnson's voice is grave, musical, and proud, with lines that still ring in school and church readings. It is a short, strong set of verse, and a key early work by a writer who shaped Black letters.
17936-poems:
Sophie M. Almon printed this small book of Poems at Windsor, Nova Scotia, in April 1889, for private circulation. The volume was printed for the author by J. J. Anslow, and it holds sonnets, rondeaux, and short lyrics on love, loss, and thought.

Sonnets include Crows, Futurity, There Is No God, Disappointment, and Triumph, while rondeaux sing I Will Forget, When Summer Comes, and It Might Have Been. Later pieces run from Echoes and Noon to Eurydice and An Evening in October. Almon's verse is grave, musical, and personal, a rare, small book by a Nova Scotia poet.
18109-graveyard-of-dreams:
H. Beam Piper wrote Graveyard of Dreams for Galaxy Magazine in February 1958, a tale of hope stolen from a whole planet. The epigraph warns that wealth and name are dross beside the theft of hope, and Conn Maxwell must rob a planet of it.

Maxwell stands at the armor-glass front of an airship, gripping the rail as mountains rise and Litchfield draws near. He has been away, and now he must face what he left. Piper writes with a sure, sad hand for lost worlds and tired heroes. It is a fine, short science fiction tale, best read for its mood of return and loss.
18424-a-midsummer-holiday-and-other-poem:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published A Midsummer Holiday and Other Poems with Chatto and Windus in London, in a third edition dated 1889. The title sequence runs through the seaboard, a haven, a country road, the mill garden, a sea-mark, the cliffside path, in the water, the sunbows, and on the verge. Sea, shore, and summer light carry the whole set.

Other poems follow: a new-year ode, lines on the monument of Giuseppe Mazzini, Les Casquets, a ballad of Sark, Nine Years Old, and After a Reading. Later pieces give Maytime in Midwinter, a double ballad of August, Heartsease Country, a ballad of appeal, and cradle songs. Readers get Swinburne at holiday ease and at memorial gravity, with music that moves from shore walks to public tribute.
18574-across-the-sea-and-other-poems:
Thomas S. Chard published this poetry volume with Jansen, McClurg in Chicago in 1875, entered in 1874. Its epigraph from Pilgrim's Progress tells of a city shining like the sun, its streets paved with gold. The title poem first appeared in outline in the winter of 1869 and now stands complete.

The contents divide the poems into childhood, youth, manhood, and age, following a life across the sea of time. Chard writes of the sea as a picture of life, a theme he admits is worn. He offers his verses as a plain, sincere record of a life's seasons, from first years to last.
18791-outlines-of-a-mechanical-theory-of:
T. Bassnett's outlines of a mechanical theory of storms, published by D. Appleton of New York in 1854, argues a true law of lunar influence on weather. Bassnett builds on gravitation, the ether, and the medium of space in motion, with vortices forming as a new principle of nature.

The book gives practical instructions to navigators, so they may calculate coming changes of wind and weather for any day and any part of the ocean. Its sections treat the present state of meteorology, the moon's action on the earth's vortex, and famous storms at Milwaukee, New York, Ottawa, and Liverpool. Lunar influence, long rejected by the learned, is here defended as the key to storms.
1892-extracts-from-adam-s-diary-translat:
Mark Twain presents these extracts as Adam's diary, translated from the original manuscript. A note explains that he translated part of it years ago and has since deciphered more of Adam's hieroglyphs. Adam records Eden with a husband's bewilderment: Eve's questions, the animals, and the garden's rules.

A passage on tigers living on grass and flowers, when their teeth suggest they were meant to eat each other, shows Twain's method: Adam reasons solemnly. The reasoning itself is the joke. The diary is short, funny, and tender, and it pairs with Eve's diary as Twain's most affectionate retelling of Genesis.
19096-indian-legends-and-other-poems:
Mary Gardiner Horsford wrote this 1855 volume of Indian legends and other poems, inscribed to her father Samuel Gardiner. The poems retell Native American tales in romantic verse, with heroes, spirits, and landscapes of river, forest, and cataract. The tone is elegiac, mourning a world seen as passing.

One pilgrim steers his frail bark toward a thundering fall, chanting his death song as mist meets sky, while banners of oppression wave over hill and plain. Council fires burn only in memory. Readers get mid-century American verse on Native themes, sympathetic yet shaped by the views of its time.
19188-poems:
Christina G. Rossetti's Poems, here in the author's revised Boston edition of 1906, gathers her best-known verse, inscribed to her mother in reverence and love. Rossetti tells American readers that the book must speak for itself, and thanks Roberts Brothers and Macmillan for bringing it across the sea. The tone is devout and lyrical throughout.

Goblin Market stands at the heart of the book, as Laura pines for goblin fruit, grows thin and grey, and plants a kernel stone in vain while Lizzie watches in grief. Other poems turn on faith, love, and death. Readers get a major Victorian poet in her own chosen form, musical, grave, and deeply felt.
1924-many-voices-poems:
E. Nesbit's Many Voices, poems published in 1922 and dedicated to her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-love Gertrude Bland, gathers lyrics written across her later years. The contents open with The Return, and the poems that follow move between love, war, and the English countryside.

A passage in which the comfortable are told they have taken the ease and the honor and left others the toil and the shame shows Nesbit's anger at wartime inequality. Other poems answer it with tenderness. Readers who know Nesbit only from The Railway Children will find a different writer here: a poet of strong feeling, plain speech, and a social conscience.
19357-the-new-penelope-and-other-stories:
Frances Fuller Victor wrote this set of stories and poems of the Pacific Coast, published in San Francisco in the late eighteen hundreds. Most of the tales first ran in the Overland Monthly and other western magazines. They draw on border life in Oregon and the far west: trappers, settlers, and families of mixed blood and fortune.

The poems, written across the author's life, are less western in scene but share the same plain feeling. Together the two halves give a woman writer's view of a new region, where old eastern rank counted for little and new lives had to be made from scratch.
19443-our-profession-and-other-poems:
Jared Barhite, a school principal in Long Island City, gathered this volume of his own poems, published in the late eighteen hundreds. Written across a quarter century in spare hours, the verses treat teaching, daily work, rest, and the quiet of woods and streams. The title poem honors the calling of the teacher.

The tone is plain and earnest rather than grand, with short lyrics meant to inspire a tired worker or a young pupil. As a record of one schoolman's inner life, the book shows how verse served ordinary professional men as a private pastime before it ever reached print.
19502-frank-merriwell-s-chums:
Burt L. Standish wrote this school story of Frank Merriwell and his friends, published in the late eighteen hundreds. Frank asks hard questions, faces plots and snares, and proves himself in games of bluff, in a haunted room, and in a race for life on broken ice.

Rival Paul Rains runs shoulder to shoulder with Frank when girls cling to an ice edge that keeps giving way. Loyalty, pluck, and fair play carry the tale, which helped make Merriwell the most famous school hero of his age. Later chapters stage a bully's match, a duel played for comedy, and a mystery around a vanished ring.
19529-nala-and-damayanti-and-other-poems:
Henry Hart Milman translated these poems from Sanskrit into English verse, with mythological and critical notes, published at Oxford in the early eighteen hundreds. The title poem tells of King Nala and Damayanti, whose love survives gambling, loss, and exile.

In one passage Damayanti weeps as Nala explains that a demon, Kali, worked within him when he lost his kingdom and fled. Milman's verse, kept in old spelling for Sanskrit names, brought Indian epic to English readers long before it was widely known. Beside the title poem stand the Death of Yajnadatta, the Brahmin's Lament, and the Descent of the Ganges.
1962-a-defence-of-poesie-and-poems:
Sir Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesie, with his poems, is the founding work of English literary criticism. It was written in the 1580s to answer the charge that poetry is a waste of time. Sidney argues that the poet, unlike the historian or philosopher, does not merely describe what is, but creates what should be, and so teaches virtue more sweetly.

The poems that follow show Sidney practicing what he preaches: sonnets from Astrophil and Stella, songs, and lyrics of love and honor. The volume pairs argument with example, and it remains essential reading for anyone who wants to know how the Elizabethans thought about poetry, and why they thought it mattered.
19661-tell-me-another-story-the-book-of-:
Carolyn Sherwin Bailey wrote this book of story programs for tellers and teachers, published in Massachusetts in the late nineteen teens. It gathers tales and verses, with thanks to many publishers for leave to reprint pieces such as The Country Cat and The Little Acorn.

Small scenes show children named Peony and Violet sharing a new little girl with their mother, a sign of the book's warm, domestic tone. Bailey's programs were made for classrooms and libraries, where a good story, well told, was the day's best lesson. The programs include Andersen's Old House and Wilde's Star Child among tales for tellers and teachers.
20024-crankisms:
Lisle published Crankisms in 1901, a small book of short, sharp sayings about everyday life. One sample warns a reader not to call a favor a mere trifle. The person helped may take that claim at face value. Then the favor may never be repaid at all.

Each saying stands alone, so readers can dip in at any page. The tone is dry, wry, and a bit cranky, as the title promises. The book gives a quick taste of the brief moral wit that filled many small gift books of its time.
2008-mazelli-and-other-poems:
George W. Sands offers his first book of verse as a young American poet, hoping his country's literature might match its soldiers and statesmen. The title poem, Mazelli, leads a set of lyrics on love, nature, and national pride. Sands published the book in the 1840s, when American poets still looked to Britain for models and praise.

Sands writes in a plain, earnest voice, with an eye on Greece as the model of a people made great by letters. The poems are uneven, as first books often are, but they give a clear view of mid-nineteenth-century American ambition in verse. His preface speaks for a generation that wanted a national literature to match a growing republic.
20185-eventide-a-series-of-tales-and-poe:
Eventide gathers tales and poems for quiet evening reading, as its name suggests. The makers call their book a waif of weary moments at the start. They hope some warm-hearted spirit will shelter it from harsh critics. Will so small a booklet even draw a critic's arrows, they ask.

That modest plea sets a gentle tone for the pieces inside. Tales and verse alternate, suited to lampside calm at day's end. Victorian gift books often took this humble, hopeful pose with readers. Readers get soft sentiment and reflection in the classic evening mode.
20256-memoir-of-the-life-of-john-quincy-:
John Quincy Adams was born on July 11, 1767, in Braintree, Massachusetts. His parents were John and Abigail Adams, of Revolutionary fame. The town of his birth later became the town of Quincy. Their lives, the memoir notes, have already been ably illustrated elsewhere.

From that famed house, Adams rose to the highest posts in America. The memoir traces his schooling, travels, and long public service. It stresses character formed by stern parents and early hardship abroad. Readers get a compact life of a president raised inside the Revolution itself. His later years in Congress, fighting slavery's spread, crown his long career with honor.
20356-hero-and-leander-and-other-poems:
Hero and Leander is a famed love poem from Greek myth, told in English verse. A dedicatory letter offers the work to a patron's favorable allowance. The writer serves both himself and the deceased, he says humbly. He stands ready at his worship's disposing, now and ever.

Hero and Leander loved across the Hellespont, which he swam nightly. A storm and a drowned light end their tale in sorrow. Marlowe began the poem, and Chapman finished it after his death. Readers get one of the most beautiful English poems of the 1590s.
20373-the-dreamers-and-other-poems:
The Dreamers and Other Poems is a book of lyric verse by an unnamed poet. The poems turn on home, longing, and the pull of the open road. Short stanzas and plain images carry most of the feeling.

In one poem, a settled woman watches gypsies pass her door. She never guesses the wistful dream that draws them close. She never guesses the longing in each breast for a home like hers, where their hearts might rest. The book holds that tension throughout: the wish to wander set against the wish to stay.
20427-custer-and-other-poems:
Custer and Other Poems is a book of verse built around the memory of General Custer and the frontier West. Around the title poem stand reflective pieces on age, death, and the passing of fame. The poems use plain, ringing lines meant to be read aloud.

One poem warns those who burn the candle down to the stick. The sputtering socket, it says, yields but little light, and long life can be sadder than an early death. We must use, it urges, the warp and woof the ready present gives us. Such verses show the book's earnest, moral temper.
2044-the-education-of-henry-adams:
Henry Adams, grandson and great-grandson of presidents, writes his own education as a study of a man outpaced by his age. From Quincy and Harvard through Civil War diplomacy in London to Paris and Chicago, he tests each chapter of his life. Adams wrote the book in the third person, as if his own life were a case to study.

Adams judges himself a failure by the standards of the new century of dynamos, science, and mass power, and his irony cuts both ways. The memoir remains a classic of American self-scrutiny, praised for its style and its frank view of change. The famous Dynamo and Virgin chapter contrasts medieval faith with modern power, and readers still quote it.
20504-the-man-of-uz-and-other-poems:
The Man of Uz and Other Poems is a book of religious verse. The man of Uz is Job, the patient sufferer of the Old Testament. The title poem retells his story in measured lines, with his children and his losses before the reader.

The patriarch, with a chastened heart, joins his children's mirth. He keeps God's fear ever before him. Earnestly he brings his offerings and his prayers for every one of that beloved group, lest they have sinned in their feasting. The other poems share that devout temper, turning Bible scenes into verse for home reading.
20609-the-voyageur-and-other-poems:
William Henry Drummond's The Voyageur and Other Poems sings of French-Canadian river men, hunters, and habitant families. Drummond, a Montreal doctor, wrote in the dialect of his patients and friends. His recitation pieces were loved across Canada and the United States.

One poem opens on the night of the young New Year. The camp is warm and the fire is bright, and the bottle is close at hand. Out on the river the north wind blows, and down in the valley the snow lies piled. In that contrast — warm camp against deep winter — Drummond sets his tales of the old voyageur days.
20842-dreams:
Black fields, bright points that rise and sink, and spots of shifting colour open Dreams. Spots spread, shrink, and trade places in a slow, strange dance. Some dreamers see hues so bright, the text says, that waking sight cannot match them.

Thinkers of the mind stand behind studies of this kind. The book probes what dreams are and how they form. Sleep science was young, mixing keen notes with bold guesses about the night mind. Such books fed the new study of sleep. It treats the night mind as a thing to be studied, not feared.
20914-a-window-in-thrums:
A bare house, a manse, and Hendry's cot watch the brae in A Window in Thrums. J. M. Barrie sets his 1896 tale in a poor row of homes in a Scots village. A broken dyke alone keeps the potato pit from the south road.

Thrums, Barrie's famed fictional Kirriemuir, fills the tales seen from one window. Weavers, elders, joys, and griefs pass in warm, wry sketches. Barrie wrote of his mother's world with love and sly humour. Before Peter Pan, books like this made his name, and they still show his tender art at its roots.
21029-the-new-morning-poems:
A silent flame of pure passion before the true and good marks one life in Alfred Noyes's poems. The New Morning, from 1918, praises a man who scorned to fawn on the crowd. All might see what he saw, the verse says, who truly would.

Noyes, famed for The Highwayman, gathers war-age poems of hope and grief here. A new morning after darkness gives the book its title and its trust. Music drives his lines, ballad-sure and bright even in sorrow. Readers who love classic, singing verse will find Noyes's gift intact across these pages of loss and dawn.
21419-the-children-some-educational-prob:
Alexander Darroch, professor of education at Edinburgh, takes up schooling in The Children, issued in 1907. He finds the system of his day full of faults, with no clear join between its parts. Each part, he says, chases its own aims with little link to the rest.

Chapters treat the state's role in schooling, its cost, and its care for health. Darroch covers medical checks of children, the feeding of poor pupils, and physical training. He also asks what education is for, and how its means should be ordered. The book is a clear survey of reform debates in Edwardian Britain.
21872-the-life-of-david-as-reflected-in-:
David's life is read through his own songs in Alexander Maclaren's study. The Life of David as Reflected in His Psalms reached its ninth edition in 1903. Maclaren, a famed preacher, calls David's life remarkable for its romantic variety of circumstance. Shepherd boy, exile, king, and penitent each gather fresh fitness, he says, for David's great work: giving voice to every phase of devout feeling.

Chapters follow the early days, the long exile in its stages, the kingship, and the tears of the penitent. A final chapter studies the songs of the fugitive. The book belongs to the Household Library of Exposition, made for Bible classes and home study. It treats the Psalms as a diary of the soul, keyed to the events of David's life.
21921-pickwickian-manners-and-customs:
Dickens's Pickwick Papers had grown a literature of its own by 1897, and Percy Fitzgerald catalogs it in Pickwickian Manners and Customs. No English book, he says, so increased the general gaiety of the country. Sixty years on, readers still devoured Pickwick, counted its misprints, and prized the earliest states of its plates. Fitzgerald inscribes his study to Augustine Birrell, himself a noted Dickens lover.

The book walks through the customs, places, and people of the novel's world. Rochester and Dickens Land, then as now, drew pilgrims to the scenes. Fitzgerald treats a comic novel like a classic under glass, with a fan's joy and a scholar's patience. For Pickwick lovers, it is a companion full of garnish for a favorite dish.
22052-standish-of-standish-a-story-of-th:
Jane G. Austin wrote Standish of Standish, a story of the Pilgrims, in 1889. Austin came of old New England stock and spent years on Plymouth records. She opens by noting how Americans pause to look back at the spot where the Pilgrims sowed their seed. Her tale gives that looking-back a human form in Myles Standish, the colony's soldier captain.

Around Standish she builds the daily life of early Plymouth. Hunger, Indians, weddings, and quarrels fill the small settlement's first years. Austin fills gaps in the record with invention, and says so honestly. Her Pilgrim novels helped fix the popular picture of Plymouth for generations of readers.
22301-valley-of-dreams:
Valley of Dreams is a work of fiction preserved from Project Gutenberg, with no author or date in the catalog record. The surviving scene is a fast, slangy talk about pictures of the moon. The speakers hope those shots will pack crowds to the doors.

They also count on broadcast rights to pull their trip out of the red. A profit, they joke, might even come through for the Academy. That mix of space travel, film, and money gives the tale its flavor. It reads as early popular science fiction, built around a showy voyage and the businessmen hoping to cash in on it.
22322-a-legend-of-old-persia-and-other-p:
A Legend of Old Persia and Other Poems collects verse built on an old eastern tale. No poet is named in the catalog record. The legend opens in a golden climate, in the fairest place on earth.

Its happy people suffer no sickness, plague, or want. They live through endless summers, and half-summers hardly colder. Growing older so slowly, they hardly guess the years are passing. That dreamlike start sets the tone for the title poem. The other poems share the volume with it. Readers get romantic verse of a kind once read aloud: smooth, storied, and set far from daily life.
22423-poems:
Poems, preserved without an author's name in the record, opens on a cold landscape. The dim sea glints chill under a shy white sun. Skeleton weeds stand white with frost by a hilltop finger-post.

Rough, long grasses by the post never dry out. Traveller's-joy smoke puffs over hawthorn berry and hazel tuft. Such images give the verse a wintry, rural English cast. The poems favor observed nature over grand statement or story. Small signs of season and road carry the feeling here. Readers who like quiet landscape poetry will find its mood familiar. It rewards attention to frost, weed, and berry alike.
22569-the-listeners-and-other-poems:
Walter de la Mare wrote The Listeners and Other Poems, a landmark verse collection. De la Mare's title poem is among the most famous short poems in English. Its traveller knocks at a moonlit door and finds only listeners.

Other poems in the volume share his quiet, haunted music. One tells of blossoms coming to berries on slender stalks. A lady is charmed away for one long summer's day. Vows sweet, merry, and tender accompany that charmed summer absence. De la Mare mixes childlike wonder with an undertow of mystery. His lyrics seem simple until their strangeness settles on the reader. The collection remains a doorway into modern English poetry's dream side.
22650-the-defence-of-guenevere-and-other:
The Defence of Guenevere and Other Poems is William Morris's first book of verse, a landmark of Pre-Raphaelite poetry. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Morris retells Arthurian tales in a voice by turns dreamy and stark, quite unlike the polished verse around him.

In the sample, a knight knows somehow that he is Launcelot, bravest of all who ever bore lance or swung sword in wrong cause or right. Guenevere's defense at her trial gives the title poem its dramatic frame: the queen pleading her life before Arthur's court. Other poems treat Froissart's chronicles and northern legend. The book still startles with its color, violence, and medieval longing.
22717-lundy-s-lane-and-other-poems:
Lundy's Lane and Other Poems, published by the George H. Doran Company in 1916, gathers verse by the Canadian poet Duncan Campbell Scott. The catalog record credits the publisher. The title poem recalls the battle of Lundy's Lane, the bloodiest fight of the War of 1812, fought near Niagara Falls in July 1814.

The sample comes from a love lyric: in her twilight garden she plucked a half-opened rose, and the speaker thought it meant for him. She hid it in her bosom instead, and the unanswered question of her meaning haunts him still. Scott mixes such lyrics with sonnets and war-haunted meditations. The volume shows Canada's leading poet of the day at his most musical and melancholy.
22732-last-poems:
Edward Thomas wrote the poems collected in Last Poems, the final gathering of a poet killed at Arras in 1917. The catalog record gives no year. Thomas came late to verse, writing all his poems in the last years of his life, most of them rooted in the English countryside he walked and loved.

In the sample lines, the poet wishes for the speech of trees and birds, a language that cannot be betrayed. What was hid should still be hid, except from those made like him, who answer when such whispers bid. That quiet creed runs through the volume: rain, roads, old houses, and the approach of war. Thomas's restraint made him a founder of modern English nature poetry, and these last poems carry his voice at its purest.
22734-bay-a-book-of-poems:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Bay, a small book of poems shaped by the First World War. The catalog record's credit line is garbled, and no year is given. Lawrence, then known for Sons and Lovers, gathered in Bay the war poems he had written through the conflict's years, fierce and grieving by turns.

The sample shows his manner: a general canters gaily past, his white plumes winking under a grey evening sky. Then the earth itself seems to stir. A red ridge heaves up in slow, magnetic answer. Landscape and artillery merge in a single ominous image. Lawrence's war verse is less famous than his novels, but it burns with the same intensity. Bay is a slim, strange book from a major writer at war's end.
22736-the-inn-of-dreams:
The Inn of Dreams is a book of lyric poems, dreamy and musical in the manner of the 1890s. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its title promises lodging for the night thoughts: an inn where fairy princes ride and beauty keeps her brief hour.

The sample calls to those princes: in the night you have been dreamed of, O fairy Princes, and her eyes shine bright. Spur your swift horses: this is Beauty's hour. Beauty's flame, the poem says, quivers and flickers out like a golden flame in a dark place, a torch and wonder of the world. Such verse prizes shimmer over statement. The collection will suit readers who like their poetry perfumed, twilit, and unashamedly romantic.
22739-the-human-aura-astral-colors-and-t:
Swami Panchadasi wrote The Human Aura: Astral Colors and Thought Forms, a handbook of occult teaching about the colored atmosphere said to surround every person. The catalog record gives no year. Panchadasi, one of the pen names of the New Thought writer William Walker Atkinson, taught thousands of mail-order students in the era's hidden wisdom.

The contents promise a key to the astral colors. Red stands for the physical, blue for the spiritual, yellow for the mental. White and black stand as the two poles of spirituality, and olive, russet, and citrine arise from mixing. With practice, the book claims, almost everyone can learn to see the prana aura's outlines plainly. It is a period document of popular occultism, written with a teacher's confidence in invisible things.
22803-helen-redeemed-and-other-poems:
Maurice Hewlett wrote Helen Redeemed and Other Poems, a volume of narrative verse by the novelist of The Forest Lovers. The catalog record gives no year. Hewlett, a romantic medievalist in prose, here takes up classical story: Helen of Troy, redeemed at last from the blame the poets laid on her.

The sample sings of Odysseus and his long road home. What weariness of wind, wave, and foam lay before him first! Only then would he see his home of scrub and crag again. What stress of pilgrimage awaited him, through roaring waterways and the cities of men. What sojourns among folk beyond mortal seafarers' ken. Hewlett's verse rolls in long, sonorous lines, more incantation than argument. The volume shows the late-romantic taste for myth retold in music, by a writer who believed the old tales still carried fire.
23314-spring-blossoms:
This Turner and Fisher toy book, with eight colored plates, offers spring blossoms for infant minds. Its opening verses promise blossoms of bright truth and seeds of virtue, sown before a single weed can grow.

Children learn to worship nature's loveliness through flowers, escaping thoughts of harm in the charm of spring. Small, bright, and moral, the book is a typical Victorian gift book for the very young. The colored plates match the verses, so spring flowers teach virtue as they bloom. Later pages meet Robinson Crusoe's man Friday and Industrious Jane with her shining needle.
2355-the-formation-of-vegetable-mould-th:
Charles Darwin's last book argues that earthworms, tiny and ignored, have shaped the landscape itself. The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms shows how worms bury stones, build soil, and slowly remake fields, with Darwin's experiments measuring their work over years. The book is a model of patient observation.

Darwin's final argument is humble and grand at once: small causes, given time, move the world. The work charmed general readers and remains a classic of natural history. Anyone curious about Darwin beyond evolution will find a delightful surprise.
23944-bulbs-and-blossoms:
Amy Le Feuvre published Bulbs and Blossoms with the Religious Tract Society, illustrated by Eveline Lance. It opens at five o'clock in the afternoon at Chatts Chase, where Miss Hunter presides at tea and Amabel stands at the window in a muddy riding habit. Hester lies back with a novel.

The sisters discuss poor children brought home, and whether an aunt in the brougham would have comforted them more than a strange maid. Graham the nurse, the children's own, will put them at ease, Amabel insists. Le Feuvre, author of Probable Sons and Teddy's Button, writes a domestic story where bulbs and blossoms stand for children growing toward light.
24216-poems:
Frances Anne Butler, late Fanny Kemble, published this little volume of poems in London in 1844, reprinted from the American edition. It is inscribed to Katharine Sedgwick with respect, gratitude, and affection. Butler, famed as an actress, writes here as a poet of night, travel, and feeling, in verse that moves between prayer and picture.

The book opens with Lines Written at Night, dated August 9, 1825. It hails the moon above a silent stream of light, with night looking from her throne of ether on a slumbering universe. A poem on Venice follows, where night steals over the ocean and the bark finds a pillow on the rippling deep. Readers get a Romantic volume of moonlight, travel, and tender address.
24298-nestlings-a-collection-of-poems:
Ella Fraser Weller wrote this book of poems, published by the Californian Publishing Company in San Francisco in 1892, with pictures by K. A. Fraser from children in the author's own circle. It is lovingly dedicated to the children whose faces are pictured within. An introduction by S. H. Weller of Los Angeles explains that the selections came of occasions, not meant for the public eye, until mother-love called them and fugitive poems became a book.

Contents include My Baby's Feet, Two Little Seeds, Edith, The Theft, and Who's Afraid. Lullaby, Two of Them, In the Meadow, Beatrice, and My Boy follow. The Fairy's Motto, A Reverie, My Choice, Elliott, and Three Little Kittens close the set. The pictures are shadows of real faces, readily matched in any small circle. Readers get a mother's album of verse for children.
24364-the-defeat-of-youth-and-other-poem:
Aldous Huxley, author of The Burning Wheel, wrote this book of poems, opening with The Defeat of Youth in three parts. Under the trees, phantoms of pale-remembered shapes, sisterly in resemblance, crowned with the same bright hair, pass like dreams that can bless or hurt no more than dreams. These ghost things were she, formless, without identity, many and dim, one face among the legions of the street, an indifferent mystery, something still uncreated and incomplete.

Later poems include Song of Poplars, The Reef, Winter Dream, The Flowers, The Elms, and Out of the Window. Inspiration, Summer Stillness, Anniversaries, Italy, The Alien, A Little Memory, Waking, and By the Fire follow. Valedictory, Love Song, Private Property, Revelation, Minoan Porcelain, The Decameron, Topiary, On the Bus, Points and Lines, Panic, and The Louse-Hunters close the book. Readers get Huxley's early verse, bright, restless, and already ironic.
24605-gleams-of-sunshine-optimistic-poem:
Joseph Horatio Chant, a Canadian minister, published this book of optimistic poems at Toronto in 1915, printed for the author by William Briggs. He dedicated it to the memory of his wife, Mary Matilda McKim. She was his helpmate for over forty-six years. Her gentle disposition and earnest Christian life made their home a place of peace and joy.

Contents include an invocation, a poem on God's plan, verses on Canada and late autumn, friendship, life, and a poem to Rudyard Kipling.
