Chant's poems are plain, hopeful, and devout, meant to cheer rather than to dazzle. Readers who enjoy old-fashioned verse of faith and encouragement will find this collection warm and sincere.
2491-love-or-fame-and-other-poems:
Fannie Isabelle Sherrick's Love or Fame, and Other Poems offers Victorian lyrics on love, ambition, and the choices women faced between domestic life and public praise. The poems are musical, sentimental, and earnest, with the title poem framing the volume's central question. Sherrick writes in the popular style of her day.

The collection interests readers of women's poetry and period verse, even where the poems feel conventional now. Its sincerity carries many pieces. Poetry lovers will find a representative voice of its age. Sherrick published her poems in magazines before gathering them here.
24944-mushrooms:
William Falconer published Mushrooms: How to Grow Them in New York in 1892, a practical treatise on mushroom culture for profit and pleasure. The book tells who should grow mushrooms, from market gardeners and florists to farmers and village folk, then shows how to grow them in cellars, houses, sheds, greenhouses, and fields.

Chapters take up manures in detail: horse manure freshest is best, with mule, cow, and city stable manure beside it, and good sod loam mixed in to hold the ammonia. Falconer gives named growers' methods, from Mr. Gardner's cellar to Mrs. Osborne's mushroom house. The book remains a clear, useful guide for small growers.
2558-poems:
George P. Morris, the American songwriter and editor, gathered his verse in this volume, from his early days in New York letters. Morris wrote songs and ballads that ordinary readers sang and quoted, and his lines favor clear feeling over showy craft.

The poems run from patriotic airs to home and nature lyrics, with the plain music that made his name. Readers will find the popular taste of early America here, warm, sentimental, and direct. The book serves as a record of a poet who reached his public through melody as much as print.
25731-ancient-egyptian-and-greek-looms:
H. Ling Roth, keeper of Bankfield Museum, Halifax, writes this study of ancient Egyptian and Greek looms, published in April 1913 with thirty-eight line block and one collotype pictures. Greek words appear transliterated between plus marks.

Halifax, in the heart of the Lancashire and Yorkshire textile trade, long housed woollen manufacture, so its museum fittingly holds early spinning, weaving, and cloth making tools. Roth notes many typical specimens still want collecting, and study material for weaving worldwide abounds, while Egyptian and Greek loom evidence needs careful gathering. Roth writes from a museum town where wool and cloth shaped daily life.
25813-isle-o-dreams:
Frederick F. Moore writes Isle o' Dreams. He had written The Devil's Admiral and The Sailor Girl. Doubleday, Page published the book in 1920. Ralph Pallen Coleman supplied the front picture. Trask commands a man to come closer so he can look into the boat, in that picture.

Robert Trask arrives in Manila from Amoy in chapter one. Dinshaw tells of his island in chapter two. Captain Dinshaw pulls a long bow, and Captain Jarrow cruises strange waters. Jarrow does queer things. Trask, Doc Bird, and a schooner off the island chase a South Seas mystery of dreams and treasure.
26001-the-bertrams:
Anthony Trollope sets a novel of love, money, and vocation in The Bertrams, printed by Chapman and Hall in 1859 in three volumes. The first volume opens with a vae victis cry and moves through breakfast and lunch, a new vicar, a prima donna, and a choice of profession. Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives follow, with Sir Lionel Bertram, Miss Todd's picnic, and George Bertram choosing the bar.

Trollope opens by noting the age of humanity in England, where wife beating shocks, flogging soldiers seems near as bad, and hanging repels many. One heroine weighs an aunt's hint that George may be his uncle's heir, and fears she would make a poor wife for a poor man. The novel probes rank, means, and marriage with Trollope's steady, ironic eye.
26008-hydriatic-treatment-of-scarlet-fev:
Charles Munde, physician, argues for the water cure in scarlet fever in this 1857 pamphlet, drawn from twenty one years of practice and several hundred cases of eruptive fevers. Munde says doctors have fought scarlet fever for two hundred years while it carries off half a million people a year, and he offers his share toward a barrier against the disease. Parents and physicians are his readers.

Treatment runs by packs, sheets, and baths, eased as heat abates: packs less often, sheets unchanged, longer stays in packs, shorter baths, and no sitz bath out of season. Even without fresh symptoms, one pack and bath a day stays needful. Munde presents the water cure as a system to save thousands of lives and healths now lost each year.
263-trees-and-other-poems:
Joyce Kilmer's 1914 volume holds the poem that made him famous and many quieter ones. Trees and Other Poems opens with a dedication to his mother, gentlest of critics, and a Patmore epigraph on humble rhyme. Schoolboy verse, praised by that mother, gives way to mature lyrics.

Trees itself praises a tree's beauty in simple quatrains, ending with the claim that poems are made by fools like me. Other poems treat faith, home, and nature with the same plain music. Kilmer, killed in France in 1918, left this book as his best-known work. It remains a favorite gift volume.
26333-maurine-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's Maurine and Other Poems, issued at Chicago in 1888, opens with a verse preface on crossing into the wonder world of art. The speaker, calling herself only a singer of a little song, finds hills, valleys, and mountain peaks trod by great artists, where tears turn to rainbows. The title poem Maurine follows, a long narrative in parts.

Mid-poem scenes show a wedding party, with Miss Trevor's six bridesmaids and Vivian Dangerfield standing as best man at a New Year Eve wedding. Shorter poems follow, from Two Sunsets and Unrest to The Coquette, Inevitable, If, Gethsemane, and The Sonnet. The volume mixes narrative romance with lyrics on love, loss, and ambition.
264-main-street-and-other-poems:
Joyce Kilmer, best known for Trees, gathers here poems of streets, houses, and faith. Main Street and Other Poems, transcribed from the 1917 edition, opens with its title poem for S. M. L. and moves through roofs, snowmen, and valentines. Many pieces first ran in periodicals.

Later poems honor Lionel Johnson, Father Gerard Hopkins, and Rupert Brooke, and visit Rheims Cathedral and wartime seas. Kilmer's verse is plain, musical, and devout, with a love of home and church. The book shows the poet killed in 1918 at his most varied. It pairs well with his Trees volume.
26505-the-old-hanging-fork-and-other-poe:
George W. Doneghy's 1897 collection, printed at Franklin, Ohio, sings of Kentucky country life in nostalgic and dialect verse. The title poem recalls fishing the old Hanging Fork with sapling pole and painted cork. It follows the stream from the railroad bridge down to the mill at Dawson's dam, from early morn till shades of night. Bare feet, stone bruises, and sun-browned hair return in later stanzas as emblems of youth.

Other poems treat sweet September days, an old cob pipe, Tim Bluster's dream, apple blossoms, and the Civil War fields of Chickamauga and Perryville. Paraphrases of Burns, tributes to Poe and Father Ryan, a mother's grave, an old church bell, and a stage coach fill the volume. Doneghy closes with hills, ponds, and straw hats of a vanished countryside.
26611-enthusiasm-and-other-poems:
Susanna Strickland, now Mrs. Moodie, published this poetry volume with Smith, Elder and Company at London in 1831. She inscribes it to James Montgomery, praising his genius as a poet and his character as a man, and she dates her note from Reydon, Suffolk, on January 1, 1831. The title poem, Enthusiasm, opens the book with a call for the spirit that fires preachers, painters, poets, and patriots.

Later poems take up Fame, the Deluge, the Avenger of Blood, and the Overthrow of Zebah and Zalmunna, with paraphrases of Psalm 44 and Isaiah 40. The Vision of Dry Bones and the Destruction of Babylon sit beside nature lyrics, hymns, and laments, from The Old Ash Tree to Morning Hymn and Evening Hymn. It is an earnest early volume, biblical in theme and romantic in feeling.
27024-the-path-of-dreams-poems:
Leigh Gordon Giltner's The Path of Dreams, published by Fleming H. Revell in 1900 and dedicated to the memory of her mother, gathers poems of woodland ways, love, and loss. Titles such as In Woodland Ways, Ashes of Roses, Afterbloom, and A Winter Landscape set the book's reflective tone.

Other poems turn to history and myth: Spartacus, Hagar, Circe, and Clytie the sunflower, beside love poems where pride is matched against love and loses. Giltner writes in a late Victorian lyric voice, musical, earnest, and fond of roses, rue, and twilight paths.
27221-the-minstrel-or-the-progress-of-ge:
James Beattie's The Minstrel, or The Progress of Genius, with some other poems, published at Edinburgh in 1805, follows a shepherd-boy poet through two books. The youth tells a courteous stranger his artless tale, roaming at eve to a wilderness where cliffs rebound a voice mourning ruined man and virtue lost.

Other poems in the volume include Retirement, an Elegy, an Ode to Hope, and the mock-heroic Battle of the Pigmies and Cranes. Dedicated to Sir William Forbes of Pitsligo, the book remains the classic Spenserian portrait of genius growing in solitude.
27333-pan-and-olus-poems:
Charles Hamilton Musgrove's Poems was published by John P. Morton in Louisville in 1913. They range from A Fugue of Hell and Hymn of the Tomb Builders to The Tornado, Voices, and A Song for the Hills. Romany, Idols, and an Ode to the New Century sit beside A Clown's Prelude and A Legend of Gold.

The Eagle and the Flower, Sunset in the City, The Admiral's Return, and The Dungeoned Anarchist lead to At the Play. There a woman tells the poet that the best painting comes from the heart's own blood. Zoroaster, The Story of Moses, and Parthenope to Ulysses close a varied book of formal verse.
27357-the-landing-of-the-pilgrims:
Henry Fisk Carlton wrote this short play about the landing of the Pilgrims for school use, edited by Claire T. Zyve and issued by the Bureau of Publications at Teachers College, Columbia University, as part of the Dramatic Hours in Colonial History set. It was written to be performed as a radio play, and the book notes that the play had already been produced on the radio.

No costumes, scenery, or memorized lines are needed: the young actors stand around a microphone with copies in hand and let their voices carry feeling, since a radio audience cannot see them. The booklet even explains how to set up a mock studio. It gives teachers a ready way to stage colonial history with a class.
27370-poems:
Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, published this volume of poems in Boston in 1910. It was issued by the trustees under her will as authorized literature of the First Church of Christ, Scientist. The poems span her long life, from verses to the old year of 1865 and an invocation for 1868 to hymns and national pieces.

Contents include Mother's Evening Prayer, Christ My Refuge, Feed My Sheep, Woman's Rights, The New Century, Christmas Morn, Easter Morn, Communion Hymn, Laus Deo, and a national thanksgiving hymn. Personal, devotional, and patriotic notes mix throughout. Readers get Eddy's faith and feeling in her own short, plain verse.
27468-ibm-1401-programming-systems:
IBM issued this brochure when companies ordered the IBM 1401 Data Processing System, explaining why programming systems mattered as much as the machine itself. Methods-programming staffs, it says, translate the requirements of management into finished applications, and good programming systems cut the cost of getting the computer into operation.

A modern high-speed computer is a marvelous instrument, the brochure argues, but it is only part of a data processing system. Well-tested programming languages must accompany it, so the computer itself performs tedious functions a programmer would otherwise code by hand. A few minutes of computer time can equal many hours of staff time. The piece is a clear window on early business computing.
27635-the-canterbury-puzzles-and-other-c:
Henry E. Dudeney, the puzzle maker called Sphinx, gathered this book of ingenious puzzles and problems, with solutions at the end. Press praise called it a book of remarkable ingenuity and interest, and the Observer warned that the puzzles tax ingenuity to the utmost.

The title section imagines Chaucer's pilgrims, met at the old Tabard Inn in Southwark, beguiling their ride to Canterbury by propounding puzzles instead of tales. Later sections bring puzzling times at Solvamhall Castle, the merry monks of Riddlewell, the strange escape of the king's jester, and the squire's Christmas puzzle party. Adventures of the puzzle club and the professor's puzzles follow, with miscellaneous puzzles before the solutions.
27677-daisy-dare-and-baby-power-poems:
Rosa Vertner Jeffrey published these poems with Claxton, Remsen and Haffelfinger of Philadelphia in 1871, entered in 1870, with light illustrations designed by D. Vertner Johnson. She dedicates the volume to her dear friend Mrs. Margaret Wickliffe Preston of Lexington, Kentucky.

The title poem opens at early morn, as Daisy Dare sweeps through scented meadows where meek-eyed kine graze on summer days. She is sparkling, graceful, and passing fair, with wondrous tresses like a crown of light glorifying her white brow and deep, impassioned eyes. An illustration shows Daisy Dare at early morn, sparkling as dew-drops gleaming on her path. The book pairs Daisy Dare with Baby Power poems.
27781-revised-edition-of-poems:
Bill o'th' Hoylus End, the Yorkshire dialect writer, published this revised edition of poems in 1891 with John Overend of Keighley, priced at two shillings. The contents run to dozens of pieces, from The Grand Old Man of Oakworth and Dr. Dobie's Lecture on Burns to The Factory Girl and A Yorkshireman's Christmas.

Written in the dialect of the West Riding, the poems mix humor, local news, and sentiment, with odes to Sir Titus Salt, Burns, and Bacchus among them. The collection preserves a popular regional voice, and its many titles show a working writer answering his neighbors' lives in verse.
27912-gloucester-moors-and-other-poems:
William Vaughn Moody published Gloucester Moors and Other Poems in Boston and New York with Houghton Mifflin in 1901. Several poems had appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, Scribner's Magazine, and the Chap-Book, including An Ode in Time of Hesitation, The Brute, and On a Soldier Fallen in the Philippines.

The title poem pictures Gloucester town a mile behind, moors stretching free in the high blue afternoon, and wild geraniums holding dew in the boulder's shade. Moody's poems join landscape, conscience, and history, and the collection shows an American poet of the generation after Emerson wrestling with empire and faith.
28218-three-unpublished-poems:
Three Unpublished Poems by Louisa M. Alcott comes from the Fruitlands Collection, with an introduction on Bronson Alcott's failed utopia. In the spring of 1843, Bronson Alcott and a group of transcendentalists cut themselves off at Fruitlands in Harvard, Massachusetts. They sought a New Eden of simple work, study, and nature, where evil could find no entrance.

The experiment ended in comedy and tragedy, yet visitors still cross pastures each year to see the old house. Helen Bell's line, that Bronson nearly died of a broken dream, frames the poems. The little volume links Alcott's verse to her father's hopeful, doomed plan.
2888-yorkshire-dialect-poems-1673-1915-a:
F. W. Moorman, professor of English language at Leeds, compiled Yorkshire Dialect Poems from 1673 to 1915 with traditional poems and a historical introduction. Published for the Yorkshire Dialect Society in 1916 and 1917, the book is dedicated to Yorkshiremen serving in trench or on battleship. Contents include a dialogue between an old wife, a lass, and a butcher, Henry Carey's Honest Yorkshireman, and verses from Snaith Marsh.

The poems speak in dialect throughout, with glosses for words such as kine for cattle and pail for a milking vessel. One song follows a lad who runs away to London with ribbed stockings, waistcoats, money, and a light heart. The collection preserves a regional voice across two and a half centuries, useful to readers of dialect verse and local history.
29209-reel-life-films:
Jacques Jean Ferrat wrote this satirical science fiction story about Hollywood and its villains. Cinema-makers, the tale says, now avoid offending national groups, after boycotts over portrayals of their nationals as villains. Space aliens have become the safe substitute, since no earthly minority can object to a Martian menace.

Ferrat asks what happens if extraterrestrial neighbors are touchy too. Two producers, Cyril Bezdek and E. Carter Dorwin, meet in adjoining rooms on the Super-Sachem, the fastest coast-to-coast train, to settle a matter on which much depends. Readers get a witty satire of the film business, where the search for an inoffensive villain runs into a very offended galaxy.
29477-the-universal-reciter-81-choice-pi:
Made for speakers and schoolrooms, The Universal Reciter gathers eighty-one choice pieces of rare poetical gems for reading aloud. Its opening counsel is plain: a weak voice should be strengthened by frequent practice, by exercise in the open air, and on all convenient occasions. Ease, grace, and fluency, it promises, come only from a great deal of practice, not a little.

The pieces mix verse and prose, humor and pathos, with some dialect pieces kept in period spelling. One quoted piece cries to a rapid stream of the valley, asking if life's morning joys awake only to vanish. Students of elocution and Victorian recitation will find a full, practical anthology for the platform and the parlor.
29521-enamels-and-cameos-and-other-poems:
Théophile Gautier's Enamels and Cameos, translated by Agnes Lee, gathers the French poet's polished, gem-like lyrics in English dress. Contents run from The God and the Opal and a pantheistic madrigal on affinity, through The Poem of Woman and A Study of Hands. Variations on the Carnival of Venice, a Symphony in White Major, Coquetry in Death, and the nostalgia of obelisks in Paris and Luxor complete the set.

Gautier crafts each poem as a jeweler cuts a stone: hard, bright, and exact, with color and form prized above confession. The god turned artisan in the opening poem sets the creed. Readers of French poetry in translation will find a classic of art for art's sake, rendered with grace and care.
29993-poems:
William D. Howells published this volume of poems in Boston in 1886, with Ticknor and Company, under a copyright of 1873 and 1885. The University Press of John Wilson and Son at Cambridge printed it. The contents run from The Pilot's Story, Forlorn, and Pleasure-Pain to In August, The Empty House, and Bubbles. Lost Beliefs, Louis Lebeau's Conversion, and Caprice follow, with Sweet Clover and The Royal Portraits.

The Faithful of the Gonzaga, The First Cricket, and The Mulberries lead to By the Sea, Saint Christopher, and an elegy on John Butler Howells. Thanksgiving, A Springtime, and The Bobolinks are Singing add seasonal notes, with The Battle in the Clouds, The Two Wives, and The Song the Oriole Sings. Pordenone and The Long Days close a full, varied book of Howells's verse.
30045-planet-of-dreams:
In a tale by James McKimmey Jr., Daniel Loveral and a chosen flock leave Earth for a small, fertile world where the sky stays blue, the air stays clean, and no one need work. Loveral picked the planet on a map two years before, calling it the Dream Planet, and his settlers land expecting their dreams to come true at last. Paul Orban drew the pictures for the short tale, which opens with Loveral already troubled in his office.

A single name, Atkinson, ticks through his mind like a machine, and Loveral fears one settler may be first in a wider break from the dream. The story asks what a perfect place costs when every wish is met and no task gives a day its shape. Its short length suits the point: paradise, once reached, still needs a leader to watch for the first crack.
30184-the-fairy-changeling-and-other-poe:
Dora Sigerson, Mrs. Clement Shorter, gathers poems first printed in magazines, in a John Lane volume dated 1898 in Roman numerals. The title piece leads a set that includes a ballad of Marjorie and the priest's brother. A ballad of the little black hound, the rape of the baron's wine, and Irish-titled lyrics such as Cean Duv Deelish and Banagher Rhue follow. Later pieces turn to love, wishes, a meadow tragedy, an eclipse, and a scallop shell.

Only one poem in the book had appeared in her earlier Verses of 1893. The rest came from Longman's Magazine, the Pall Mall Magazine, the National Observer, and Cassell's Magazine, plus American journals such as the Century and the Bookman. Sigerson thanks those editors in her note, and the collection shows a lyrical, often melancholy Irish voice, fond of fairies, ballads, and the dead.
3039-forty-two-poems:
James Elroy Flecker collected Forty-Two Poems as a slim volume of lyrics, sonnets, and exotic fantasies. The poems move between London streets and imagined lands. Evening falls on smoky walls, railings drip with rain, and a tram glides solemnly like love's still-mysterious car, lit gold and white with a single dark red star. A garden beyond the Thames holds a rose where flowers are pale and few. The first sonnet of Bathrolaire opens over a moonless land, showing Flecker's taste for invented kingdoms and musical names.

His verse favors color, mystery, and a young man's longing. The collection suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century lyric poetry before Flecker's early death cut his promise short.
30672-eidolon-or-the-course-of-a-soul-an:
Walter R. Cassels writes Eidolon, or the Course of a Soul, and Other Poems, published in London in 1850 by William Pickering and inscribed to Charles Peel by his friend Cassels. Contents open with Eidolon, Alceste, and Pygmalion, followed by miscellaneous poems.

Those shorter pieces include Ode to Fancy, What is a Sigh, Ione, Reality, Retrospection, and The Stormy Petrel. Later poems add The Mermaid, The Spirit of the Air, Why Do I Love Thee, Lady Annabel, To Jenny Lind, and The Gold Seekers. Sonnets close the named sections, with verses written at Ullswater and on life as pilgrimage. Cassels blends classical myth with Victorian feeling.
30687-the-lord-of-misrule-and-other-poem:
Alfred Noyes gathered this 1915 poetry book in New York, with a color frontispiece by Spencer Baird Nichols. Its title poem, The Lord of Misrule, opens the volume, and the contents list runs through The Repeal, The Search-Lights, Forward, A Spell, Crimson Sails, and Blind Moone of London, among others. Noyes was already known for Drake, Sherwood, and his collected poems in two volumes.

The poems move between pageant and war, London streets and old roads, ghosts and songs of hope. Titles like The Great North Road, The River of Stars, A Knight of Old Japan, and The Day of Remembrance show that range. Readers who enjoy clear, musical verse with a strong sense of place will find Noyes at his most varied here, writing in the shadow of a war that had just begun.
31159-essentials-of-economic-theory-as-a:
John Bates Clark, professor of political economy at Columbia University, sets out his economic system in this 1907 work, reprinted in 1915 by Macmillan. Thirty chapters move from wealth and its origin through varieties of goods, value, wages, interest, rent, and land. They then move into economic dynamics, population, and the accumulation of capital.

The later chapters apply those principles to live questions of the day: railroads, labor organization, arbitration of wages, boycotts, protection, monopoly, and money. Clear and systematic, the book shows a leading American economist of the Progressive era trying to give reformers and students a usable theory of how wealth is made and shared.
31184-poems:
G. K. Chesterton's 1916 volume, published by John Lane in New York, gathers his poems under six heads. Three dedications open the book, to Edmund Clerihew Bentley, Hilaire Belloc, and M. E. W., followed by war poems including Lepanto, The Wife of Flanders, and The Crusader Returns from Captivity, and love poems such as Glencoe and A Marriage Song.

Religious poems follow, with The House of Christmas, The Truce of Christmas, and The Nativity. Then come rhymes for the times, including The Secret People and A Song of Swords, miscellaneous poems, and ballades. The collection shows Chesterton's range in verse: martial, devotional, comic, and polemical, all in his unmistakable rolling music.
312-young-adventure-a-book-of-poems:
Stephen Vincent Benét, aged twenty, dedicates his first book to a friend who was Perseus, D'Artagnan, and Lancelot to him. Young Adventure, from the 1918 American edition, gathers poems first printed in periodicals. Titles were conformed for ease of searching.

Benét's early verse mixes romance, war, and youthful ambition in musical lines. The book predates his Pulitzer work by years, yet shows his gift for story in verse. Readers meet a poet learning his craft in public. The volume charms as a debut of real promise. Benét later won Pulitzers for poetry and for John Brown's Body.
31548-a-succinct-account-of-the-plague-a:
A Succinct Account of the Plague at Marseilles, its symptoms, and the methods and medicines used for curing it, was drawn up and presented to the governor and magistrates of Marseilles. Its authors were M. Chicoyneau, Verney, and Soullier, the physicians sent thither from Paris by the Duke Regent of France. Translated from the French by a physician, it was printed in London for S. Buckley and D. Midwinter in 1721, the year given as M.DCC.XXI.

The account describes the plague's symptoms as the doctors saw them, and the treatments they tried, with the authority of men on the spot. For readers of medical history, it is a firsthand record of an epidemic and of early eighteenth-century medicine facing it. Its plain, professional tone makes the horror of Marseilles in 1720 all the more vivid.
31585-the-amazing-mrs-mimms:
David C. Knight's science-fiction story The Amazing Mrs. Mimms opens with tea having a wonderful effect on its heroine, as she sips slowly and feels strength returning to her tired system. A muffled rush and a faintly acrid smell of ion electrodes mark the Time Translator setting Mrs. Mimms down in 1958, at the rear of a large supermarket, between two packing cases that once contained breakfast foods. Two heavy black suitcases are her only luggage, and a smile never left her rotund countenance during the intervening centuries.

The headnote, quoting the author, says long may the good lady serve poor folks in the dim past, and argues that science fiction misses much because it lacks the human angle. Readers will find a warm, funny time-travel tale, where an ordinary woman carries kindness across the centuries.
317-the-culprit-fay-and-other-poems:
Joseph Rodman Drake's fairy poem opens with purged eyes seeing old fairyland's tinsel show. The Culprit Fay and Other Poems, from the 1836 Dearborn edition, was inscribed by the author's daughter to Fitz-Greene Halleck. Drake died young, and friends gathered his verse.

The index lists To a Friend, Leon, Niagara, and The American Flag among the shorter pieces. The Culprit Fay itself tells of a fairy punished for loving a mortal. Drake's Hudson River scenery and romantic fancy charmed early American readers. The volume preserves a brief, bright career. Drake's fairy verse still charms readers of early American poetry.
31706-milton-minor-poems:
Samuel Thurber's school edition of Milton's minor poems, copyrighted in 1901 by Allyn and Bacon, gathers L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, Comus, Arcades, On the Nativity, Lycidas, On Shakespeare, and At a Solemn Music. It also gathers the sonnets, with introduction and notes. Its preface says the study of Milton in high school has two aims: acquaintance with a great classic poet, and practice in conquering real difficulties.

The notes explain meter, allusion, and word use line by line, comparing passages with Paradise Lost, Shakespeare, and Ovid. Readers get a classroom Milton, designed to be read with help, rather than a bare text of the poems alone.
31712-the-garden-of-dreams:
Madison Cawein's Garden of Dreams was published at Louisville by John P. Morton and Company in 1896, with copyright the same year. Cawein was already known as the author of Intimations of the Beautiful and Undertones, and this book gathers his verse on gardens, dreams, and the meeting of the two. Its opening verses remember a garden the spirit once walked, full of wild, wet dream-flowers.

The poems move between waking life and dream life, with flowers, hours, and a figure met among them. Cawein's garden is a place of mystery and gleam, and his verse keeps it half real and half dreamed.
31764-days-and-dreams-poems:
Madison Cawein's 1891 poetry collection, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons and dedicated to James Whitcomb Riley, gathers short lyrics in several parts. The opening poems watch a loved woman through June days, evening owls, buckeye shade, and wood-violet and bramble-rose, with a lover waiting at a trysting place.

Across the volume, Cawein returns to Kentucky woods, moonlight, birds, and the moods of youth and love, in verse that favors musical lines and natural images. Readers get a late nineteenth-century book of lyric poetry, gentle and romantic, meant to be read slowly rather than for plot.
31877-sea-poems:
Cale Young Rice's 1921 collection Sea Poems, published by The Century Company and dedicated to Harrison S. Morris, gathers lyrics of the sea in many moods. Its contents include Sea-Hoardings, The Shore's Song to the Sea. They also include To a Firefly by the Sea, A Sea-Ghost, Off the Irish Coast, The Song of the Homesick Gael, and Pageants of the Sea.

Later poems travel farther, to a song of the old Venetians, Typhoon, Penang, nights on the Indian Ocean, and sighting Arabia. Readers get a book of sea verse that moves from a single shore to the wider oceans, with the music and melancholy of a poet who loved ships, storms, and distant coasts.
31927-the-portal-of-dreams:
Charles Neville Buck's 1912 novel The Portal of Dreams, published by W. J. Watt and Company with illustrations by Frank Snapp, opens with a small, frail doctor whose trim Van-Dyck beard rescues his narrow face from inconsequence. When the doctor speaks, his mentality expands to commanding proportion, and he bullies his patient with the large authority of a Bonaparte.

Chapters follow a vision upon a warning, pursuing a will-o'-the-wisp, a fool's errand, premonitions become realities, and a search for orchids in which the narrator finds himself a demi-god. Readers get an adventure romance of dreams, warnings, and strange circumstances, told by a narrator who embarks on the improbable.
31935-sumerian-liturgies-and-psalms:
Stephen Langdon's Sumerian Liturgies and Psalms, published at Philadelphia by the University Museum in 1919, presents ancient Sumerian religious texts in translation. Langdon, professor of Assyriology at Oxford University, was working from tablets in the museum's collections, numbered and cataloged in his contents.

The volume includes a lamentation of Ishme-Dagan over Nippur, a liturgy of Ishme-Dagan, a liturgical hymn to Innini. They also include psalm to Enlil with a long intercession by the mother goddess, a lamentation on the pillage of Lagash by the Elamites, and a lamentation on the destruction of Ur. Readers get primary texts of Mesopotamian religion, with introduction, tablet descriptions, and indexes.
32898-the-handbook-of-conundrums:
Edith B. Ordway gathers riddles, wordplay, and party games in a New York handbook from George Sully and Company, copyright 1914 and 1915. Ten chapters run from early English wit through mythological, biblical, historical, and Civil War conundrums. Later chapters add geographical and literary riddles, alphabet games, general conundrums, and charades.

The early English chapter traces the modern conundrum from sayings current around 1600 onward. Its jokes turn on puns: lawyers' clerks write wide lines to keep the peace between plaintiff and defendant. One joke likens a spendthrift to a brush worn out dressing others. The closing chapter turns the collection into contests, with stories and charades for social gatherings.
33190-a-book-of-epigrams:
Ralph A. Lyon's gathering collects short, sharp sayings on poetry, the seasons, the sun, and much else, drawn from many writers. Published in Evanston in 1902, it opens with verse on poetry itself, then moves through the year's minstrelsy, from spring's low prelude to winter's pause. Each epigram is brief, often just a few lines, yet meant to be savored slowly.

The book suits readers who like wit in small doses, to dip into rather than read straight through. Lyon chose pieces that shine by brevity, pairing famous names with lesser-known voices. As an anthology, it preserves a taste of early twentieth-century verse craft, where a keen phrase could carry a whole thought in a handful of words.
33417-later-poems:
Bliss Carman's Later Poems, published in Toronto, gathers verse that dreams under an April moon, with a frontispiece portrait of the poet. Carman's poems speak of beauty, twilight woods, and silver music from a marshy flood, asking how life can seem a shadow in moonlight, a murmur in a dream. An appreciation by R. H. Hathaway and decorations by J. E. H. MacDonald frame the volume.

The poems suit readers who love lyrical, nature-haunted verse, with a Canadian poet's ear for music and image. Their tone is gentle and reflective, best read slowly, poem by poem. For fans of Carman, Later Poems offers a rich, musical collection, full of the beauty and melancholy of the natural world.
33486-songs-of-the-silent-world-and-othe:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps gathers poems of loss, absence, and faith in this 1885 collection. The opening sequence, which gives the book its title, speaks to a household after a death. These include a chair that seems occupied, a silence that still feels like listening, and grief held in check by love. Later sections range more widely, through friendship, the sea, legend, and figures such as Guinevere and Eurydice.

Phelps writes in plain, musical verse that treats death not as an ending but as a quieter form of presence. Birthday verses, tributes, prayers for morning and evening, and short lyrics about parting and endurance fill the six sections. The collection suits readers who want nineteenth-century devotional and elegiac poetry rather than showy display.
33553-in-a-belgian-garden-and-other-poem:
F. O. Call, writing from Bishop's College in Lennoxville, Canada, gathers wartime and reflective lyrics in this 1917 volume. Many of the poems had appeared before in the Canadian Magazine, the University Magazine, the Westminster, and Canada West. The title poem contrasts a Belgian garden of tall white lilies, poplars, wheatfields, and poppies with the same garden after battle, where shattered trunks stand and small white crosses guard the dead.

Other poems visit a Lincolnshire maiden's coast, fishing boats, and quiet English scenes, giving the collection a balance of home feeling and war grief. Call writes in a plain, musical style, honoring soldiers from lands beyond the sea who laid down their lives so the garden might bloom again. The book suits readers of First World War poetry in its gentler, elegiac register.
33686-accolon-of-gaul-with-other-poems:
Madison J. Cawein gathers romantic and lyrical verse in this 1889 Louisville volume, headed by the long poem Accolon of Gaul. Its prelude dreams of wandering dim with someone beautiful, good, true, and sad through suffering, with curl-crowned brow and soft eyes and voice. They cross a flower-showered lea where pansies, peas, and rain-rinsed poppies spread. Keats's line on triumphs gay of old romance sets the poem's key.

Further poems include Der Freischutz, To Revery, Late October, An Anemone, The Rain-Crow, Loveliness, The Last Scion of the House of Clare, On the Jellico-Spur, Señorita, Leander to Hero, Musagetes, The Quarrel. A sequence called Chords, with Dead and Gone, A Mabinogi, and Genius Loci. Cawein writes lush, musical verse in the late Romantic manner, rich in nature imagery and Arthurian echo.
33770-impertinent-poems:
Edmund Vance Cooke, author of Chronicles of the Little Tot, offers impertinent poems in this Dodge volume, copyrighted in 1903 and 1907, with illustrations by Gordon Ross. The pre-impertinence anticipates the intelligent critic by remarking that the chief impertinence is in calling them poems at all. It thanks the editors of the Saturday Evening Post, Success, Ainslee's, Metropolitan, Independent, Booklovers', and the New York Herald for first promoting their publicity.

An epigraph verses that death comes with a crawl or a pounce, and it is not the fact of being dead that counts but only how one died. Cooke's verses are witty, cheeky, and lightly philosophical, poking at vanity, mortality, and modern life. Readers who enjoy humorous verse in the manner of early twentieth-century magazines will find a bright, irreverent collection, illustrated with spirit.
33774-mice-other-poems:
Gerald Bullett's first book of verse appeared in Cambridge in January 1921, with a general note by Sir Arthur Quiller Couch. The short poems take plain, everyday things as their subjects, and the title poem gives the set its name. Bullett was then a young writer, and the book was sold as one of a small series of verse by new poets.

Readers meet brief lyrics that watch small creatures and small moments with close care. The poems favor clear images over grand claims, and they show how much feeling a few lines can carry. For a reader new to Bullett, the book is a compact first look at his early voice.
33902-1914-and-other-poems:
Rupert Brooke's poems of 1914 and other years appeared in London in 1915, after his death in the Aegean on April 23, 1915. Brooke, born at Rugby in 1887 and a fellow of King's, served as a sub-lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve and sailed with the Mediterranean force in February 1915. He had not prepared this book himself.

The 1914 sonnets, Peace, Safety, The Dead, and The Soldier, stand at the head of the set. Later poems turn to the South Seas, Tiare Tahiti, the great lover, and heaven. The book preserves a young poet's voice at the moment war cut it short.
33940-a-voice-on-the-wind-and-other-poem:
Madison Cawein published this book of poems at Louisville in 1902, inscribed to Edmund Gosse. Several poems had first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's, the Century, and other magazines. The title poem gives a voice to the wind on a windy height, calling lost children home through the night.

Cawein's proem asks for a soul that fills music like a bird, or a flower that blooms careless of praise. Nature, song, and longing run through the set, in lines rich with image and sound. The book shows a Kentucky poet at his most musical, writing for readers who love lyric verse.
34331-minor-poems:
Minor Poems is volume fifteen of the Little Classics, a pocket set edited by Rossiter Johnson, printed at Boston and New York in 1900. The book gathers short poems by many hands, each named in the contents. It is the kind of small, well made volume meant for the coat pocket and the quiet hour.

Burns opens the singer's list with Ae Fond Kiss, and Tennyson stands near with Break, Break, Break and the Bugle Song. Longfellow gives The Children's Hour and Haunted Houses, while Holmes gives The Chambered Nautilus. Milton's sonnet on his blindness, Browning's Evelyn Hope, and Hemans's Graves of a Household show the range, from high verse to fireside song.
34462-adventures-and-enthusiasms:
Lucas wrote these essays of adventures and enthusiasms for general readers. Doran printed the book in New York, copyright 1920. Contents open the perfect guest, then the sparrows friend essay. The golden eagle, a morning call, and the true wizard follow.

Innocence and impulse, possessions, and Drake and his game fill early. Admirals all to be and a study in symmetry come next. Davy Jones, the man of Ross, and the innocent progress appear. A long backlist of Lucas travel and essay books fronts it. Thoughts at the ferry, a little child, and a Devonshire inn close the seen contents.
3525-music-and-other-poems:
Henry van Dyke gathers poems in this volume, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in October 1904. The contents divide into odes, sonnets, legends, and lyrics. Odes include Music, Peace, and God of the Open Air, while sonnets treat work, life, love, and the child in the garden. Legends such as A Legend of Service and The Vain King sit beside shorter lyrics.

Van Dyke writes in a warm, musical style, often turning to nature, faith, and the duties of a good life. His poems favor clear images and steady rhythms over experiment. The collection suits readers who enjoy traditional verse for reading aloud, with themes of service, home, and the seasons running through it.
353-in-flanders-fields-and-other-poems:
War poems by Canadian doctor and soldier John McCrae anchor this small volume, drawn from the 1919 New York text. Most pieces date from 1894 to 1917, and a short essay on McCrae by his friend Andrew Macphail opens the book. The verse moves from love, sleep, and old towns to the strain of war.

The title poem speaks in the voice of dead soldiers in Flanders, urging the living to keep faith with them. Other poems mourn fallen men, praise duty, and mark places such as Quebec and Isandlwana. Read as a whole, the book shows a poet shaped first by peace, then by loss on the front.
3530-love-at-arms:
Rafael Sabatini sets this romance in Renaissance Italy, opening with a dedication to Guidobaldo da Montefeltro and an epigraph from Ariosto on ladies, knights, arms, and loves. Chapters carry titles such as Vox Populi, On a Mountain Path, Sackcloth and Motley, Monna Valentina, and The Amorous Duke. The hero moves through courts, wine shops, and mountain roads in a world of dukes and intriguers.

Love and swordplay drive the plot, with a fool's motley and a duke's desire both shaping events. Sabatini writes with speed and color, giving his hero duels, disguises, and a love that must survive politics. Readers who enjoy historical romance in the manner of his Captain Blood books will find a brisk, old fashioned adventure here.
35497-three-sunsets-and-other-poems:
Three Sunsets and Other Poems is a volume of serious verse by Lewis Carroll, with twelve fairy-fancies by Gertrude Thomson, published by Macmillan at London in 1898 at four shillings net.

The preface explains that nearly the whole volume reprints the serious portion of Phantasmagoria and Other Poems, first published in 1869 and long out of print. The Path of Roses was written soon after the Crimean War, when Florence Nightingale's name had become a household word. Only a Woman's Hair grew from a circumstance in the life of Dean Swift. A packet found among his papers held a single lock of hair, inscribed with those words. After Three Days followed Holman Hunt's picture of Christ found in the Temple, and two poems are reprinted from the Sylvie and Bruno books.
35679-pieces-of-hate-and-other-enthusias:
Heywood Broun wrote Pieces of Hate and Other Enthusiasms, issued at New York in 1922 by George H Doran. Broun gives the book to his father, Heywood C Broun. Short, sharp pieces fill the volume. Heads range from sport and stage to faith, drink law, and war.

One piece treats a sheik film and one treats John Roach Straton. G K Chesterton gets a piece in brief initials. Babe Ruth, Jack Dempsey, and college sport draw more pieces. The Unknown Soldier and a tortoise shell home sit side by side. Broun writes with wit and bite on the news and fads of his day. The pieces suit readers who like brief, brisk takes.
35687-history-of-american-socialisms:
History of American Socialisms, by John Humphrey Noyes, is a study of the socialist communities of the United States. The hosted copy is an exact reprint of the scarce edition of 1870, limited to five hundred copies. In his preface Noyes states the book's aim. Its object is to help the study of socialism by the method of working from facts.

It is first and chiefly a collection of facts, he says, and his attempts at reading and generalizing are secondary and not meant to be dogmatic. It is high time, he holds, that socialists begin to take lessons from experience. Noyes had unusual chances to watch the movements himself, and good fortune in gathering the records of others. Noyes founded the Oneida Community, and knew his subject from inside. His history remains the first full survey of America's many experiments in common living.
35761-the-man-who-pleases-and-the-woman-:
The Man Who Pleases and the Woman Who Charms is a book of manners by John Cone, with copyright in 1901 and a third printing in 1904. Cone gave the book to his mother. Its motto runs: look out lovingly upon the world, and the world will look lovingly in upon you.

Cone owns in his preface that he is more a gatherer than a maker, and that his truths are known to all. His point is that we forget them in daily life. Chapters treat the art of talk, good English, tact, the voice, dress, and good manners. He holds that courtesy rests on the wish to be pleasant, attractive, and kind in the sight of others.
35779-the-cornflower-and-other-poems:
The Cornflower and Other Poems, by Jean Blewett, was printed at Toronto by William Briggs in 1906. Blewett had also written Heart Songs. She gives the book to Lillian Massey Treble, in a verse that calls her a woman with a heart of gold.

The poems sort into tale poems, lyrics, and mixed pieces. Tale poems hold The Cornflower, The Quarrel, and In Sunflower Time. Others name Katie wooing, a sick children hospital, and Christy and the pipers. Lyrics treat harbor lights of home and the preacher down at the cove. Later verses honor Queen Victoria and give thanks. Blewett writes in warm, plain tones of home, faith, and the sea. Verse readers get a kind Canadian voice in full bloom.
35780-two-fishers-and-other-poems:
Two Fishers and Other Poems, by Herbert Palmer, was published in London in 1918 by Elkin Mathews of Cork Street. A motto from O'Shaughnessy heads the volume: we are the music-makers, and we are the dreamers of dreams. Palmer dedicates the book to three friends, among them a captain. The title poem speaks to Charley, a friend away at the war.

When the war is over, Charley, we will go fishing once again, the poem promises. The two will seek a leaping river far among the fells, where springing water wells. There Charley will forget the war among bracken, bilberry, and rolling leagues of heather. The speaker owns he never loved England till she kissed him in the West. Palmer's lyrics turn on nature as healer, written under the shadow of the war years.
35848-gaudeamus-humorous-poems:
Gaudeamus holds humorous poems turned from the German of Joseph Victor Scheffel and others. Charles G Leland made the English verse. The book came out in London in 1872.

A memoir of Scheffel opens the set, by way of introduction. The poems sing of granite, basalt and a great comet in jest. A song of the ichthyosaurus gives a beast's lament in rhyme. The Teutoburger Battle and old Assyrian Jonah get the same droll touch. Student songs and the Rodenstein ballads close the set. The humour is learned but light, aimed at readers who like wit with their verse. Leland's own preface tells how he came to the task.
36214-virginia-a-tragedy-and-other-poems:
Virginia: A Tragedy and Other Poems is a verse volume by Marion Forster Gilmore. It was published at Louisville, Kentucky, in 1910 and dedicated to her father. The long title piece is a tragedy in verse named for Virginia. Around it Gilmore gathers shorter poems, several of which had already appeared in The Cosmopolitan Magazine and Leslie's Weekly.

The shorter pieces move between family, faith, and famous places: My Mother, The Cradle Song, and a sonnet to Niagara Falls. There are verses on the Winged Victory of Samothrace and the Lion of Lucerne, and songs of the sea and the West. The tone is earnest and devout, in the manner of genteel American verse of its day. The volume preserves one regional poet's full range, from stage tragedy to the occasional magazine lyric.
36620-the-three-hills-and-other-poems:
Three Hills and Other Poems is a verse book by Squire of London. Latimer published it on Great Queen Street in the year 1913. Squire dedicates the volume to Francis Burrows on its front page. Contents open with Antinomies on a Railway Station and the title poem. A Chant, Artemis Altera, Starlight, and Florian's Song follow in his list.

Dialogue, Crepuscular, At Night, and For Music vary the shorter lyrics. The Roof, Treetops, In the Park, Song, and Town fill more pages. A Memorial, Friendship's Garland, and lines on the earthly paradise ensue. Twelve translations from Baudelaire close the book in French dress. Spleen, the cracked bell, and a voyage to Cythera stand there.
3665-maurine-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers her long poem Maurine with other poems in this popular edition of 1910. Maurine itself, a narrative poem of love and fate, fills the first hundred pages. Shorter pieces follow, such as All Roads that Lead to God are Good, Dust Sealed, Advice, Over the Banisters, The Past, Secrets, Applause, and The Story. Wilcox adds many new poems to this edition.

Wilcox writes in clear, musical verse about love, faith, and the choices of women. Her speakers move from morning mail and a lover's scorn to thoughts of God and the past. The book suits readers who enjoy popular American poetry of the late nineteenth century, earnest, romantic, and meant to be shared.
36913-the-divine-vision-and-other-poems:
The Divine Vision and Other Poems is by A E, the pen name of George William Russell. Macmillan in London and New York issued the book in nineteen oh four. Russell had earlier issued Homeward, Songs by the Way and The Earth Breath. He gave the book to seven friends, named by initials, as comrades in the craft. Some forty poems fill the volume.

The title poem lends its name to the whole book. Other poems include The Gates of Dreamland, Freedom, Dana, and The Nuts of Knowledge. Twilight, stars, faery lights, and old gods of Ireland fill the verse. A child of earth burns in his heart for the night and the deep unknown. Readers of Irish mystic verse will find Russell at his most dreamlike here.
37105-hints-to-pilgrims:
Charles Brooks wrote essays printed at New Haven in 1921, with pictures by Florence Minard. Brooks had written Journeys to Bagdad, There's Pippins and Cheese to Come, and Chimney Pot Papers, and a novel, Luca Sarto. The essays first ran in the Century Magazine, the Yale Review, the Atlantic Monthly, and the Literary Review, the publisher notes. Hints to pilgrims opens the set.

I plan a vacation, at a toy shop window, and Sic Transit follow. The posture of authors, after dinner pleasantries, little candles, and a visit to a poet fill the middle. Autumn days close the contents shown. A sly creature in one tale fetches in an embroidered wallet to hold an extra shift, and hints in return for a true nail from the holy cross. Brooks writes the familiar essay in its last graceful age.
37722-the-hindoos-as-they-are-a-descript:
Shib Chunder Bose, a Bengali writer, described his own people's life for English readers in this book. Stanford printed The Hindoos as They Are at London in 1881, with a Calcutta house beside him. Hastie, head of the General Assembly's Institution at Calcutta, adds a first note.

Manners, customs, and the inner life of Hindoo society in Bengal: the subtitle holds the whole plan. An insider's account was rare in such print. Bose writes of caste, faith, home rule, and feast days from inside the house, not from the veranda. The book speaks to two crowds at once: the British who ruled Bengal, and the Bengalis who read English. A plain, proud piece of self-portrait.
37751-the-deluge-and-other-poems:
The Deluge and Other Poems is a verse book by John Presland, published at London in 1911. Chatto and Windus issued it. Presland had written Manin and the Defence of Venice. The title piece is a poem in dramatic form. Its motto comes from Genesis: the sons of God saw the daughters of men. A Seeker after Truth, his wife, and his mother people the scenes. A chorus completes the cast.

Scene one shows the wife and mother spinning together. The wife sings a love song her husband made before they wed. Nightingales, jasmines, and moonlight fill its lines. The mother asks her to sing it again for its soothing music. Sonnets and lyrics fill the rest of the contents. A ballad of a sea nymph and In the Valley of the Shadow close the list.
37999-poems:
Poems is the verse of Macy, with a word at its front by a friend of his craft. It came out at Boston in the mid first years of the last age. Its rights were held that year by the poets wife. All rights were kept.

A front print, from a photo, shows the poet. The book owns that heads of great sheets let some poems stand in print once more. Sheets for the young and for wit are in that list. Its first pieces run in a soft strain: a piece in memory, an old cafe, a meal at a famed house. The pass of a rose and a love note for the feast of hearts come next. Loss of charm and like themes of love and time fill its span.
38001-sans-cravate-or-the-messengers-lit:
A volume of novels by Paul de Kock, printed at Boston and New York in 1903. George Barrie's Sons issued the set by arrangement with the Jefferson Press. This third volume holds Sans-Cravate, or the Messengers, and Little Streams. De Kock wrote hugely popular Parisian comic fiction. His name on a title page promised boulevard laughter.

Sans-Cravate opens on the Boulevard des Italiens. Three young men loiter arm in arm at noon. They scrutinise women, crack puns, and smoke cigars. The narrator maps Paris by its quarters and costumes. A Marais annuitant dresses nothing like a Chaussée d'Antin dandy. A practised eye reads strangers at a glance, he boasts. The frontispiece shows a wine-shop quarrel, plate raised high. De Kock's world is clerks, grisettes, and small adventures.
38135-etain-the-beloved-and-other-poems:
Etain the Beloved and Other Poems, by James H. Cousins, came out in Dublin in 1912. Its title piece retells an old Irish tale in verse. King Eochaidh holds the Feast of Tara, where custom bars a wifeless chief. An aged bard steps in to voice what the court cannot say.

Shorter poems and lyrics fill the rest of the volume in full. Pieces on death and life, schoolboys, and spring sit beside them here. One group works as paraphrase and retelling of old tales and scenes. Sonnets on a paper seller, a prisoner, and a homecoming close the set. An envoy piece, The Loving Cup, ends the book with notes.
38410-the-star-treader-and-other-poems:
The Star-Treader and Other Poems, by Clark Ashton Smith, was published by A M Robertson of San Francisco in 1912. Smith dedicates the book to his mother. He was then a young poet of Auburn, California, and this was his first book. Its verse looks away from the modern world to stars, old gods, and lost continents. A list of some fifty poems fills the contents.

Nero opens the volume, dreaming over a burning Rome made the fuel of his vision. A chant to Sirius and the title poem follow. Medusa, an ode to the abyss, the soul of the sea, and the mask of forsaken gods show the book's temper. Atlantis and the return of Hyperion reach for drowned worlds and old myth. Lethe, nirvana, the nemesis of suns, and a song of a comet close the round on notes of doom and distance.
38438-the-melody-of-earth-an-anthology-o:
The Melody of Earth gathers garden and nature poems by present-day poets, chosen and set in order by Gertrude Moore Richards. The book was published in Boston and New York in March 1918 and dedicated to the editor's sister, a lover of gardens. Thanks pages list the presses and poets who let their work be used.

Names in the thanks include James Whitcomb Riley, Alice Meynell, Katharine Tynan, Edward Thomas, and Louis Untermeyer. Poems treat poppies, daffodils, larkspur, haunted gardens, and views from a car window. Richards groups short lyrics by theme and season, making a calm gift book for readers who love both verse and the outdoor year.
38741-the-isle-of-palms-and-other-poems:
John Wilson gathered long poems and shorter verse in a volume printed in Edinburgh in 1812. The lead work, The Isle of Palms, runs through four cantos of sea and island scenes. Wilson gave the book to two Glasgow teachers, George Jardine and John Young. A wide table of contents sets out the full range of the verse.

Shorter pieces treat the Lake District, old abbeys, childhood, loss, and love. Sonnets on Wastwater, Skiddaw, and Helm Crag close the set. One poem marks the end of the slave trade, and one honors poet James Grahame. Readers of early Scots verse will find both grand scenes and quiet, close views.
38933-by-canadian-streams:
A celebration of Canada's rivers by Lawrence J Burpee. The Musson Book Company published it at Toronto in 1909. Burpee opens with a hymn to the waterways. Their scenery runs from the gentle Sissibou to the Fraser's grandeur. Legends of Micmac, Iroquois, Cree, and Blackfoot cling to their shores. Acadian villages and fortified St Lawrence towns add history.

Two centuries back, he notes, little was known beyond the St Lawrence valley. A century later, scores of rivers stood explored from source to outlet. Canoe men crossed the height of land by countless portages. They reached the Western Sea by a water road joining three oceans. Winnipeg, the Saskatchewan, and the Churchill carried them north and west. Burpee argues the rivers are the nation's true arteries.
39218-the-everlasting-arms:
Joseph Hocking wrote a novel of a wreck, an heir, and a count's creed. Hocking also wrote All for a Scrap of Paper. A woman's face starts the tale, and a wire note comes next. A ship wreck then throws the leads on a strange shore. The foe of your soul is named in a dark early part.

Wendover Park and Lady Blanche set the high house stage. Count Romanoff spreads his own gospel in that house. Beatrice Stanmore and the true heir twist the line of wealth. A scrap of paper and a day of fate mark the turns. Hocking blends faith tests with house plots.
39969-a-civic-biology-presented-in-probl:
George William Hunter, head of biology at De Witt Clinton High School in New York, wrote A Civic Biology, issued in 1914. The book was made for school use and is built as a set of problems, not as a smooth text. Hunter gave it to his fellow teachers, whose aid, he says, made the book possible.

Hunter cut hard science terms to the fewest he could, and kept the speech plain. A poll of more than three thousand pupils in four states showed the keenest pull toward the care of the human body and the betterment of the home scene. Boys and girls, and town and country pupils, pulled in split ways, and the book bends to those pulls. City crowding fronts the art.
400-helen-of-troy-and-other-poems:
Sara Teasdale gathers early lyrics in this 1911 volume, opening with a sequence on Helen of Troy. Poems on Beatrice, Sappho, Guenevere, and Erinna follow, each giving a famed woman a brief, clear voice. Later pieces turn to love songs, city scenes, and quiet laments in New York parks and streets.

Teasdale writes in short, musical lines, with plain words and sharp feeling. Love, loss, and beauty recur, never dressed in heavy show. The book marks her early gift: to say much in few lines, and to let a single image carry a whole mood.
4009-the-victories-of-love-and-other-poe:
Coventry Patmore's poems trace love through marriage, doubt, and faith, with Leah and Rachel as figures for two kinds of devotion. The speaker weighs the weary work of forcing love on one who has enough of it, and the honor owed to a woman whose thoughts stand too high for flattery.

Other poems in the volume carry the same theme in shorter forms, joining domestic life to spiritual hope. Patmore writes in measured, earnest verse, closer to prayer than to show. Readers who enjoy Victorian religious poetry will find a serious, tender book about love that seeks to serve rather than to win.
40444-the-union-or-select-scots-and-engl:
The Union, or Select Scots and English Poems, reached a second edition in 1759. R Baldwin printed it at London in Paternoster Row. A Juvenal line in Latin heads the title. Doubtful palms from poems, it hints in brief. Mind loves variety, the preface opens.

A judicious pick of small poems best entertains, it says. Great poets' shorter works fill the plan here. A finished landscape gives the same pleasure, it claims. Each object charms alone yet gains in company. Sweetly interchanged, Milton's phrase, names that gain. Dryden's miscellany was Britain's first of fame, it notes. Tonson carried that line on after him. Careless picks marred later such books, it charges. Swelling pages with weak verse was their fault. A Scots-English verse garland of 1759 shows the miscellany trade sorting gold from padding for polite readers.
41381-bible-emblems:
Bible Emblems is a book of talks on faith by Edward E Seelye, a church man of Schenectady. The American Tract Society in New York put it out, with rights held from 1866. Seelye builds each talk on a short line from the Bible. The first talk takes its text from a psalm about a high rock.

Twelve talks use signs drawn from the text, such as the sun and the voice of blood. One talk calls good men the lamps of God, lit to shine in the world. The raven and the dove, the bow in the cloud, and the altar all get a talk each. Each part asks the soul to look past self for help and growth.
41985-poems:
Poems is a volume of verse by Elinor Jenkins, published by Sidgwick and Jackson at London in 1915. The dedication, dated 15 August 1915, offers sad flowers from a bitter harvest field in place of frankincense or gems. The opening poem is a requiem for a dead friend, and The Dead Comrade follows.

Many poems answer the war then raging. Titles include Night in the Suburbs, August 1914, The Battle of the Rivers, and A Legend of Ypres. One poem marks Rupert Brooke in April 1915, and another asks a question about tears. Poppyfields, an epitaph on a child buried abroad, and poems of moonlight and waking fill out the wartime garland.
42034-poems:
Poems is a volume of verse by John Draper, published by the Poet Lore Company at Boston in 1913. The first poem, From a Grecian Myth, builds the sun a palace in the west, fringed with gold and dressed in every heavenly hue. Dated January 1911, it sings the sun lying down to rest in that vermeil hall. Carpe Diem follows, calling love to wake as dawn tinges the sky.

The contents range widely over myth and letters. Songs of Lorenzo and of Wo Hou stand beside poems to Shelley and on Thomas de Quincey. The Vision of Dante, the Spirit of Schopenhauer, and Arthur to Guenever follow. A glass of absinthe, the palace of pain, and the death of Chatterton show Draper's darker register.
42097-musical-criticisms:
Musical Criticisms collects the concert reviews of Arthur Johnstone, critic of the Manchester Guardian. The University Press published the book at Manchester in 1905, after Johnstone's death. A memoir by two friends opens the volume. The book is inscribed to the conductor Hans Richter, the author's friend.

The reviews are sorted by composer, from Bach to Elgar. Bach's mass and passion music take the first chapter. Beethoven's symphonies and Berlioz follow in turn. Wagner's ring at Covent Garden and at Bayreuth fills a long section. Tchaikovsky and the new English school of Elgar close the survey. Johnstone wrote for a city proud of its orchestra. His notices set a standard for plain, learned music writing in the provinces.
42301-poems:
Alexander Smith wrote the Poems in a volume of youth’s high hopes. David Bogue issued the third edition in London in eighteen hundred fifty four. A Life-Drama, his long stage poem, fills most of the book. Short tales in verse and sonnets share its last pages.

Walter, the young poet of the Life-Drama, tears his page at midnight. For Poesy his heart and pulses beat, he cries in the first scene. One passion eats the rest in him, as Aaron’s serpent ate the snakes. He would give rich laden years for one smile from his cold muse. A great heart with weak hands is the deadliest pang, he finds. Tears of self contempt spring like nightshade in a shrine’s ruins. An Evening at Home and Lady Barbara turn to softer strains. Fame for this book made Smith a marked young Scot of letters.
424-general-william-booth-enters-into-he:
Vachel Lindsay gathers poems of faith, reform, and American life in this 1913 volume, reprinted in 1916. The title poem marches Salvation Army founder William Booth into heaven to drums, banjos, and a host of saved sinners. Other pieces praise Lincoln, Shakespeare, and St. Francis, and scold drunkards, gamblers, and unrepentant cities.

Lindsay writes in chanting, musical lines meant to be read aloud, with strong beats and plain speech. Springfield, cornfields, and street corners ground his visions. The book marks Lindsay as a people's poet, eager to preach beauty and justice in the same breath.
42439-the-santa-fe-trail-and-other-poems:
Joseph R Wilson wrote this book of poems, printed by the International Printing Company of Philadelphia in 1921. He gives it to his wife. A short history of the famous Santa Fe Trail opens the book, before the long title poem. A plate shows a hunter creeping closer to the trail, from page fifteen.

Poems follow on the Blind Beggar of Albuquerque, sunrise from the Alvarado, the Grand Canyon of Arizona, and the Harvey House chimes. The tumbleweed gets a jolly piece of its own. Later pages turn home: boyhood, memories, a country romance, and Napoleon's tomb. Wilson writes as a western lawyer-poet, mixing trail lore, travel views, and soft home verse in one keepsake book.
42947-little-ann-and-other-poems:
Little Ann and Other Poems is a book of verse for children by Jane and Ann Taylor. Kate Greenaway drew the pictures. The London edition pairs plain moral tales in rhyme with soft, famed art.

The poems warn and praise in turn, each through a small scene. Careless Matilda and Meddlesome Matty show faults in action. Dirty Jim and Greedy Richard get the same sharp treatment. Other pieces praise the violet, the orphan and the good natured girls. A true story of little Ann and her mother opens the set. Young readers get clear lessons wrapped in lively rhyme. Greenaway's soft drawings made the book a gift book favourite.
43089-chaucer-s-works-volume-1-romaunt-o:
The Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, edited from numerous manuscripts by Walter Skeat, begins with this first volume: the Romaunt of the Rose and the minor poems. The Clarendon Press at Oxford published the second edition in 1899. A frontispiece portrait of Chaucer is taken from a Harleian manuscript.

The contents open with a long Life of Chaucer and a list of his works. The Romaunt, Chaucer's translation of the great French love poem, takes the bulk of the volume. The minor poems follow: Merciles Beautè, a balade to Rosemounde, Lak of Stedfastnesse, and envoys to Scogan and Bukton. The Compleynt of Venus is printed with its French original beside it. Skeat's edition, with its account of the manuscripts and its care over Middle English forms, became the standard Chaucer for generations of students.
4331-sun-up-and-other-poems:
Lola Ridge wrote this collection of poems after her Ghetto book, and she dedicated it to her mother. The opening dedication cradles the speaker back into darkness, half shapes, and the dust of unused air. It sets a tone of memory, loss, and stubborn tenderness that runs through the book.

The contents divide into Sun-Up, Monologues, Windows, and Secrets, with poems on jaguars, wild ducks, trains, skyscrapers, and Wall Street at night. Ridge moves between nature and the city, between a train window and an inner room. Her free verse keeps the immigrant city and the American landscape in the same frame.
4332-the-ghetto-and-other-poems:
Lola Ridge wrote the title poem of this collection for the American people, offering a harsh feast, with iron still hot from the furnace. The Ghetto pictures the crowded Jewish quarter of New York, with its markets, faces, fog, and debris, in free verse of great force.

Other poems range across Manhattan, Broadway, the Bowery, and Brooklyn Bridge, with pieces on iron, labor, and the war years. Frank Little at Calvary and The Song of Iron show Ridge's political edge. The book stands as an early modernist portrait of immigrant New York, written from inside its streets.
43612-katydid-s-poems:
Katydid's Poems gathers the verse of McKinney, who wrote under the name Katydid. The volume was entered for copyright in 1887 at Washington. The Courier-Journal job office printed it, and a warm letter of praise opens the book.

Williams of Harrodsburg, Kentucky, writes that her lines please him more at each reading. He calls them womanly, natural, musical, and sweet, and free of all affectation. Only the restraint of rhyme and measure, he says, checks her muse at all. The contents run from To a Katydid and A Day Dream to The Old Ravine. Love poems, a sister's love, and a memorial to Nannie Johnson White fill the middle. Later pieces give the heliotrope a soliloquy of its own. The set keeps the tone of a parlour songster of its day.
43615-poems:
Frederic Manning published a slim book of verse called Poems with John Murray in London in 1910. The first long piece, Theseus and Hippolyta, retells a Greek war tale in bold, ringing lines. Other early poems take up Tristram, the soul of man, night, spring dance, and love. A set of short lyrics under a French head closes the book.

Titles in that last group include The Pool, Noon, The Swallow, Light, and Death and Memory. Some poems had first run in The Atlantic Monthly, The Spectator, and The English Review. The volume shows Manning as a young poet drawn to myth, nature, and brief, keen moods.
44444-the-mother-s-dream-and-other-poems:
Hannah Gould wrote these poems, printed in Boston in 1853. Crosby, Nichols issued the book of verse for home readers. Contents open with Blowing Bubbles, Infant Faith, and Patty Proud. Short nature and faith pieces fill much of the long list.

The title poem, The Mother Dream, stands well into the volume. Pieces treat a little blind boy, a humming bird anger, and shells. A Name in the Sand, The Pilgrim Way Song, and Time appear. Hymns, dirges, and album verses close the gentle, pious verse set. The Widow Only Son stands near the end of the list.
44635-military-manners-and-customs:
Military Manners and Customs is a study of military usages by James Anson Farrer, issued by Chatto and Windus of London in 1885. Farrer had written Primitive Manners and Customs and Crimes and Punishments. A Seneca motto, man is a sacred thing to man, stands on the title page.

Farrer limits himself to European civilisation, drawing no hard line between ancient and modern. Topics include the treatment of prisoners of war and of surrendered garrisons. He covers rules about spies and surprises, and feelings about new weapons. Others explain parts of military dress and customs like kissing the earth before a charge. Honour figures too, in reprisals, and in fairness allowed in stratagems and deception. He warns that big subjects often receive only a page or a chapter here.
45280-the-wonderful-one-hoss-shay-and-ot:
The Wonderful One-Hoss Shay is a set of poems by Oliver Wendell Holmes. The chief poem first stood in a famed month book in 1858. The set here came out in 1897 with plates drawn for the verse. Its full name adds the deacon whose work the shay was in life.

The deacon built a chaise in a strict way of thought in 1755. Each part was made as strong as each other part of the build. No weak spot could make the shay break down in one place. It ran a full round of years to a day with no flaw. Then it fell to dust all at once, in a heap on the road. Holmes tells the tale as a jest with a grave point at its core.
45643-poems:
Poems, by Iris Tree, was published in London and New York in 1920. Curtis Moffat made the decorations. A head of the poet by Jacob Epstein fronts the book. Some poems had run in Poetry, Vanity Fair, and the Wheels anthology. Contents split into three parts: Rockets and Ashes, Smoke, and Flame. Titles are given by first lines, in the manner of early verse books. The first cries out against laws that tie her limbs and choke her songs.

War enters in the Smoke part, with a poem called Zeppelins. Holy Russia and pity for the slain appear there. Love, nerves, and the complex life fill other pieces. Tree's voice is bold, restless, and modern, set against hymns and rules.
46374-mr-punch-s-book-of-arms:
Mr Punchs Book of Arms is a jest book of mock grants by E Reed. Both text and coats come from the hand of the same gay artist. The Punch house in London put the joke book out for its fans. The book bears the year eighteen ninety nine in old Roman marks.

Great men of the day get false ranks and arms in a long droll list. A press chief, a law chief, and a famed war lord lead the roll. A tale smith is made a peer of his isle, and a stage chief a lord. Each grant pairs a drawn shield with a tart line of praise in jest. The book mocks the lust for rank that marked its rich age.
47055-gipsy-night-and-other-poems:
Gipsy-Night and Other Poems is a book of verse by Richard Hughes. The first American edition came out in Chicago in 1922 from Will Ransom, with a lithograph portrait by Pamela Bianco. A note states the limits of that edition. Sixty-three copies of it, each signed by author and artist, were made.

Of those, thirty were for sale in America and twenty-four in England. The copy in view is number 46. A page lists where the poems first came out. In England they stood in The Athenaeum, the London Mercury, the Spectator, and more. In America they stood in The Dial, the New York Evening Post Literary Review, The Bookman, and Poetry. The book is a first gathering of the poems of a young Welsh writer of his day.
48213-religious-studies-sketches-and-poe:
Religious Studies, Sketches and Poems is Volume Fifteen of the Riverside Edition of Harriet Beecher Stowe's writings. Houghton Mifflin printed the set at Boston in 1896, with biographical introductions and portraits. The pieces gathered here date back in copyright to 1855 and after. They show the side of Stowe her fame sometimes hides.

The biographical introduction notes a constant in all her work. Running through the whole of her writings, it says, is the appeal to the religious sensibilities. Her greatest book took captive the humblest reader and the genius alike by that appeal. These studies and poems are the source made plain: sermons in essay dress, devout sketches, and verse. The volume rounds out the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin as a theologian of the hearth.
48306-selected-poems:
Selected Poems gathers the best-known lyrics of Rupert Brooke. Sidgwick and Jackson published it in London. The first edition appeared in March 1917. Impressions followed yearly to 1922. Brooke had died in the war. The selection became his memorial in verse.

A long contents list maps his range. Early pieces treat a hippopotamus goddess and town life. The Old Vicarage, Grantchester, stands among the famous titles. The Great Lover catalogues his joys. Poems of love and mutability fill the middle pages. The volume closes with the 1914 sonnets. Peace, Safety, and The Dead lead to The Soldier. That final sonnet became the emblem of a generation.
49277-twixt-earth-and-stars-poems:
Twixt Earth and Stars, by Marguerite Radclyffe-Hall, is a volume of lyric poems. Bumpus issued it at London in 1906, from Oxford Street, in full. A dedication to my inspiration opens the set with a short love verse. In a Garden leads, with roses, jessamine, sweetpeas, and sunflowers in bloom.

A drowsy bee on a rose and a thrush in the ivy set the scene. Songs ask what if you were a rose and I were the sun. Earth and dew trade places in the lover playful what if game. Drifting praises lying in a boat on a languid stream of dreams. Love, gardens, and longing tune these early Edwardian lyrics.
49321-a-sheaf-of-verses-poems:
A Sheaf of Verses is a book of poems by Marguerite Radclyffe-Hall. Bumpus of London issued it in 1908. The writer is listed here under her early style of name. Press notices for her first book open the volume. That book, Twixt Earth and Stars, drew warm praise. Reviewers called her rhythms truly musical. Her nature verse won special notice.

The sheaf is dedicated to sad days and glad days. Kinship opens the contents. The Moon's Message and a battle-field piece follow. A hymn to earth as mother sings in one poem. Sunlight, moorland, and daffodils crowd its lines. Hall later won fame and trouble with a bold novel. These early verses are fresh, glad, and young.
49649-the-bombardment-of-reims:
Barr Ferree wrote The Bombardment of Reims, at New York in 1917. The Leonard Scott company published the book, with rights held by Ferree. A front plate shows the west front of Reims cathedral. Contents give the bombardment year by year in a chronology. The years 1914, 1915, 1916, and 1917 each take their section.

A postscript and a survey of the buildings of Reims follow. The destruction of those buildings closes the contents list. Plates show the front at Reims in May 1917, and the west portals. The cathedral after the April bombardment of 1917 stands pictured too. The bombardment has excited the indignation of the civilized world, Ferree opens. Its sacrifice seemed so wanton and so unnecessary, he writes. Those who knew the church feel an intense personal loss, he adds. Ferree, an American far from the war, surveys the ruin.
49721-poems:
George Santayana selected and revised this Poems volume himself, and Constable of London published it in 1922. The contents show a poet's whole career gathered between two covers.

Fifty sonnets come first, written between 1883 and 1895, followed by miscellaneous sonnets on subjects from a volume of scholastic philosophy to a statue of Achilles. Odes follow, then various poems: Cape Cod, Avila, a chapel at King's College, Spain in America, and a minuet. Translations from Michael Angelo and from Gautier close the book. In the sonnets Santayana returns often to faith and knowledge, arguing in one that it is not wisdom to be only wise. In another, Columbus trusts a chart that faith deciphered in the skies.
49755-brief-diversions-being-tales-trave:
Brief Diversions gathers tales, travesties and epigrams by Priestley, printed at Cambridge by Bowes and Bowes in 1922. The motto on the title page runs: short, but there's salt in it, borrowed from The Double-Dealer. Nearly all the pieces had appeared in the Cambridge Review. A few travesties and epigrams were added for the book, and others revised.
