Priestley's note is candid about the tales' origin. Most were written during the war, many of them while he was in Flanders. Being away from books at the time, he imagined he was doing something new. To such gentlemen he offers an apology if he seems to have trespassed. It stands at the head of a long career, before the novels and plays that made its author famous.
50043-poems:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote these poems in French, and Bernard Miall put them in English verse. The book was printed at London in 1915. The man who did the work in English wrote a word at its front. Once in a span of years, he says, an author breaks the bounds of his own land. Of such world-wide men of art, Maeterlinck is the most bright case in his view.

Twenty years past, Miall had tried in vain to stir the print men of England to take up the plays of the Belgian. Now he is asked to give one of the less known, first works of the man. The hour draws near for the full set of all his works, a crown few men gain in their lives. His readers in England and America are more in count than those who read him in French.
5015-state-of-the-union-addresses-of-joh:
John Quincy Adams's State of the Union addresses open with thanks for providence. Health prevails within American borders. Abundance covers the land despite the seasons. Peace holds with all nations, and calm holds at home. The sixth president frames his messages as reports on a republic blessed and obliged to use its blessings well.

Internal improvements, commerce, and the nation's standing abroad fill the later messages, delivered in Adams's learned and moralizing style. The set covers a presidency that prized science, roads, and canals over party combat. Readers get a primary record of the 1820s, when America debated what a national government should build.
50603-minute-mysteries-detectograms:
Minute Mysteries is a book of detective puzzles by Ripley, printed by Houghton Mifflin at Boston in 1932. The puzzles are called Detectograms. Lewis Lawes, warden of Sing Sing Prison, supplies a foreword. Ripley dedicates the book to his mother. The author's preface opens in a detective bureau.

Chief Inspector Kelley, a grizzled veteran, talks with his nephew Jim Barry, who wants to enter the field of criminology. The average policeman, Kelley says, looks on the lay criminologist as any professional regards an amateur. In thirty years of police work, though, he has met no one who so well combines theory with practice as Professor Fordney. Fordney is the book's detective: each Detectogram gives the reader a small scene, a set of facts, and a hidden flaw to find. The puzzles made Ripley's name in the mystery magazines.
50852-the-bells-and-other-poems:
The Bells and Other Poems is a gift edition of Edgar Allan Poe's verse, published by Hodder and Stoughton of New York and London. Edmund Dulac illustrated the volume in his rich colour manner. The Bells leads the contents and gives the book its name.

The Raven, Annabel Lee, and Lenore stand among the famous pieces. Ulalume, The Haunted Palace, and A Dream Within a Dream deepen the selection. The City in the Sea and Eldorado carry Poe's music of doom. Sonnets to science and to Zante show his formal range. Al Aaraaf, his long youthful poem, closes toward the end of the list. Dulac's plates turned Poe's sound haunted lyrics into a drawing room treasure. Few American poets have been so often and so beautifully dressed for the gift trade.
51277-a-summer-s-poems:
A Summer's Poems, by Lys, was printed in London in 1893 by Seeley and Company. Nearly all the poems were written during a stay of six weeks, in August and September of that year. The place was Hallstatt, among the mountains of Upper Austria.

Lys says in a short note that the poems go out at once, faults and all. He hopes they may give some small pleasure to a few friends and other readers. The first piece, To the Muse, is a sonnet that asks the muse to take him as her servant again. A second piece praises a flower that gives its scent to all and does not fear the dark. A third, called Life's Voyage, sends glad ships out over deep water.
5134-discoveries-made-upon-men-and-matte:
Ben Jonson's Discoveries gathers the short notes, judgments, and reflections he made from his daily reading, arranged as a wood, or storehouse, of thoughts on men, letters, and conduct. The volume pairs those prose fragments with poems, including his famous memorial lines to William Shakespeare and an epitaph for the boy actor Salathiel Pavy.

Jonson writes with a scholar's eye and a playwright's bluntness, praising, correcting, and moralising in turn. Readers get a direct look at how a leading Jacobean writer thought about his craft and his contemporaries, in pieces short enough to dip into and sharp enough to quote.
51415-poems:
Jamie Harris Coleman of Louisville, Kentucky, wrote the poems in a small book issued by John P Morton and Company with a copyright of nineteen eighteen. The price on the cover is twenty five cents. Some forty short poems fill the book. Titles include Days of Youth, Life, The Ocean, and Signs of Spring. Faith, home, and race run through the list.

An opening essay asks what poetry is and tells of a prize contest on that theme. A short life of Coleman follows. She was born in Mayfield in eighteen ninety three and left day school to work and help her young brother and sister. Poems in the book recall Booker T Washington, Lincoln, slavery, and freedom, and plead for justice. Her verse is plain, warm, and full of hope.
51536-poems:
Poems, by Jennie Earngey Hill, was printed at Boston in 1918. The Gorham Press issued the volume. Hill gives the book to her beloved aunt, Jennie Hewes Caldwell. Contents list some thirty short pieces. Song of the Brook opens the set. It asks the whispering brooklet why love must die. A note says the words were set to a piece of music called The Brook. A Sleighing Song follows, all slipping and sliding over ice and snow. Hearts attune, and the air seems drunk with revelry.

The Dresden Maid, the goldfinch, and Bonny Bunny show her range. Snowflakes, the family cow, and the meadowlark fill the nature side. Consecration, Enchantment, and Death's Spectre take graver tones. Hill writes small, earnest lyrics of love, seasons, and home, in the manner of her day.
51798-when-santiago-fell-or-the-war-adve:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote When Santiago Fell, a boys' tale dated eighteen ninety-nine and reissued in nineteen hundred and five. Bonehill had written A Sailor Boy with Dewey and other tales for lads. The book opens the Flag of Freedom series.

Bonehill aimed to give American boys a true picture of Cuba in its war with Spain. The tale covers the last year of that war and the march that led to the fall of Santiago. Two chums share the risks and fights of the campaign. Bonehill grants that their adventures may seem drawn large. He holds that real cases were just as bold. Patriot pride runs strong.
51904-poems:
Henry Reed Conant published this book of his own verse at Kaukauna, Wisconsin, in 1893. The Sun Publishing Company made it, and Conant entered it in his own name. A line from Byron heads the book, with a grin: a book's a book, although there is nothing in it.

He gives the volume to his brother Carlos, a professor of languages. The Telulah Spring stands as front plate and as a long poem within. Life, Dream of a Fairy, and Be Not Discouraged open the list. God's Love, Contentment, and The Fox River mix faith with home ground. A Little Grave, The Crown of Fame, and To a Brown Thrush fill a plain, earnest shelf of small-town verse.
5209-miscellaneous-poems:
This collection of miscellaneous poems opens with Sir Eustace Grey, a dramatic poem set in a madhouse, where a visitor, a physician, and a patient speak in turn. The ruined lord of Greyling Hall, once admired by rich and poor alike, tells how pride and rash deeds brought him to his cell. The physician urges the visitor on to happier scenes.

The remaining contents, The Hall of Justice, Woman, The Birth of Flattery, and Reflections, extend the volume's moral range. Readers will find verse that mixes dramatic monologue with satire and reflection, in the style of early nineteenth-century narrative poetry at its most earnest.
52115-songs-for-all-seasons-and-other-po:
Cora Bass wrote Songs for All Seasons and Other Poems, printed by Lawler at Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1901. Her preface thanks papers such as the New York Observer and Zion's Herald for kind use of her verse. She also thanks friends who gave her first book of poems a warm welcome. The first poem gives best wishes of the season to each reader. It hopes fair gifts attend them till the day of time is done.

Contents run from songs of the seasons to verse on Washington, Memorial Day, and freedom. Poems bear names like Bravely Do and Bravely Bear, The Sum of Life, and The Way Will Open. Faith runs through the set, with songs for the King of Kings above. Bass writes plain, hymn-like verse for home, church, and holiday use.
52366-the-veil-and-other-poems:
Walter de la Mare gathered these poems in The Veil and Other Poems, printed by Henry Holt at New York in 1922. De la Mare was by then a loved hand at verse of dream and quiet strangeness. A note at the front tells where some pieces first stood.

Seven poems were written for drawings by Pamela Bianco, and first came out in a book named Flora. One piece, Tidings, comes from Crossings, a play for children. Leave to reprint came from Pawling, Beaumont, and the editors of journals that first ran the verse. Readers get de la Mare in his own vein: short, clear songs with a chill of the unseen at their edge.
52448-the-house-of-the-trees-other-poems:
The House of the Trees and Other Poems is Ethelwyn Wetherald's volume of nature verse. It was copyrighted in 1895 by Lamson, Wolffe and Company, with William Briggs of Toronto. Many poems are new; others first appeared in the Youth's Companion and the Toronto Week.

The title poem begs the spirit of the wood to open its doors, wash the speaker clean of dust and din, and lock her into the sunless peace of the trees. The contents then keep the year's round: the sun on the trees, pine needles, the sound of the axe, and the prayer of the year. The hay field, a rainy day, leafless April, and September follow in season. The humming bird, the chipmunk, the blind man, and children in the city widen the set. October, winter, and the snow-storm close the calendar of a poet who lived outdoors.
52546-poems:
Poems is a small volume of verse by Thomas Hall Shastid. The author published it himself at Pittsfield, Illinois, in 1881. He had earlier issued a book called Newspaper Ballads. A preface thanks friends and editors for kind treatment. It asks for no harsher judgment this time.

One fact dominates the preface. The author is fourteen years of age. Many poems were written at a much earlier age. The first poem treats Christmas night. It calls for peace on earth and good will to men. A fallen apple tree earns an elegy. Angels of peace and death fly over the land in another piece. Spectres haunt a sad palace in a third. The verse is earnest, simple, and very young.
52584-tides-a-book-of-poems:
John Drinkwater gathered these poems in Tides, the first book sent out by the Beaumont Press. Fine copies came on Japanese vellum, signed and numbered, and 250 more on hand-made paper. Drinkwater gave the book to General Sir Ian Hamilton.

His gift verse praises the brave graces that light a battle line. A Man's Daughter opens the set, then Venus in Arden and Cotswold Love. The Midlands, May Garden, and Plough root the verse in his own hills. Birmingham in 1916 and a verse for a war fountain bring the great war near. Roundelays, estates of the heart, and treason of the pen fill the list shown here.
52623-poems:
Poems, by Crocket McElroy of St Clair, Michigan, was printed at Chicago by the Scroll Publishing Company in 1900. McElroy gives the book to the Honorable Thomas W Palmer of Detroit, the Honorable Joseph B Moore of Lansing, and his other friends.

The index sorts the verse into poems of patriotism, poems of sentiment, and poems of feeling. Our Country and Our Flag opens the set, then the Flag of Hobson Choice and the Old Soldier. Washington, a Voice for Freedom, and the Reconcentrados follow. The Milk of Human Kindness, the Working Girl, and the Wayward Girl stand in the sentiment part. One poem opens at morning light on October twelfth, in fourteen hundred ninety two. Columbus and his happy crew sang land ahoy, with shouts of joy and dreams of wealth. Verse fans get a small town muse.
52796-poems:
Nora May French left poems printed at San Francisco in 1910, three years after her death. French was born at Aurora, New York, on April the twenty sixth, 1881, and died at Carmel, California, on November the fourteenth, 1907, aged twenty six years. The Outer Gate opens the book, then Rain, Best Loved, The Rose, and Between Two Rains. The Message, By the Hospital, and Oh Dryad Thoughts follow.

Music in the Pavilion, Rebuke, In Camp, The Nymph, Vivisection, The Stranger, and The Constant Ones fill the early pages. The Spanish Girl runs in three parts, and The Garden of Dolores, Indifference, and After Knowledge come later. Two Spendthrift Kings, Growth, Change, Wistaria, and My Nook close a slim sad harvest. Carmel's young poet is still read for her clear, brief, grieving songs.
52803-canadian-melodies-and-poems:
George Merkley wrote Canadian Melodies and Poems, published at Toronto by Hart and Riddell in 1893. He dedicated the volume to the Marquis of Lorne, whom Canadians held in grateful remembrance. In his preface he makes no apology for the book, though he admits the poems were written in haste.

Merkley says several pieces began as relief from the routine of college life, and many were written under foreign skies. He laments the lack of a national literature in Canada, a country whose history, he argues, has a poetic background. Canadians, he notes, read good home journals and import many foreign books, yet produce little of their own. The poems that follow are his small offering toward filling that gap.
52865-home-poems:
Home Poems is a book of verse by Kate Louise Wheeler, out in the rights year of eighteen ninety-seven. Wheeler calls her self a girl of the Granite State in her front note. She wrote the verse for the work of a youth faith band, and her friends urged the print for their joint gain. The book is writ to her dear mother, past a verse on the wealth of a mothers love.

The list of verse runs past one hundred heads, from the old state to a last stand fast. Faith, home lights, prayer, babes, and the go home fill the rows. One verse sings the hills and streams of her state as they wake to praise it. A class ode of a past year and a verse for the feast of thanks stand in the list.
52898-the-magic-house-and-other-poems:
The Magic House and Other Poems, by Duncan Campbell Scott, was printed in London in 1893. Scott gives the book to his mother. Contents run to more than fifty short poems. First lines are printed by each title as a guide. A Little Song opens with a sunset in the rosy west. Poems on winter, a summer storm, and life and death follow in quick order.

Place poems name Scarboro Beach, Les Eboulements, and Riviere du Loup. Ottawa gets a poem of its own near the end. One piece is written in a fellow poet's book, for Lampman. Love, memory, youth, and time recur as themes. Scott mixes farm, river, and city scenes in a clear lyric voice. The set shows early Canadian poetry in a London dress.
53385-for-your-sweet-sake-poems:
For Your Sweet Sake is a book of poems by James McGirt, printed at Philadelphia in 1906 by the John Winston Company. The contents list some sixty short lyrics. They include Born Like the Pines, The Spirit of the Oak, Home Sick, and The Siege of Manila, plus dialect pieces such as Des Fo' Day and Uncle Is'rel.

Love songs, nature pieces, prayers, and success poems fill the small volume, along with a tribute to the late Queen Victoria. McGirt wrote as a Black poet building a name in print on his own terms. The book survives as an earnest, hopeful record of that climb.
53435-at-minas-basin-and-other-poems:
At Minas Basin and Other Poems is a book of verse by Theodore Rand. William Briggs published it in Toronto in 1897. Copies were also sold in Montreal and Halifax. The dedication thanks a companion of perfect summer days at Partridge Island.

The poems belong to the shores of the Minas Basin in Nova Scotia. A willow at Grand Pré and the bowing dyke stand among the titles. The rain cloud, the rose, and the cumulus cloud show the nature range. The night-fisher and a deep-sea shell bring the coast itself into the verse. Glooscap, the hero of native legend, earns a poem of his own. Another honours Silas Tertius Rand, a kinsman famed in the same region. The opening poem lets Poesy herself speak to her maker. She asks for a soul of truth breathed into her fair form.
53545-canadian-battlefields-and-other-po:
Canadian Battlefields and Other Poems is a verse collection by J R Wilkinson, printed for the author by William Briggs of Toronto in 1899. Wilkinson was a lieutenant-colonel, late commanding the 21st Fusiliers. His portrait fronts the book. The preface is written from Leamington in 1899.

Battle poems of the War of 1812 lead the contents. Chateauguay, Lundy's Lane, and Chrysler's Farm each get a poem. Laura Secord's walk is told under the Battle of the Beaver Dams. Queenston Heights, Stony Creek, and Lacolle Mills follow. The Taking of Detroit and the Battle of Abraham's Plains widen the field. Dulac des Ormeaux is named the Thermopylæ of Canada. Waterloo stands among the Canadian fights without apology. Other poems treat the Ojibways, the Hurons, and the Jesuit. Nature, home, love, and faith fill the rest.
53623-the-snowflake-and-other-poems:
The Snowflake and Other Poems, by Arthur Weir, was printed at Montreal by John Lovell and Son in 1897, under an 1896 copyright. Weir had written Fleurs de Lys and The Romance of Sir Richard. The title poem opens the book, followed by The Masque of the Year.

The contents run from The Muse and the Pen and The Beaver Meadow to a Voyageur Song and a Dedicatory Ode. Entering Port, Wild Flowers, and Timor Mortis Conturbat Me stand in the mid list. Baby Stocking, The Sleeping Soul, The Mother, and Pluck Flowers in Youth fill the later pages. Sonnets in California, The Pool of Sant Oline, and Winter in the South show his range. One verse tells of Neptune daughter laughing in cool grottoes under the water. Verse fans get a Canadian poet of nature and home.
53800-orpheus-and-other-poems:
Orpheus and Other Poems is a memorial volume of verse by Edward Burrough Brownlow. The Pen and Pencil Club of Montreal published the poems in 1896 after his death. Brownlow was born in London in 1857 and died in Montreal in September 1895. Fellow club members collected the work in memory of their friend and poet.

Orpheus leads the contents, followed by Dead Summer, Autumn, and The Sky Lark in turn. Ballades, sonnets, a pantoum, and a rondeau show his love of set forms. A Roman girl prayer, the whip poor will, and the death of the laureate fill the list. Canadian letters of the 1890s keep a voice here that death cut short.
53818-poems:
Geoffrey Dearmer published a book of war poems in New York in 1918. He gives the book to Christopher, killed at Suvla Bay on October 6, 1915. The dedication poem tells how Christopher shuddered to the ground under shrapnel without a word and hid his darkening eyes. Your blood shall help to purify the world, Dearmer writes.

The first part holds poems of the Dardanelles, from W Beach, a prayer, a Turkish trench dog, and a sentinel. Mudros after the evacuation and the dead Turk follow. A second part turns to the western front, with missing men, trench poems, Gommecourt, and the Somme. Later poems turn homeward, to children, Keats, and spring.
54036-armenian-legends-and-poems:
Boyajian compiled Armenian Legends and Poems for Dent in London and Dutton in New York, giving the profits to the Lord Mayor's Armenian Fund. Viscount Bryce wrote the introduction, and Aram Raffi added a long essay on the epics, folk-songs, and medieval poetry of Armenia.

The contents mix cradle songs, love songs, charm verses, and laments with great legendary tales: Ara and Semiramis, Artashes and Satenik, the founding of Van, and the Lake of Van. A chronological index of authors and an index of first lines close the book. Boyajian dedicated the volume to the undying spirit of Armenia, and it carried a people's old songs to English readers in a time of Armenian suffering.
54147-dorothy-dale-and-her-chums:
Dorothy Dale and Her Chums is a girls' novel by Margaret Penrose, printed at New York in 1909. It is one of the Dorothy Dale series, which also holds Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School and Dorothy Dale's Great Secret. The first chapter is called Stolen Birds. Dorothy, perching on the high shelf at the side of the pump, sighs that a thing has happened just now, and isn't it too mean.

She gazes beyond the wire fence into the pigeon loft, where a few birds pose in fond dove fashion. The chapters bring a gypsy girl, Dorothy at the camp, and a midnight alarm. Miette and her troubles hold the middle of the book. A runaway, a rumpus, a girl's mean act, and Dorothy to the rescue follow. Tavia's double, the capture, and surprises lead toward the close.
544-anne-s-house-of-dreams:
Lucy Maud Montgomery follows Anne Shirley into married life at Four Winds in this Anne novel. Done with teaching geometry, Anne leaves Green Gables garret for a small house of dreams with Gilbert Blythe. Captain Jim, Miss Cornelia, and Leslie Moore, a girl in a sad marriage, fill the harbor town.

Montgomery writes with warmth and wit, mixing joy, loss, and gossip. A first child, a life book, and a ship of dreams mark Anne's new life. The book endures as a tender chapter of Anne's growth, where a young wife learns that dreams hold both light and shadow.
54505-poems:
William Anderson collected his poems for the first time in a volume printed at Edinburgh in 1845. He inscribed the book to his friend Henry Edwards, author of works on piety and intellect. Landscape lyrics open the contents. Sunrise, morning farther advanced, noonday, and a sunbeam lead the day through its hours in verse.

To a wild flower, summer, midsummer, and the sunshine of poetry follow. Autumn in two aspects, sunset, twilight, and moonlight on land and sea round out the landscape set. Anderson warns that the poems must be taken as parts of a whole, distinct only in their subjects. The same measure runs throughout by design, he says, a note that frames the book as one long meditation.
54774-fortunes-and-dreams:
Astra Cielo wrote Fortunes and Dreams, A Practical Manual of Fortune Telling, Divination and the Interpretation of Dreams, Signs and Omens, issued at New York in 1917 by George Sully and Company. A horoscope print heads the book. Parts treat astrology first, with a past review and readings. Tables and lucky days fill that part.

The ancient oracles hold Napoleon's Oraculum and its table. Fortune telling by cards fills the next long part. Suits, symbols, and the sense of each card are set out. Methods named hold the Italian, French, English, Gypsy, and Creole ways. Dice and dominoes get a part too. Palmistry, with the chief lines of the palm and their sense, closes the part shown here. The book is a home guide to popular fortune arts.
54887-beaufort-chums:
Beaufort Chums is a boys adventure novel by Edwin Sabin, published by Crowell in 1905. Charles Copeland supplied the pictures that run through the hosted text of the book. Early chapters promise a June rise of the river and a great lumber fire. A breakwater accident and a camp at Deep Creek follow in the contents.

Turtles, fish, frogs, and snakes fill one chapter of outdoor boy sport. A ghost of the Indian mounds, a county fair, and a campaign parade come next. Trouble at Breede Hill and the routing of Big Mike raise the action. Skating, hunting bags, and river peril keep the chums busy to the end.
54907-the-white-sail-and-other-poems:
The White Sail and Other Poems is a book of verse by Louise Imogen Guiney, out in eighteen eighty-seven. Its first poem lends the book its name. A verse past a famed bard of the past age heads the book, a hail by night past the dead to the live. Parts stand past tales of old, past songs, and past sonnets.

Tale poems tell of a maid of old Rome, of a chief and a beg man, and of a saints bell. Songs sing of youth, of the last faun, of men of the storm, and of dawn. Sonnets treat a spring wish, a rite in a sport hall, and a hail. The name poem sets an old king on a lone rock porch past dusk, his white hair lit past the foam of the surf.
54912-poems:
Julia Dorr wrote these poems, here in a complete edition of her verse. Scribner printed the book in New York in 1892. A portrait of the poet fronts the volume for the reader. An opening sonnet gathers golden rod on hills in August light.

The sonnet weighs June roses against late golden sunshine at feet. Song lives on though summer birds have flown, it closes. A second piece begs the words stand as they were writ. Long love tried by years and showers frames the plea. The lines are set as they were writ in August 1884, the dedication note says plainly.
54948-poems:
S C Mercer gathered his Poems from fifty years of news paper verse. John P Morton and Company issued the book in Louisville in nineteen hundred eight. Mercer had first printed in the Louisville Journal in the late eighteen fifties. George D Prentice, that paper’s famed chief, was his close friend.

Prentice once asked Mercer to help run the great daily sheet. Duty to kin kept Mercer from that fine post, he says. He still wrote leaders and verse for it through long years. The Nashville Press and Times next took his hand in war’s wake. As state printer under two governors he ran that sheet. Partisan songs of the stormy sixties keep their old fire here. One hospital angel poem was claimed for a dead officer. Mercer had printed it first, and tells the tale in plain grief.
55079-poems:
Poems is a selected volume by Theodore Maynard, issued at Toronto with copyrights running from 1917 to 1919. G K Chesterton contributes the introduction, On Theodore Maynard's Poems. The selection is the author's own, made for a permanent collection.

Most of it reprints three British volumes: Laughs and Whifts of Song of 1915, Drums of Defeat of 1917, and Folly of 1918. None had appeared in America before. Chesterton takes A Song of Colours, seen in The New Witness, as his key to the poet. A long dedication poem to Maynard's wife opens the book, dated April 1918. It sings of a love that has waylaid God among buttercups and lilies. Sacraments, a bitter Lenten fast, Gethsemane, and Golgotha mark its road. Magdalen mistaking the risen Lord for the gardener closes the figure.
55086-poems:
Poems by Edward Dowden gathers the verse of a man of letters. The book came out in London and Toronto in the year 1914. Dowden dates most of his poems, and the dates head each piece. The first run of verse comes from his young years of study.

A stroll piece and a spring piece open the book in his youth. In the halls of art he sings of famed forms of stone and paint. Five great dames of myth have a set of their own in the book. Sea pieces, rock pieces, and a song of the new day fill the midst. A child's noon sleep and a peach in the yard stand in the list. The verse is grave, wrought, and full of the old tales of Greece.
55303-winona-a-dakota-legend-and-other-p:
Winona, a Dakota Legend, and Other Poems collects the verse of Captain Huggins. Huggins served in the cavalry of the United States Army. Putnam published the book in New York and London in 1890. The title poem retells a Dakota legend in three parts. A proem introduces it. Miscellaneous poems, translations, and memorial verses follow.

The translations range widely over French verse. Hugo, Gautier, and Musset appear among them. Spanish and Russian pieces join the set. A memorial section is dedicated to the Grand Army of the Republic. It holds verses for Memorial Day and a poem on Abraham Lincoln. Twenty-five sonnets close the volume. An opening excerpt mourns a changed Lake Minnetonka. Electric lights now swarm where Indian camp-fires once flickered.
55507-the-story-of-justin-martyr-and-oth:
The Story of Justin Martyr, and Other Poems, by Richard Chenevix Trench, perpetual curate of Curdridge Chapel in Hampshire, was published in London in 1835 by Moxon. Dedicatory lines open the volume, then the title poem on the early Christian apologist and martyr. Sonnets and short pieces follow, many written on travels: Madeira, Gibraltar, the Rhone, Vesuvius seen from Capri, and Rome.

A legend of the Alhambra, an address to Poland, and lines to the Emperor Nicholas on his conduct toward the Poles show Trench's range. Poems to Silvio Pellico, to a child playing, and to a friend entering the ministry stand beside sea pieces and mountain sonnets. Trench, later Archbishop of Dublin and a famed word scholar, here appears as a young churchman poet of the romantic school.
55963-shepherd-singing-ragtime-and-other:
Shepherd Singing Ragtime and Other Poems is a verse book by Louis Golding, printed in London by Christophers. Golding had issued Sorrow of War and Forward from Babylon before this set. The book is for Jack, killed in France on April the fifth, nineteen eighteen. Twenty seven poems are listed, from Ploughman at the Plough to Courage the Dreamers.

The first poem, Numbers, counts a small farm world in short, plain lines. Three sheep graze under five sycamores while cows munch in twos and fours. Nine and twenty crows croak on an elm, and six owls haunt a cracked house. Fourteen stacks of hay stand guarded by the poet's prayer in the stackyard. His three children play at a table while geraniums glow at the window. War grief and peace run under the farm scenes of the whole book.
56037-sorrow-of-war-poems:
Sorrow of War, a book of poems by Louis Golding, was first published in London in 1919. Golding gives the book to his mother and to the other mother. Some poems had run in journals such as the Nation and the Manchester Guardian. Contents list more than eighty pieces. War titles stand out: Dead in Gallipoli, During the Battle, and Over in Flanders. A Soldier Dying and Wounded Soldiers come late in the list.

The first poem, Lilac and Laburnum, asks how flowers can bloom in spring 1918. Streets of Gold turns Bethnal Green into a vision of pearl and silver. Home front pieces treat women, slums, and statesmen. Later poems move through Kent fields, downs, and still life in France. Grief and stubborn life run side by side.
56060-presidential-problems:
Presidential Problems, by Grover Cleveland, gathers four essays by the president. The Century Company printed the book in New York in October 1904. Two essays began as addresses at Princeton, and two in magazines, the publisher notes.

All four were revised by Cleveland for this book form. The subjects are the independence of the executive and the Chicago strike of 1894. The bond issues and the Venezuelan boundary dispute complete the set. The first essay starts at the birth of the presidency. Cleveland recalls how the thirteen states framed their break with the Crown. The charges against the king ran to eighteen counts of injury and usurpation. A prince so marked, the founders held, is unfit to rule a free people. Against that root, Cleveland tests his defence of the office.
56074-pan-worship-and-other-poems:
Pan Worship and Other Poems is a verse book by Eleanor Farjeon. Elkin Mathews of London issued the collection in nineteen o eight. Farjeon gives the book to her father on the dedication page. Contents run from the title poem through songs, tales, and nature pieces.

The title poem sets a crystal spring in Arcady, ringed with reeds. A worn image of a half forgotten god crumbles on its stone base. Earth tips her cup at the shrine and spills daffodil nectar there. The poet longs for the past and for Pan as he was of old. King Laurin Garden, The Quest, and Dream Ships stand among later pieces.
5616-the-madman-his-parables-and-poems:
Kahlil Gibran wrote The Madman as a book of parables and poems, opening with the story of how he became a madman. One day, long before many gods were born, he woke from deep sleep to find all seven masks he had fashioned and worn in seven lives stolen. Running maskless through crowded streets shouting thieves, he was laughed at, feared, and finally named madman by a youth on a housetop.

When he looked up, the sun kissed his naked face for the first time, and he felt freed rather than shamed. The parables that follow speak in that freed voice, about gods, men, love, and sorrow. Readers get Gibran's early masterpiece in miniature: short, lyrical pieces that read like proverbs.
56228-poems:
Cora C Bass, who also wrote as Harley Vane, issued a book called Poems at Lowell, Massachusetts, in eighteen ninety nine. Lawler and Company printed the book on Central Street. Bass thanks journals such as The New York Observer, The Churchman, and the Boston Transcript for leave to reprint verse. Some seventy short poems fill the volume. Faith, nature, war, and home run through the list.

Titles include The Sweetest Songs, Sea and Cliff, The March of Time, and A Gift. War verse includes He Lies in State, Dead on the Field of Battle, and a Memorial Poem. Place verse treats Bunker Hill, Kearsarge, and the spot where Passaconaway was wont to stand. The first poem holds that the sweetest songs are left unsung and the sweetest themes unread. Bass writes in a plain, earnest voice for home and church readers of her day.
56418-new-york-nocturnes-and-other-poems:
Charles Roberts published this book of poems with Lamson, Wolffe and Company at Boston, New York, and London in 1898. It follows Orion and Other Poems, In Divers Tones, and Songs of the Common Day. The first part, New York Nocturnes, opens with The Ideal, a poem to a woman whose cool white fingers on the poet's face stilled the city's clamour.

Seventeen nocturnes follow her through the city at night. The list includes In the Crowd, Night in a Down-town Street, At the Railway Station, Twilight on Sixth Avenue, The Street Lamps, and A Nocturne of Exile. In the crowd poem the night is loud and the pavements roar, yet the crowd only brings her closer, and he hears only her low replies. The Other Poems section turns outward to The Atlantic Cable, The Solitary Woodsman, The Hermit, Ice, and the falling leaves.
57492-engraved-gems:
Maxwell Sommerville wrote a short book on cut gems through the ages. The book came out in Philadelphia and London in 1901. Sommerville taught gem lore at the University of Pennsylvania. He wrote Sands of Sahara and a book on Siam. His past big work on gems was too large for most hands, he says.

He cut that work down and added fresh stuff for this book. Each age of gem cut is traced from first to last in it. Stones, tools, and great gems of fame fill the pages in turn. Kings, priests, and rich men wore such work in all ages. Art and past fans share the worth of his store. Plates show the gems' fine faces.
57676-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Project Gutenberg Index of the Works of Samuel Hopkins Adams is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. Samuel Hopkins Adams was an American novelist and muckraking journalist. The index gathers the contents of his books as issued in the Gutenberg collection.

Titles listed include The Unspeakable Perk, Average Jones, The Mystery, and The Clarion. The Great American Fraud, his famous exposure of patent medicines, stands among them. Wanted: A Husband, Common Cause, and The Health Master also appear. For each work the index prints the table of contents, chapter by chapter. A reader can thus survey a whole shelf of one author's books in a single file. The index is a reader's tool, plain and useful, for finding one's way among linked electronic editions.
57720-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of George R Sims is a finding list compiled by David Widger. It gathers the tables of contents of Sims's books held by Project Gutenberg. The works indexed include Rogues and Vagabonds, The Mysteries of Modern London, and How the Poor Live and Horrible London.

For Rogues and Vagabonds, printed in 1892, the chapter list runs from the wreck of the Bon Espoir to a burglary at the hall. Characters named include Topsey Turvey, who sees a ghost, and Mr Edward Marston, who meets an old friend. Later chapters tell of a forged cheque and of Gertie Heckett, a kind lady, a good dog, and a wicked bird. A critique of socialism stands among the contents as well. The index is a reader's map to Sims's tales of London rogues and London poor. Widger compiled many such guides to authors in the Gutenberg library.
57937-the-dread-voyage-poems:
The Dread Voyage is a book of poems by William Wilfred Campbell, a Canadian poet, published at Toronto by William Briggs. Campbell had won his name with Lake Lyrics. The title poem sets a fated bark sailing past iron hail and thunder. Its crew pass the mystery and the wonder, and the moaning of lost voices. Nature poems fill much of the book. The lake country of Ontario is their ground. Winter, harvest, and the turn of the year give them their themes.

How One Winter Came in the Lake Region and Midwinter Storm in the Lake Region stand in the list. The Were-Wolves brings a darker folk note. A poem to mighty death speaks of Robert Browning, and The Dead Leader mourns a chief. Campbell sings the lakes as a man who lived by them. His verse is plain, strong, and full of weather.
58233-a-surgeon-in-arms:
Manion, a cure man with the Canadian Army, told his war tale in brief. His book came out in New York and London in 1918. A front plate shows Manion with his war cross won. He gave the book to his wife and boys with love. Life in the trenches starts his tale of the line.

Over the top, a march by land, and a man named Kelly come next. The talk of the line and a look round fill the mid parts. Gas, rest, dugouts, and the sick line show a cure man's day. Care of the hurt and cheer in dark times mark his view. Vimy Ridge and a trip to Arras crown the war parts. Plain, warm prose rules it.
59096-the-seven-streams:
Warwick Deeping wrote The Seven Streams, a dream romance given to his dear sister Kathleen, issued by Cassell and Company in MCMXI. Deeping had earlier written The Rust of Rome and Uther and Igraine. Spenser and Shakespeare lines on sleep and dreams head the book. Chapter one opens on a knight vigil. Tristan le Sauvage is the hero.

For a night and a day Tristan watched his arms before the high altar of the chapel of Purple Isle. Long tapers glimmered towards their silver sockets under the painted roof. Dawn and evening light dusted the stones with colour, the tale says. Not a sound broke the silence of the tombs. Two months past, a great ship with gleaming sails had swooped like a falcon on Purple Isle. It carried thence Columbe the Fair, a white dove. A quest beyond the sea follows in lush romance prose.
59167-poems:
Edna St Vincent Millay wrote the Poems gathered in a London volume of verse. Martin Secker issued the book in nineteen hundred twenty three. Renascence, her famed long lyric, leads the whole set of songs. Sonnets and short lyrics fill three parts of the slim book.

Three long mountains and a wood bound the girl’s world in Renascence. Three islands in a bay meet her turned eyes in the next lines. God’s World and Afternoon on a Hill sing the joy of free hills. Witch-wife, Blight, and The Little Ghost turn to darker strains here. Recuerdo recalls a night of ferry rides and fruit at dawn. Thursday and Portrait by a Neighbour show her dry light wit. Travel longs for the train that takes the world each day. Wild Swans and an Ode to Silence close the last pages in song.
59198-the-seven-conundrums:
Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Seven Conundrums, for McClelland and Stewart at Toronto in 1923. Wallace Morgan drew the pictures, and the book came out in February. A front plate shows a woman whispering over a rose. They will know from whom that rose comes, she says in the caption. An opening piece called The Compact sets the frame for the tales.

Seven numbered puzzles follow, each with its own title. The stolen minute book and what happened at Bath come first. The spider's parlour and the courtship of Naida fill the middle. A tragedy at Greymarshes and a duke's dilemma come next. The greatest argument closes the set as the seventh conundrum. Performers shorn of their mummer's disguise make a melancholy spectacle in one tale. Oppenheim gives mystery in short, neat doses.
592-the-chinese-nightingale-and-other-po:
Vachel Lindsay gathers chanting poems of America at war and at peace in this volume, dedicated to Sara Teasdale. The title poem, which won the Levinson Prize in Poetry magazine for 1915, tells of a Chinese nightingale in musical, painted lines. Later sections watch the war from August 1914 to April 1917, then America at war.

Lindsay writes in strong, singing rhythms meant for voice, with prairie, flag, and factory in his sights. Poems on Bryan, Jane Addams, Mark Twain, and Joan of Arc mix politics with fancy. The book shows Lindsay as a people's poet, eager to sing a nation through hard years.
59214-the-world-of-dreams:
Havelock Ellis wrote this study of dreams, printed by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1922. Ellis, known for The Soul of Spain and other wide-ranging books, asks whether dreams can be studied at all and how error creeps in. He asks if we dream through all of sleep, and he sorts the sources of dreams into two main kinds with their branches.

Later chapters take up the stuff of dream life: images that flow and fuse, colour, words that shift shape, and the push of the senses. Smell, taste, touch, sound, and the inner organs all leave marks on dreams, as do love and fear. The book is a calm survey by a keen watcher of the mind.
5953-many-kingdoms:
Elizabeth Jordan's Many Kingdoms opens with children, imagination, and a kingdom of the mind, under an epigraph comparing the state of man to a little kingdom suffering nature's insurrections. Margaret Hamilton Perry listens remotely as Raymond Mortimer explains that a little girl comes to play, seen by no one but him, and Margaret answers candidly that pretending seems little fun. With delicacy, she adds that she will like the girl and play with her if Raymond does.

The story follows a novel of inner kingdoms, where childhood fancy, adult feeling, and social life contend for rule. Jordan, author of May Iverson and Tales of the Cloister, writes with sympathy for imagined companions and real loneliness. The book suits readers who enjoy novels of childhood imagination grown serious, and stories where a private kingdom shapes a public life.
59603-three-stories-ten-poems:
Ernest Hemingway's Three Stories and Ten Poems was published by the Contact Publishing Company with copyright in nineteen twenty-three held by the author. The dedication is short. The book is for Hadley. Five of the poems had first been printed in Poetry, a magazine of verse, and the contents name the whole of this small first book.

The stories are Up in Michigan, Out of Season, and My Old Man. The poems carry war and expatriate titles like Mitraigliatrice, Champs d'Honneur, Riparto d'Assalto, Montparnasse, and Along With Youth. Up in Michigan starts in Hortons Bay, where Jim Gilmore, a Canadian blacksmith with big hands and big mustaches, notices Liz Coates, the neat girl who works at the Smiths' house.
59642-old-days-at-beverly-farms:
Mary Larcom Dow wrote these memories of Beverly Farms, on the Massachusetts shore, in her old age. The North Shore Printing Company of Beverly issued the book in 1921. Katharine Loring held the rights and saw the work into print.

A sketch of Dow's life opens the volume, by another hand. For sixty years, a friend says, she led the real life of the place. Her own Old Days follows, then a memory of Lucy Larcom, her famed kin. Letters by Dow and praise by Sarah Miller fill the back. Lines from friends' letters close the book. A warm, small town keeps its past in one woman's mind here.
59897-new-poems:
Charles G D Roberts wrote the New Poems gathered in a London book. Constable and Company issued the first edition in nineteen hundred nineteen. Roberts sang for Canada, his home land across the wide sea. War verse and hill songs share the slim new volume here.

His first poem speaks to Shakespeare in the war year nineteen hundred sixteen. White wrath must shake the bard’s bones at the foe’s foul deeds, he cries. Lusitania’s slain and Malines’ wrongs stain the foe’s name in it. Yet kin feet tramp from earth’s ends to right the wrong, he trusts. The Unknown City dreams of a place no grief or war can reach. Hill Top Songs and valley airs of Luchon turn to peace and heights. Cambrai and Marne close the war strand of the book in song. Earth sufficing all our needs sounds his deep ground note.
59999-argentina-and-her-people-of-to-day:
Argentina and Her People of To-Day, by Nevin Winter, was published in Boston in 1911. Winter wrote matching books on Mexico, Guatemala, and Brazil. The subtitle promises an account of the customs, character, amusements, history, and progress of the Argentinians, and of the growth and wealth of their country. Photographs, many by the author, fill the book.

Contents move from the country at large to Buenos Aires, called the metropolis of the southern hemisphere. Chapters then cross the camp, the River of Silver, and the garden of the republic. Later parts treat the people at play, schooling and the arts, the armed forces, and railroads. Winter wrote for American readers at a moment when Argentina's farms and ports drew world notice.
60003-negro-poets-and-their-poems:
Negro Poets and Their Poems is an anthology and study by Robert Kerlin. Associated Publishers of Washington issued it with rights in 1923. A front plate reproduces Emancipation, a sculpture by Meta Warrick Fuller. Kerlin also wrote The Voice of the Negro before this survey. He dedicates it to the Black and unknown bards of the plantations.

Those bards gave the world the spirituals, canticles of love and woe. Their lullabies entered the souls of Poe, Lanier, Dunbar, and Cotter. Contents open with the present day Negro heritage of song in chapter one. Untaught melodies, the spirituals, and the seculars fill its first heads. Dunbar, Braithwaite, and the younger poets get their chapters after.
60108-the-legend-of-the-blemished-king-a:
The Legend of the Blemished King, and Other Poems is a small volume of verse, issued in Dublin. Its opening pages are filled with the publisher's matter for The Little Library, a series of small books meant to make Dublin a book-producing place. A few copies remaining, the heading warns.

The notices quote the press on the series' first volume, Idylls by Laura Jean Douglas. The Moderator calls it some of the most exquisite prose read for many a day. The Irish News of Belfast finds in the ten idylls a group of the sweetest prose poetry possible, a gallery of lovely pictures. The Irish Figaro thanks all who work in a sincere spirit at the task of making Dublin produce books. The Irish Daily Independent calls the volume beautifully produced and a credit to Dublin. Such praise pages sold the books.
60142-hymns-and-poems:
A lady who wrote as A L O E sent out this book of hymns and poems through Nelson in 1868. She had written The Triumph over Midian and Rescued from Egypt. Her initials stand for A Lady of England, as her readers knew.

The Willing Sacrifice opens the hymns, then the Resurrection and a hymn for Communion. The Beacon, the Blossoming Rod, and a hymn for the penitent convict follow. A hymn for the blind, the Sexton's Hymn, and the Second Advent fill the early list. A Soldier's Hymn stands among them. Plain faith in verse, made for singing and for quiet hours, marks the whole set.
60237-poems:
Poems by Clive Bell came from the Hogarth Press in 1921. Leonard and Virginia Woolf printed the slim book at Richmond. A short contents list holds some twenty poems in the volume. The Card House stands first, a tale of a house of cards. Letters to a lady in verse open and close the set's frame.

Month poems for March, April, June, October, and December mark the year. A poem To Lopokova Dancing shows the ballet love of that circle. Spring, Reply to Mrs Jowitt, and a self-address fill the mid list. One card house tale sets the tone of the whole small book. Its builder piles card on card with pride and high delight. A shout, or a too-bold fling, brings the whole pile down flat.
6025-the-englishman-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers poems headed by The Queen's Last Ride, written on the day of Queen Victoria's funeral. The Queen takes a drive with the carriage way hung in purple, army and navy leading, kings and princes riding behind as a humble band, and flags of all nations at half-mast.

The silent lady of royal birth rides away from earth's courts and unrest toward a mystical goal on a secret quest. Wilcox writes in plain, musical verse, fond of direct feeling and large occasions. The collection moves from royal mourning to other English themes, with sentiment worn openly.
60252-advice-a-book-of-poems:
Advice is a book of poems by Maxwell Bodenheim, printed by Alfred Knopf at New York in 1920. Bodenheim dedicates it to Minna, whose smile is his throne. Some of the poems had appeared in the Yale Review, the Dial, the Little Review, Poetry, and other journals of the day.

The contents run as a list of counsels. Advice is given to a street-pavement, a buttercup, a river steamboat, a horned toad, a forest, a bluebird, a butterfly, and a pool. Two Rattlesnake Mountain fables and a set of foundry workers stand among them. A poem to a woman and one to a friend vary the address. Bodenheim was a sharp voice of the Chicago and New York little-magazine world. The book is his wry, image-dense manner in a slim first gathering.
60504-a-naughty-biography-and-other-poem:
A-Naughty-Biography, and Other Poems is a book of verse printed at Cincinnati by Robert Clarke and Company in 1878. Its author signs herself as the wife of Enoch Taylor, and dedicates the book to My Dear Five Hundred. The title poem tells her own life in rhyme, in parts named My Infancy, School Life, and Girlhood, ending with a Good-Bye-ography.

The mixed poems that follow run with the seasons and the heart. Titles include The Village Belle, The Rainy Day, Autumn, and October. She Sleeps Beneath the Roses, Found Drowned, and Our Baby stand beside lighter pieces like The Song of the Slush. An appeal for the Memphis orphans and verses on Washington's birthday close the home-made volume.
6061-some-poems:
This small volume adds a few poems by Sir Walter Scott to a larger collection, since room remained for more verses. The introduction notes the first was written in 1811 during the struggle with Napoleon in the Peninsula, and the second in 1815, after Waterloo.

The contents list The Vision of Don Roderick, The Field of Waterloo, The Dance of Death, Romance of Dunois, The Troubadour, and Pibroch of Donald Dhu. Over all hangs a thin haze of battle, through which only finer feelings and nobler hopes show. Scott's war poems look toward a day when war shall be no more.
6062-pike-county-ballads-and-other-poems:
John Hay's Pike County Ballads lead this collection, with Jim Bludso, Little Breeches, Banty Tim, the Mystery of Gilgal, and the Pledge at Spunky Point. An introduction by Henry Morley frames the poems, which mix western humor with river and prairie voices.

Wanderlieder follow, from sunrise in the Place de la Concorde and the Sphinx of the Tuileries to the curse of Hungary and the monks of Basle. Later pieces include Miles Keogh's Horse, the Advance-Guard, a haunted room, and songs of liberty, remorse, and homecoming. Hay writes with vigor and plain feeling.
6121-jack-winters-gridiron-chums:
Mark Overton opens Jack Winters' Gridiron Chums with grueling football practice. A shrill whistle halts almost two dozen sturdy boys in their middle teens, clad in old and new football togs and struggling furiously. The coach, acting as referee in practice, stops the commotion as if by magic.

Chapters follow a boy in trouble, Big Bob confessing, a friend in need, a message from Marshall, and Jack and Joel investigating. The great game opens, struggle fills the gridiron, and glory follows, before bed fire burns in Chester and a burning house tests the chums. Overton praises team play on and off the field.
61286-selected-poems:
Selected Poems gathers the best-known verse of John Masefield from across his books, in the Heinemann edition printed in London. The choices open with the sea songs of Salt Water Ballads, among them Trade Winds and Sea-Fever, and go on to Cargoes from Poems and Ballads. Long narrative work stands beside the lyrics, and the poet's wife receives the dedication.

Later sections draw on The Everlasting Mercy, The Widow in the Bye Street, Dauber, The Daffodil Fields, Gallipoli, Reynard the Fox, Right Royal, and the plays in verse. There are sonnets, a poem dated August 1914, and the meditations on growing old from Enslaved. The selection shows why Masefield's plain music and salt-water subjects made him one of the most widely read English poets of his generation.
61440-shylock-reasons-with-mr-chesterton:
Humbert Wolfe wrote Shylock Reasons with Mr Chesterton and Other Poems, a book of verse put out at Oxford in 1920. Wolfe had won a name with a set of London sonnets. Some of these poems had run in the Saturday Review and in two church town sheets. He gives the book to a loved one, with thanks for her laugh.

The poems split into two groups with sly names that mean self and not self. Shylock leads, in talks on Judas, sin, and the pound of flesh in the old play. Pheidias, Paul, Caesar, and the first man to fly get a poem each. Short tomb verse honors Edith Cavell and a child who sleeps. France, the skies, the wind, and a room in Bohemia fill the back. Wolfe writes with wit, faith, and a sharp eye for fame.
617-poems:
Alan Seeger gathers his short life's verse in this volume, with an introduction by William Archer. Juvenilia, sonnets, Paris poems, and translations from Dante and Ariosto fill the early pages. Last poems from the Aisne and Champagne in 1914-15 close the book, including I Have a Rendezvous with Death.

Seeger, an American poet killed in France on 4 July 1916, writes in polished, romantic lines, full of beauty, youth, and fate. His war poems face death with grave acceptance, not swagger. The volume endures as a poignant record of a young poet who kept his rendezvous.
62961-the-tyranny-of-shams:
The Tyranny of Shams is a book of social criticism by Joseph McCabe, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1916. McCabe calls it a frank criticism of most of the dominant ideas and institutions of his time. He also calls it a confession of faith in daring heresies.

The preface explains the book's making. It was conceived, and much of it written, on the long voyage from Australia to England. Readers of McCabe's earlier books on stars, dinosaurs, and ancient empresses had asked him for light on the problems of the hour. His answer sketches a new social order and even a new planetary arrangement. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
63155-the-white-comrade-and-other-poems:
The White Comrade and Other Poems is a verse volume by Katherine Hale of Toronto. McClelland, Goodchild and Stewart published it in Canada in 1916. Dorothy Stevens designed the cover. Hale had written Grey Knitting before it. The title poem speaks in the voice of a Canadian soldier wounded at Ypres. He marvels at green England, the land of his youthful dreams.

He and one comrade survive of three who started out together. Edward fell in the wood at Saint Julien. The two survivors keep watch for a shared knowledge in others' eyes. In the fields of France, some of them heard a rumour and saw a Form. That form is the White Comrade of the title. Other poems treat mothers' hearts, the soul of the earth, and departure. The book is a Canadian voice of the Great War.
6332-playful-poems:
Henry Morley edits this volume of Companion Poets, with an introduction, gathering playful poems from Chaucer to Hood. Chaucer's Manciple's tale of Phoebus and the crow, modernised by Leigh Hunt, opens, with Sir Thopas, the Friar's tale of summoner and devil, and the Reeve's tale. Wordsworth modernises the Cuckoo and the Nightingale, Gower gives treasure trove, and Lydgate, Dunbar, and Drayton follow.

Pope's Rape of the Lock, Cowper's John Gilpin, and Burns's Tam o'Shanter carry the fun forward. Hood's demon ship and tale of a trumpet follow, with a note on ombre and a glossary to close. Morley, emeritus professor at University College London, presents old humour in modern dress, so that readers can enjoy it without a scholar's apparatus. The 1891 book is light verse with a learned frame.
63399-the-glebe-1914-09-vol-2-no-2-poems:
The Glebe was a monthly magazine that gave each issue to a single writer. This number, volume two, number two, came out in September 1914 at fifty cents. The poems in it are by George Cronyn, and his work fills the whole issue.

The editors state one rule: full freedom of speech for all who write for them. Work may run from the most radical to the most staid, so long as it has clear merit. Twelve such books a year made the plan. A set fee from subscribers freed the Glebe from chasing the crowd. Readers got one poet in bulk, enough verse to grasp the man whole, not in scraps.
64030-my-valued-ruby-poems:
My Valued Ruby is a book of poems by Perry Honce McGee. It came out in a small town in the year 1920. A shot of the poet and a shot of his wife stand at the front. He gives the book to his race, in love and in hope.

The poems are short and plain, on love, faith, and the day's work. A rose that droops, a town hall meal, and a cold dawn start the run. His wife, his dark days, and his strength as a poet get songs of their own. Songs of a sailor, of fate, and of a broke heart fill the midst. One song looks to a star of a far land as a sign of hope. The book is the work of a self-taught voice of his town and time.
64148-saga-of-the-oak-and-other-poems:
Saga of the Oak and Other Poems, by William Venable, was published at New York in 1904. Dodd, Mead and Company issued it with copyrights from 1884 and 1893 in the front. A portrait of the poet fronts the volume as its first plate. The title poem opens the contents at page one of the book.

A Diamond, My Catbird, and the tunes Dan Harrison used to play follow in the list. Fairyland, summer love, and Clover Hill fill the lyric part of the contents. The wedding deferred and a poem to the Little Miami river come next in the roll. Johnny Appleseed gets a long poem of his own near the end of the book. Ohio rivers, founders, and folk heroes share this volume with love songs and nature verse.
64318-april-twilights-and-other-poems:
Willa Cather's April Twilights and Other Poems was published by Alfred A Knopf at New York in 1923. Cather dedicated the book to her father for a valentine. The first part reprints her early volume April Twilights of 1903 entire. The second part holds later poems, reprinted from Scribner's Magazine, McClure's, and the Century. A front list names her novels to date, from Alexander's Bridge to A Lost Lady in preparation.

The poems of the first part open with Grandmither, Think Not I Forget, in dialect. Fides, Spes, The Tavern, and The Hawthorn Tree follow. Antinous, London Roses, and Winter at Delphi show the young poet's classical bent. The later poems turn home: Prairie Dawn, Prairie Spring, and Macon Prairie. Spanish Johnny and Street in Packingtown stand among them.
64408-hours-of-childhood-and-other-poems:
Hours of Childhood and Other Poems is a small volume of verse published at Montreal in 1820. Bowman issued the book in August of that year, as its illustration page states. A motto from Kirke White claims the night for the poet in its lines. The day has duties requiring the vigorous hand of steadfast application, the motto allows.

 Let the day be another, let it pass, the lines conclude: the night is my own. The preface owns that few authors are indifferent to the stamp their writings bear in public minds. The volume is among the earliest books of poems printed in Canada for a local author. Its verses of childhood and the night belong to the first thin shelf of Canadian poetry, printed when Montreal had scarcely a reading public to buy it.
64415-mind-worms:
Mind Worms is a short tale of a ship's crew in the grip of fear. Moses Schere wrote it for a pulp book of the spring of 1948. Its hook asks what force could drive a crew mad in space. Such a force glows soft in the black and twists as it waits.

The tale opens on a man of state at the end of a long talk. A world of folk saw his last bow and roared their luck cries. His screen on the ship Ceres then goes blank at his back. The wire man, a good hand, shakes as he works the beam to Earth. The man of state has more cause for fear than the young hand. His talk with the heads of Earth is cut short in mid breath. What waits out there turns the proud ship's calm to ice.
64454-illuminated-illustrations-of-frois:
Illuminated Illustrations of Froissart gathers plates chosen from the manuscript Froissart in the Royal Library at Paris and other sources. The book was put out in London in 1845 by Humphreys. A plate list keys each picture to volume and page in Smith's two-volume Froissart. Old English lettering in the source is marked for the reader.

Subjects run from Queen Isabella's voyage to England and the coronation of Edward the Third to battles, funerals, and sieges. Froissart himself sits in his study in one plate. Other plates show Philip van Artevelde haranguing the people and a combat between Nicholas Clifford and a French knight. The book lets Victorian readers see medieval war and court life in medieval art.
64545-marguerite-or-the-isle-of-demons-a:
Marguerite, or the Isle of Demons, and Other Poems is a verse book by George Martin. Dawson Brothers of Montreal issued the volume in eighteen eighty seven. Martin gives the book to his wife in a warm dedication page. The poems were written at sundry times in a busy life, he says.

Most shorter poems ran first in Canadian journals before this gathering. Some hold the local hue of the city where they were made. Marguerite is the newest poem and appears here for the first time. Martin says the verse draws on the history and scenery of Canada. He hopes to fix in lasting form aspects that are peculiar to that land.
65068-terrible-tractoration-and-other-po:
Terrible Tractoration is a satirical poem by Fessenden, under the name Christopher Caustic. The third American edition came out at Boston in 1836. Its mock titles fill the title page with honours. The preface tells the poem's strange origin. In 1801 the author met Perkins in London. Perkins sold patent Metallic Tractors. Those tools were said to draw sickness from the body. Electric fluid was the theory behind the cure.

The poem mocks that quack cure in verse. Stripping folly of its disguises is its stated aim. It first ran as a short newspaper piece. A pamphlet of fifty pages followed in 1803. A second edition was called for within two months. The satire made Fessenden's name in his day. It stands as an early American hit at medical humbug.
651-phantasmagoria-and-other-poems:
Lewis Carroll gathers his comic and serious verse in this volume, first published in 1869 and reprinted by Macmillan in 1911 with illustrations by Arthur B. Frost. Phantasmagoria, in seven cantos, tells of a man who finds a ghost in his study one winter night, cold, tired, and cross, and learns the ghost's five rules. Echoes, A Sea Dirge, Hiawatha's Photographing, and The Three Voices follow.

Carroll writes with logic games, parody, and sudden tenderness, dedicating the book to a dear child and golden summer hours. The poems show the Alice author's other side: a wit who could rhyme a ghost into manners. The volume charms as a varied Carroll set, where nonsense and feeling sit side by side.
65347-i-ll-see-you-in-my-dreams:
William Campbell Gault wrote I'll See You in My Dreams, a tale printed in Imagination in September nineteen fifty-one. A head note teases that Ted loves his wife, yet a blonde next door keeps entering his dreams. The tale opens among bodiless minds in talk.

Two minds, El and Bee, speak in outer-thought and inner-thought. Their bodies went when Lust was killed, and they judge that a mistake. They miss colours they cannot see and streams they cannot hear. The Assembly meets in a glade it cannot sense. Bee raises new business that may be mutiny. Peak agrees to listen, so long as Valdora is left out. Talk turns to raising a minor god who grew major.
65357-ismael-an-oriental-tale-with-other:
Ismael is an east tale in verse by Bulwer, in the first flush of the great novel pen he would grow to be. He wrote it, the title page owns, between the age of thirteen and fifteen. A row of more poems stands with it.

It came out at London in eighteen twenty, from a shop in a famed row. A Latin tag at its head, from an old bard, owns that the taught and the untaught alike write poems at large. His word at the front takes up the theme of fame. Craft and a thirst for fame are kin by birth, it holds. The young rover may then be let to seek a good name by the spread of his work, and the book goes out on that plea.
65367-guide-to-fortune-telling-by-dreams:
Courtney of Boston issued this dream book as number ten of the Multum in Parvo Library in October 1894. It calls itself the smallest magazine in the world. Fifty cents a year, or five cents a copy, bought it at 671 Tremont Street.

Oneirology, the science of foretelling future events by dreams, heads the text. Since the world began, it says, coming events have cast shadows before. Many great turns of our lives are shown us in dreams, if only we grasped their sense. A pleasant dream almost always means good health, wins, and fair luck; an evil one warns of ill health and trouble. Abuse begins the list: to dream you are insulted means a dispute with some person. A pocket oracle of the old sort.
65574-the-freeman-and-other-poems:
The Freeman and Other Poems is a volume of verse by Ellen Glasgow, published by Doubleday, Page and Company of New York in 1902. Glasgow dedicated the book to Louise Collier Willcox. The long title poem carries a hard motto: hope is a slave, and despair is a freeman.

Around that title poem stand shorter pieces: A Creed, The Traveller, and A Battle Cry. Others include The Vision of Hell, To My Dog, and England's Greatness. A closing piece is addressed to Mary. The poems treat faith, loss, pride, and freedom in a formal, late-Romantic voice. Glasgow became famous as a novelist of the American South. Her early verse shows the same stern interest in character under pressure. This slim book preserves the poetic start of a major fiction career.
65583-new-brooms:
New Brooms is a book of light essays by Robert Shores, issued at Indianapolis in 1913. Its contents open with a philosophical cook. A bachelor on women and a piece on pensioning writers follow close behind. A puritan in bohemia and an attack on originality fill the early list, in the droll manner of the whole.

A flattering tribute, the riddle of a dream, and beds for the bad come next in the contents. Is Chesterton a man alive, one essay asks in jest. Letters from stock figures follow: a hunchback, a hotel sponge, and women with punning names. Clothes and the soul, a protesting mister body, and a piece on fashion writers' airs carry the middle. The literary life and poetic licence close the visible heads.
6568-sociology-and-modern-social-problem:
Charles A. Ellwood, a professor at the University of Missouri, wrote this short text for classes that had little time for sociology. The first eight chapters lay out its basic ideas through the family, seen as a typical human group, with its growth, shape, and work. Later chapters turn those ideas on live problems of his day, side by side with lessons from economics.

Ellwood teaches by cases, not by dry rules, and aims at readers in extension courses and teachers' reading circles as much as at college students. The book is plain, orderly, and meant to be used, not just read. It offers a clear, early view of how a new science tried to make sense of modern social life.
65908-illuminated-illustrations-of-frois:
Humphreys chose these lit pictures from Froissart Chronicles in the British Museum. William Smith printed the book in London in 1844. A front note says this volume ends the Museum manuscript set. Those books hold only the Fourth Book of Froissart history.

Subscribers urged a matching set from the first three books in Paris. The Paris manuscript drawings are finer in many respects, it says. Twelve more numbers were planned at three shillings sixpence each in price. The set grew from strong sales of Monstrelet and Froissart reprints. Color plates copy the manuscript art with great care and skill.
66000-selected-poems:
Selected Poems, by Aldous Huxley, is a gathering of his early verse in one volume. Appleton printed the book in New York in 1925, though it was made in Great Britain. Some fifty poems stand in the contents, from Song of Poplars to Return to an Old Home.

The titles map a young poet's range: nature pieces like The Reef, The Flowers, and The Elms. Town and mood get theirs in On the Bus, Panic, and Perils of the Small Hours. Minoan Porcelain and a faun's afternoon show the classical strain. The opening Song of Poplars bids a shepherd tune his flute to the tall trees. It asks whether their spears lift toward sorrow or toward joy. Do they seek a name, or only an upward ache of undefined desire? The questions hang unanswered as the trees rustle on.
66002-an-epic-of-women-and-other-poems:
An Epic of Women and Other Poems is a poetry book by Arthur W E O'Shaughnessy, printed at London in 1870. He dedicates the book to his friend John Payne. The contents open with Exile, where the poet walks among a common folk and speaks dull things in their tongue. All the while within he hears a song he does not sing for fear.

When he comes where none are near, he opens all his heart and sings. The poems include Three Flowers of Modern Greece, Bisclavaret, and The Story of the King. The epic itself runs through Creation, the Wife of Hephaestus, Cleopatra, the Daughter of Herodias, and Helen. Later pieces are named The Fountain of Tears, Love After Death, and The Poet's Grave. One poem asks whether, in praising others with his voice, the poet does not celebrate his own secret heart.
66080-a-life-s-story-in-poetry-other-poe:
Dennison Woodcock wrote A Life's Story in Poetry and Other Poems at Wrights, Pennsylvania, at the age of ninety one, printed at Port Allegany in 1908 by Chas O Laymon. The lead poem is named A Life's Story, From One to Ninety One. Woodcock looks back down a long life in verse. Joy and grief, smiles and tears mark the years, he says.

As a child he asked his brother what made the wind blow. His brother said the slim, lofty trees made it by waving to and fro. The boy took the pines as full proof and bore a grudge against them in snow. A mill saw that rose and fell as water ran stayed a mystery too. He rigged a stick and saw on a creek to test the theme and failed. Plain verse in rhyme tells a farm boy's growth to old age.
6623-the-coming-of-the-princess-and-othe:
Kate Seymour MacLean of Kingston, Ontario, gathers her poems in a volume introduced by G. Mercer Adam, editor of The Canadian Monthly. Adam, who had often printed her verse, acts as foster father to the book, and bespeaks a kind welcome from Canadian readers. He calls her a child of the first winds and suns of a young nation.

The title poem on a princess's coming leads a set of lyrics on home, land, and feeling, in the clear style of her day. MacLean writes with a Canadian eye and a gentle hand. The Coming of the Princess is a pleasant, early Canadian poetry book, worth a look for lovers of Dominion verse.
66520-poems:
Poems by Lionel Johnson is the poet's first book, issued in 1895. Elkin Mathews published it in London, Copeland and Day in Boston. The edition was limited to seven hundred and fifty copies. A Latin tribute to Winchester College fronts the book. Johnson was schooled there and at Oxford. The contents open with Winchester and Morfydd. Poems on Ireland, Wales, and the Church follow.

Parnell, war, and dead friends fill many pages. The Dark Angel is the book's most famed piece. Saints, cardinals, and Oxford woods all appear. Johnson wrote in a high, musical, sombre style. He belonged to the Rhymers' Club of the nineties. His friendship with Yeats is part of his tale. This slim volume holds his early best.
66583-the-magic-of-jewels-and-charms:
George Frederick Kunz wrote on the magic of jewels and charms, printed at Philadelphia and London with ninety pictures in color and line. A Hindu lady in the jewelry of north India fronts the book. A jade bell of the K'ien Lung period stands among the color plates, with an emerald that was a deposed sultan's. Kunz had spent twenty five years collecting the lore of precious stones, his companion volume shows.

Sentiments and folklore of gems, their use in protection and healing, in religion and fortune telling, fill the pages. Crystal gazing, birth stones, lucky stones, and talismans take their turns. Astral, zodiacal, and planetary ties are set out stone by stone. Gem lovers and the curious get a rich store of tales pinned to real stones by a great gem expert.
66892-the-pacifist-and-other-poems:
The Pacifist and Other Poems is a verse collection by Howard Futhey Brinton, published by the Gorham Press at Boston in 1918. Its title poem profiles Ben, an American type through and through, as the tocsin of war sounds in the land.

The contents mix character sketches and local pieces: Adam's Apple, Mac's Psychologic Cigar, the Poor Man's Club, a poem on Gungha Din, Barney, and the Mother. Jumbo's Dream, the Blues, the Man About Town, Elk Creek, Murphy's Purchase, the Legend of Deborah's Rock, and the Gangster follow. A final poem waits for when Ty Cobb comes to town. Ben, in the title poem, carries Celt fire and Saxon strength, shot up the town and sowed wild oats in youth, yet has a heart like an ox and muscles like steel.
67012-the-man-with-the-hoe-and-other-poe:
The Man with the Hoe and Other Poems is a verse book by Edwin Markham, printed at New York in 1899. Markham gave the book to Edmund Clarence Stedman, the first to hail and caution him. Many of the poems had first run in Scribner's, The Century, The Atlantic, and the San Francisco Examiner.

The title poem shows a farm worker bowed by the weight of ages, leaning on his hoe and gazing at the ground. Markham asks who made him dead to hope, a brother to the ox. Around it stand poems on brotherhood, toil, the hills, and dawn, mixing pity for the poor with a strong faith in man's worth.
67791-marlborough-and-other-poems:
Marlborough and Other Poems, by Charles Hamilton Sorley, was published at Cambridge in 1916. Sorley had been a captain in the Suffolk Regiment when he fell in the war. He was late of Marlborough College, as the title page records of him. The book reached a third edition by October 1916, enlarged with prose pieces.

A front note dated September 1916 hears a voice singing across the sea. That song is of Marlborough and the Odyssey in the poem that follows. Sorley fell at Loos in 1915, leaving these poems behind him at twenty. School, marching, and death in France fill the verses of the collection. War poetry by a soldier poet cut down young gives the book its lasting fame.
679-poems:
Frances E. W. Harper gathered her verse in this 1895 volume, with poems on home, faith, and public life. Titles such as "My Mother's Kiss", "The Dying Bondman", and "An Appeal to My Country Women" show the range: tender family scenes sit beside direct calls for justice. Her voice is plain and musical, meant to be read aloud and felt at once.

Many poems speak from the experience of Black Americans after slavery, praising courage, mourning loss, and urging moral action. Others turn to nature, childhood, and prayer. The book stands as a key record of a leading Black woman poet of the age, joining lyric craft to a public conscience in short, clear verse.
6815-old-spookses-pass-malcolm-s-katie-a:
Isabella Valancy Crawford, dedicating her poems to her uncle John Irwin Crawford, opens Old Spookses' Pass with a camp on Yaller Bull Flat. Possum Billy, Tom, and the speaker, all smart at throwing a lariat and riding a bronco, argue square with a devil rolled in a mule's hide. The verse speaks in a rough, western voice, full of sinew and humor.

Malcolm's Katie and other poems follow, with Canadian scenes, loves, and frontier talk. Crawford writes with a pioneer's vigor and a poet's ear. Old Spookses' Pass is a lively, distinctive book of Canadian verse, rough-edged and full of life.
68287-dragons-and-cherry-blossoms:
Mrs Robert C Morris wrote Dragons and Cherry Blossoms, held in 1896 at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company. Morris gives the book to her husband. A front piece shows her clad in native costume in Japan. Many have been before her on Japan, she owns. The theme can hardly be called new, she says.

Japan has been viewed from every side and through all kinds of eyes, Morris holds. Still she jots down her own observations and experiences. She hopes readers may feel some rays of Orient sunshine and beauty in them. Burton J Hendrick is thanked for kind aid on the manuscript. Contents treat foreign residents, shopping, and a dinner at Kioto. The Miyako Odori dance, the rise and fall of the kakemono, and a glimpse of royalty follow. Fin de Siecle Japan and a tale named Cho and Eba close the book.
68458-motley-and-other-poems:
Walter de la Mare published a volume of poems at London in 1918, thanking the editors of the English Review, the Times, the New Statesman, and the Yale Review for reprint permissions. His other books are listed: The Listeners, Peacock Pie with drawings by W Heath Robinson, and a child's day of rhymes. A novel, Henry Brocken, is also named. The Little Salamander heads the contents.

A selection from the volume appeared in a limited Beaumont Press edition. De la Mare's poems mix childhood, dreams, and quiet dread. Motley gathers his wartime lyrics for adult readers. Constable published the book in the last year of the first World War.
68531-elfin-land-and-other-poems:
Elfin Land and Other Poems is a volume of verse by Benjamin West Ball, printed at Boston and Cambridge in 1851. Ball dedicates it to a friend, as a token of warm regard. The opening poem addresses that friend directly. Ere thou wert seen, it begins, a morning dream revealed a shape in perfect beauty moulded, wearing the fabled zone of love.

The phantom fled, the poet says, yet its memory stayed in his heart until he found the friend herself. Later verses turn eastward, watching trains roll toward the distant beloved. Stars, blossom, and golden light serve as measures of her worth to him. The stars are not more dear to night, he writes, than thou art to my bosom.
