Ball writes in the formal lyric manner of his day, full of classical allusion and courtly praise. The volume preserves a young American poet's craft of 1851.
68573-petunia-blossoms-ballads-and-poems:
Petunia Blossoms is a book of ballads and poems by Dorothea Auguste Gunhilde Schrage, printed by the Gate City Press at Kansas City in 1921. Schrage dedicates the book to her beloved husband, William Schrage. A photograph of the author fronts the volume. The title poem opens the contents.

The pieces are home verse of the plain kind. A tribute to Thirty-Second Street, Baby, and Jack's Christmas lead off. Is Marriage a Failure asks its question at page sixteen. A Big Red Apple, Little Mischiefs, and Christmas in Norway follow, with Our Flag for patriotism. Later poems treat a big red apple's kin: Good-By Daddy, My Faithful Shoes, a soldier's son, an old clock, and a wedding anniversary. Mother, Swope Park, and Sweet Sixteen keep the Kansas City hearth in view. The book is a family's fireside in rhyme.
6859-songs-of-labor-and-other-poems:
Morris Rosenfeld, translated from Yiddish by Rose Pastor Stokes and Helena Frank, sings songs of labor in a factory where machines roar so wildly that workers can scarce hear themselves think. Contents run from In the Factory and My Boy to The Nightingale to the Workman, Despair, Whither, and From Dawn to Dawn. A candle seller, a pale operator, and a beggar family join the chorus.

Rosenfeld writes as a sweatshop poet, with anger, pity, and hope in plain, musical verse. His songs gave voice to immigrant workers. Songs of Labor is a moving, historic book of Yiddish labor poetry in English dress.
69248-atlanta-offering-poems:
Atlanta Offering is a book of poems by Frances Harper, published at Philadelphia in 1895. Harper printed the volume at Bainbridge Street and took the copyright herself. A verse from Isaiah heads the book, on the forsaken made an eternal excellency. My Mother Kiss opens the poems, on a kiss felt still on the brow.

Bright happy days, clustering hair, and a love light in the eyes fill the memory. A gentle voice in warning or in love sounds through the opening poem. Harper was the famed Black poet, lecturer, and abolitionist voice of her century. Her verse joins family tenderness to the long public fight for her people.
69484-bonnie-joann-and-other-poems:
Bonnie Joann and Other Poems, by Violet Jacob, is a book of Scots verse from Angus. Murray printed it in London in 1921, and Jacob gives it to her nephew, William Kennedy-Erskine. Most of the poems had stood in Country Life.

A front note praises her earlier Songs of Angus, now in a fifth impression. Buchan's preface, quoted there, hears the east wind and the rain in every song. Humour, a haunting lilt, and pathos all get praise. The contents run from the title song through the wind from the Baltic, Hallowe'en, and the Kelpie. Baltic Street, Bailie Bruce, and the banks of the Esk follow. A last section turns into English: a young man's song, the shadows, a winter phantasy, and the seasons. The title song opens at harvest, the sheaves stooked and waiting to be gathered in.
69560-leisure-hours-among-the-gems:
Leisure Hours Among the Gems is a book on precious stones by Augustus C Hamlin. The Boston edition was printed in eighteen ninety one, from a copyright of eighteen eighty four. Hamlin also wrote a treatise on the tourmaline. A Rabelais quotation at the front urges knowledge of all nature's works. A crystal of sapphire from Ceylon is pictured at exact size near the start.

The dedication honours a man who first told the academies of Europe that coral is the product of animal life. Hamlin held seats in learned societies at home and abroad, his title page notes. He was a fellow of an American association for the advance of science. The Rabelais motto bids the reader know every metal hid in the earth. The precious stones of the east and south are named in it too.
6957-canada-and-other-poems:
T F Young offers these poems with great diffidence, yet with a purpose that steadies him: to do something for his country, as Burns did for his. Canadian literature, he warns in his preface, stands in its infancy, and it must not stay so if the nation is to grow great. Literature, he writes, gives life to a nation, or mirrors its life and thought in a glass that cheers, strengthens, and ennobles.

The poems that follow sing of Canada and other themes, aiming to help a young literature grow with its people. Young asks readers to judge the verses by their intent as much as their polish. The book stands as an early Canadian bid for a national voice in verse, modest in claim and earnest in hope.
69611-the-tower-rooms:
The Tower Rooms is a story book by Mary Grant Bruce, published by Ward, Lock in London and Melbourne in 1926. A frontispiece shows a man producing jelly from nowhere to feed the young narrator. Bruce's Billabong books are listed in the front matter, with a word of praise from The Queen. She has a story to tell, the reviewer says, and tells it in her own straightforward way, smiles and tears blending as in life.

The contents, preserved in the copy, run in the first person. The narrator becomes a member of the band, hears of robbers, and sees double. Strange confidences follow, then adventuring, and the narrator finds herself a conspirator. She sails with her band and finds a lucky sixpence. One late chapter is called I Use a Poker.
69648-roger-williams:
Roger Williams is a life of the founder of Rhode Island by May Emery Hall, published by the Pilgrim Press at Boston in 1917. The frontispiece shows a detail of the Williams statue in Roger Williams Park, Providence. Hall wrote other books of the old world, named on the title page as Dutch Days and Jan and Betje.

Sixteen chapters follow Williams out of the shadows and westward to New England. They tell of the war of words that drove him out, his corner for the persecuted, and the Pequot War. His Indian key, his quests for the charter, and his time as colonial president follow. The coming of the Quakers and King Philip's War close the life, back to the shadows.
69761-the-sinking-of-the-titanic-and-oth:
The Sinking of the Titanic and Other Poems, by C. Victor Stahl, was printed at Boston in 1915. Stahl had also written Zorabella. The title poem leads a book of verse that runs from grave themes to light humor.

The list holds Spring Ballad, The Spirit of War, The Riddle of Life, and The Chord Unsung. Other poems treat flags, faith, love, nature, and the need to be strong and push onward. A humor part at the back holds His Legacy, The Word Misspelled, and A Mash in Court. The Titanic poem looks back at the lost ship in high, sad tones. Readers meet the mix of grief, faith, and cheer that marked much verse of the war years.
69855-letters-sentences-and-maxims:
Letters, Sentences and Maxims gathers the private letters and short sayings of Lord Chesterfield, the statesman Philip Dormer Stanhope. The edition pairs a prefatory note by Charles Sayle with a critical essay by Sainte-Beuve. Sayle notes the odd fate of a man famous for writing he never meant to print. Chesterfield served as Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland and knew Addison, Swift, Pope and Voltaire.

The letters give his advice on manners, speech and the conduct of life. Praise quoted from 1845 and 1846 reviews calls the style clear, elegant and terse. The maxims pack his worldly wisdom into single lines. Together they show why this polished courtier still stands for the guarded, careful manners of his century.
70013-acoustics-of-auditoriums:
Acoustics of Auditoriums is a short technical bulletin by Watson, issued by the Engineering Experiment Station of the University of Illinois. It is bulletin number 73 in the university's weekly series, dated March 16, 1914. The price was twenty cents.

The station issued such bulletins to spread the results of its tests. This one treats the sound of halls built for speech and music. Its subject is how a room's shape and surfaces help or harm hearing at the back seats. The bulletin speaks to builders, architects, and college men who must plan lecture rooms and halls. The university's seal and lists of station work frame the text.
7034-fleurs-de-lys-and-other-poems:
Arthur Weir gathers Fleurs de Lys and other poems, dedicating the volume lovingly to his parents William and Elizabeth Somerville Weir, his most severe and kindly critics. An epigraph holds that only he is a poet who finds happiness in sorrow, light in darkness, and love everywhere, leading fellow kind by flowery paths toward life's sunny height. Weir chose the name Fleurs de Lys for the Canadian poems opening the book.

Their scenes belong to the monarchial, or Fleur de Lys, period of France in Canada, whose royal crest graced the cover. Many poems first appeared in the Montreal and Toronto press, and their kindly reception led the author to collect them. The volume sings Canada's French past and its present in verse.
70526-the-canterbury-pilgrims:
The Canterbury Pilgrims is a comedy by Percy MacKaye. Macmillan published it in New York in 1903, with reprints to 1909. An illustration of the Tabard Inn fronts the play. A Keats passage from Endymion serves as a motto verse. MacKaye asks his muse not to let his weak tongue falter. He would stammer where old Chaucer used to sing, the verse says. The persons of the play are divided into groups. Characters based on The Canterbury Tales form the first group. Geoffrey Chaucer himself appears as poet at King Richard's court.

The Knight appears under a stage name in that group. His son the Squire and his yeoman accompany him. MacKaye dedicates the comedy to a friend in warm terms. The play revives Chaucer's company for the modern stage. Pilgrims jest and journey in verse once more.
71036-john-williams:
A moral tale for children, John Williams or the Sailor Boy, was printed at Boston in 1827 by Bowles and Dearborn. Its motto urges readers to purify the heart first, then light the mind with religion's lamp. The copyright was entered in Massachusetts on March 23, 1827, in the fifty first year of independence. That legal notice fills the front pages.

The tale opens on a severely cold January morning after heavy snow. The narrator sees from a parlour window a child of ten or eleven lingering at a gateway. The boy is miserably clad in tattered garments. On the third morning, a servant named James brings him in to the fire. One foot is frozen and his hands are chilled.
7110-rose-and-roof-tree-poems:
George Parsons Lathrop gathers Rose and Roof Tree poems, opening with an illustration of Jessamine and verses on the enchanted ladder of rhyme, climbed round by round and patiently. A dedication says the verse needs no hint of whom it sings for, since the rose, knowing her own right, makes light rays her servants to carry her color. Every line, the poet promises, breathes of her whom it seeks, however unworthily, to serve and honor.

Contents list Windfalls, Rose and Roof Tree, Music of Growth, A Song Long Ago, and Melancholy Contentment, then an April aria, the bobolink, the sun shower, and June longings. A rune of rain, the song sparrow, Fairhaven Bay, and a chant for autumn follow, with moods of love in absence and heart's fountain. Lathrop sings nature and love in measured verse.
71163-the-parted-family-and-other-poems:
The Parted Family, and Other Poems, by Mary Dana, author of The Southern Harp, was published in New York in 1842 by Dayton and Saxton. The subtitle calls the book an offering to the afflicted, and a tribute of love to departed friends. A text from the Book of Kings heads the title page: is it well with the child? And she answered, it is well.

The contents are a litany of loss: The Dying and the Dead, The Mother to her Departed Child, The Burial, The Death-Bed Scene, The Second Burial. Poems to a sister, a brother, a husband's picture, and an absent husband follow. A dialogue between the Savior and the mourner, and pieces like Don't Cry, My Mother, voice the era's pious grief. Dana writes consolation verse for a culture that mourned in print.
7130-london-films:
W D Howells sketches London Films in twenty chapters, from meteorological emotions and civic and social comparisons, mostly odious, to shows and side shows of state. The dun year's brilliant flower, the sights and sounds of streets, and misgivings as to the American invasion follow. A seat in the gallery of the Commons and the means of sojourn come next. Certain traits of the London springtime and voluntary and involuntary sightseeing lead to glimpses of the lowly and the lowlier.

Twice seen sights and half fancied facts, an afternoon at Hampton Court, and a Sunday morning in the country precede fishing for whitebait and Henley Day. American origins, mostly northern and mostly southern, close the set with aspects, intimations, and parting guests. Illustrations show Parliament, Fleet Street, Hyde Park, and Rotten Row.
71508-the-coat-without-a-seam-and-other-:
The Coat Without a Seam and Other Poems, by Helen Gray Cone, is a book of verse published in New York in 1919. Cone had earlier issued A Chant of Love for England, whose title poem answered a German hymn of hate.

The title poem opens the volume, telling of a web woven on the loom of God in the blue of heaven and the red of man's blood. A group of sonnets on the great peace follows. A long section called Moods of War holds The Sword, Mothers of Soldiers, The Airman, and verses to France and Belgium. A poem on Roosevelt, dated 1919, ends that group. The quiet days close the book with poems of faith, roads, and an old burying hill. Many pieces first appeared in magazines and newspapers.
71951-brothers-in-arms:
Brothers in Arms, by Alexander Powell, was published in June 1917 by Houghton Mifflin. Powell gives the book to General Kuhn and his fellows of the Army War College. The theme is America entering the Great War beside France.

We fight once more for freedom, Powell opens: for the fifth time the nation draws the sword. The Revolution won the nation's freedom, and 1812 the freedom of the seas. The Civil War kept the Union and freed the slaves, and the war with Spain freed Cuba. Now, he says, the cause is democracy and the freedom of the world. France, an ally again after nearly seven-score years, has sent her most famed men across perilous seas. Their mission, Powell argues, will rank as a turning point in the nation's history.
7228-laura-secord-the-heroine-of-1812-a-:
Sarah Anne Curzon wrote the drama Laura Secord to rescue a brave woman's name from oblivion and set it in its proper place among Canadian heroes. She dedicates the volume to all true Canadians, of whatever derivation, and pairs the play with other poems. The epigraphs invoke white-robed bards telling tales of old and the search for what is beautiful, true, and noble in a book.

Secord's walk through danger in 1812 becomes a stage story of courage, told in verse drama rather than in prose history. Curzon's preface frames the play as an act of national memory, claiming a heroine for a young country. The poems that follow widen the book from one deed to a fuller Canadian voice.
73237-synonyms-and-antonyms:
A word reference book by Edith B Ordway, published at New York in 1913. George Sully and Company issued the volume. Ordway also wrote on etiquette and quotations. Her list covers words in common use only. Each entry groups synonyms, then gives antonyms. Abbreviations mark the parts of speech.

Abandon opens the alphabet with a flood of near-kin. Desert, forsake, relinquish, and abjure crowd its line. Claim, cherish, and defend answer from the opposite camp. Abandoned splits into two senses, discarded and depraved. Abasement counters with elevate, exalt, and dignify. Such quick-reference lists served writers, students, and crossword solvers. The format descends from Roget but aims at the desk, not the study.
7325-dreams-and-days-poems:
George Parsons Lathrop's Dreams and Days gathers poems in four parts, opening with a call to young men, a star, sunshine, jessamine, the bobolink, and a sailor's song returning. Bride brook, May-rose, the singing wire, the heart of a song, and south-wind follow, with a lover's year, new worlds, night in New York, and the song-sparrow widening the book's range.

Later poems turn to war's bride, a rune of rain, breakers, a child-year, christening, and thanksgiving. Then come youth, the sword, the golden gate, charity, Helen at the loom, and a casket of opals. Lathrop dedicates the book to Rosl, and his verse mixes domestic feeling with public occasion. The collection shows a minor American poet at his most musical.
7336-home-lyrics-a-book-of-poems:
H. S. Battersby's Home Lyrics, volume two, appeared after the author's death, published by her children in fulfilment of her last wishes. It is dedicated to the memory of the dearest of mothers, whose whole life was consecrated to their happiness. Her children write that she fully reciprocated their self-denial, devotion, and love, and the book stands as a family memorial in verse.

Its index runs from a son who passed from earth in April 1887 through birdies, a little five-year-old, and the angel on war. A rink, a Binghampton home, and Mrs Langtry as Miss Hardcastle in She Stoops to Conquer follow. Domestic affection, loss, and home scenes fill the lyrics. The volume preserves a mother's voice, kept by those who loved her.
7392-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Every year, Holmes wrote for the reunion of his Harvard class of 1829, and this volume gathers those class poems from 1851 to 1889. Bill and Joe, about two old classmates bent and gray who still talk like boys, sets the tone: affectionate, a little teasing, and honest about aging. Songs of Twenty-Nine, questions and answers, and verses for class meetings follow across nearly forty years.

As the years pass, the poems darken and deepen. The Civil War enters with a voice of the loyal North and a tribute to Sherman in Savannah, and old friends are remembered as they die. The volume is less a book of lyrics than a friendship kept in verse, a record of one Harvard class growing old together through the most testing decades of American life.
7393-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
The Chambered Nautilus and The Deacon's Masterpiece, better known as The Wonderful One-Hoss Shay, both live in this volume. They come from Holmes's breakfast-table years, 1857 to 1859, when The Autocrat and The Professor turned a Boston doctor into a national sage. The Nautilus builds its shell chamber by chamber as an image of the soul outgrowing its past; the One-Hoss Shay collapses all at once after a hundred years of perfect service.

Around those famous pieces sit Contentment, Under the Violets, Sun and Shadow, and a parting health to Motley. The poems share the breakfast-table voice: warm, witty, and reflective, with a moral that never quite preaches. This is the Holmes most readers remember, at the height of his powers.
7398-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Over the Teacups was Holmes's last breakfast-table book, and this volume gathers its poems. It opens with thanks to the eleven ladies who gave him a silver loving cup. It then moves through The Peau de Chagrin of State Street, The Rose and the Fern, and Bar Harbor. The Broomstick Train, or The Return of the Witches, sends Salem's witches riding again over modern New England.

A run of secret poems follows: the banker's secret, the exile's secret, the lover's secret, the statesman's secret, the mother's secret, and the secret of the stars. Holmes closes by addressing his old readers directly, as a host at the end of a long evening. The volume is late Holmes at his most sociable, witty and tender by turns, still talking across the table.
7431-confessions-and-criticisms:
Julian Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel Hawthorne, writes here both as a confessing author and as a critic. The opening confession tells how, at twenty-three in 1869, he sent sonnets to Putnam's Magazine with no thought of becoming a writer. His early novel Bressant, finished in three weeks, was judged too immoral to publish, recast, and then lost in the post to a Boston publisher.

From that start, the essays range widely: novels and agnosticism, Americanism in fiction, literature for children, the moral aim in fiction, and Emerson as an American. Hawthorne also weighs modern magic and American wild animals in art. The book is a lively record of a literary life lived in a great father's shadow, frank about failure and generous toward fellow writers.
75121-who-were-the-pilgrims:
Who Were the Pilgrims, by William T Davis, is an essay from Harper New Monthly Magazine, volume sixty four, number 380, for January 1882. Davis answers the title question by tracing the Pilgrims roots in the English church fights.

The Pilgrims, he says, were Separatists from the English Church, and the offspring of Puritanism. Puritanism was the child of the Reformation. He follows the chief steps by which that stage was reached. As early as 1350, Bradwardine, chaplain of Edward the Third, moved his king to resist the grabs of Clement the Sixth. The Statute of Provisors set prison or exile for any who sought church posts from Rome. In 1377 Wycliffe, an Oxford teacher of divinity, rose in open revolt against the Pope. History fans get a clear, short line from Wycliffe to Plymouth.
75201-a-farewell-to-arms:
A Farewell to Arms is a war tale by Ernest Hemingway, out at New York in nineteen twenty-nine. A list at the front names his past books, tales and short sets of the same spare hand. The book is given to a man by his marks. It stands in five books, of which the first opens in late summer of a war year.

The voice of the tale lives in a house in a town that looks past a stream and a plain to the hills. Troops march past the house and raise dust that coats the trees. At night the flash of guns in the hills is like storm light with no storm. Rain in the fall strips the trees and turns the land wet, brown, and dead. That flat voice and that wet land set the tone of the whole tale.
75333-on-dreams:
On Dreams is Professor Sigmund Freud's short account of psycho-analysis applied to dreams, in the only authorised English translation by M D Eder. The Rebman Company of New York published it from the second German edition, with an introduction by W Leslie Mackenzie. Mackenzie calls dreams the awaking of dormant complexes, trailing clouds of emotion into consciousness.

The chapters contrast the scientific and popular views of dreams, then assert the thesis: dreams have a meaning. Freud distinguishes manifest from latent content and reads dreams as the realisation of unfulfilled desires, plainest in children. The dream-mechanism follows in parts: condensation and dramatisation, displacement, the ego in the dream, and regard for intelligibility. Repression connects dreams to other unconscious processes. Why the dream disguises its desires brings in the censorship, and the dream as guardian of sleep answers it. Symbolism, myths, and folklore close the essay.
75479-willow-s-forge-and-other-poems:
Willow's Forge and Other Poems is a book of poems by Sheila Kaye Smith, issued at London in 1914. The publisher's pages at the front puff her novels with warm reviews. Her first novel is called a remarkable first attempt, quite without crudeness, by one daily paper. Its air is sweet, the notice says; it smells of summer and shines of the stars.

Another paper found it hard not to be too warm over her second book, a fine, tragic, poetic tale. A third reviewer, in a famous comic paper, spoke of the high place she would take among the great masters of English fiction. Kaye Smith became the novelist of Sussex farms and marshes. These early poems come from the same ground of forge, field, and lane that her novels made her own.
75489-poems:
Poems is a book of verse by Josephine Daskam, published by Scribner's in New York in 1903. The Merrymount Press printed it in Boston. Daskam dedicates the collection to the first and cordial critic of many of the verses. The contents open with Motherhood, The Sleepy Song, and The Golden Days.

Songs of the sea, of Iseult deserted, and of a gypsy maid follow. Two sonnets come from the Hebrew, and a Christmas hymn is written for children. Three songs give a sailor, a hunter, and a prince in turn. The poems are lyrics of home, love, and childhood in the polished manner of their day.
75529-deirdre-wed-and-other-poems:
Deirdre Wed and Other Poems is a volume by Herbert Trench, published by Methuen in London in 1901. The title poem retells the Irish legend of Deirdre in a dramatic sequence of five parts, spoken by ancient chanters. Shorter poems follow, from an ode on a silver birch to a Shakespeare sonnet sequence and songs of night and funerals.

The chanters call across the ages to Fintan, elder than the yews and too old for tears. Fintan's voice tells of the marriage night: word gone out to every rath and ring of the slaughter of sheep and boar for the feast at Eman. The girl, bred in a peaty hillock by an old crone, barefoot in red wool, was seen by King Connachar and trained by queens for this night. Trench writes Celtic twilight verse at high pressure, all mist, spears and doom.
75834-two-new-poems:
Two New Poems pairs Rohallion, The Little Dragon, a Scots poem by Violet Jacob, with a second poem. The Porpoise Press of Edinburgh printed the small book in 1924. Designs by A. Mason Trotter decorate it, and fifty numbered copies were printed on hand-made paper.

Rohallion speaks in broad Scots. A shepherd-poet with no coin in his pocket looks back to a small house in Strathtay, his mother baking bannocks and his father folding the sheep at dusk. No house from there to the sea could hold him when the wind comes off the hills. Snow, rowan leaves, and the stars on the loch pull him south and home at once. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
75892-a-manual-of-the-book-of-psalms:
Martin Luther gave a short guide to what each psalm in the Bible is about. Henry Cole turned the work into English for the first time. Cole had turned more of Luther's works in those years. The book came out in London in 1837. Cole taught at Clare Hall, Cambridge, in his past.

Cole says no praise is needed, for the work speaks its own worth. Luther opens each psalm's theme in brief, clear lines. Cole's front words warn of mere form in faith with no life. True, felt truth is the book's clear aim through all. Church readers get the great reformer's hand at their side. Each psalm finds its core in a few lines.
76391-fairy-dreams:
Fairy Dreams, or Wanderings in Elf-Land, is a book of fairy tales by Austin. Tilton published it in Boston in 1859. Billings drew the illustrations. Six tales make up the volume. Their titles promise princes, frost-maidens, and castles. The first and longest is Prince Rudolf's Flower.

That tale opens at a palace audience. King Merowald asks who would beg a boon. His only son Rudolf kneels before the throne. The prince asks leave to seek a dreamed flower. He cannot recall its form, colour, or name. Yet he would know it on sight, he says. Without it he cannot live. The king sends him first to a wise counsellor. A crooked little doorkeeper with a hump admits him. Other tales follow under the sea and on a cliff.
76700-good-friday-and-other-poems:
Good Friday and Other Poems is a verse book by John Masefield, out in nineteen sixteen. A Macmillan house of New York brought the book out that year. Good Friday, its name piece, is a stage poem of the cross day. Pilate, his wife Procula, and the guard chief Longinus head its cast list. The scene is the paved court of the Roman fort in Jerusalem town.

Bronze doors of green hue and side stairs frame that high court set. Pilate bids Longinus free Barabbas, since the mob chose that man. Scourge and gate for Jesus is his soft plan for the feast day. Procula comes to plead word of what Herod said of the case. Quake air and blood in the sun weigh on the mind of Pilate.
76846-the-three-sphinxes-and-other-poems:
George Sylvester Viereck published poems in a Little Blue Book, number 579, edited by E Haldeman Julius at Girard, Kansas, with copyrights from 1907 to 1924. A first section is titled The Poet Psycho Analyzes Himself. The poems begin with Slaves and Iron Passion. The Three Sphinxes gives the book its title. The Cynic's Credo and The Ghost of Oscar Wilde follow.

The Parrot, The Candle and the Flame, and A Ballad of King David continue. Benediction, Spring, A Vision of Man, and Inhibition close the visible list. Haldeman Julius sold millions of his five cent blue books by mail. Viereck's decadent verse reached a mass audience in this cheap dress.
772-moral-emblems:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote and illustrated these short poems, first printed at the Davos Press by his stepson Lloyd Osbourne. Each poem pairs with a woodcut, and the emblems turn on labour, cross, and crown, on duty, death, and hope. A preface by Osbourne sets the small book in its place.

The verses are brief, earnest, and a touch quaint, the work of a sick man writing for friends. Their charm lies in the mix of word and image, and in Stevenson's moral seriousness beneath the play. The book is a curiosity for Stevenson lovers, showing the poet at his most private and devout.
77299-eire-and-other-poems:
Robin Flower wrote Eire and Other Poems, issued in London by Locke Ellis in nineteen ten. Certain poems had appeared in Country Life and the Academy. Contents divide into Eire, Lyrics, Sonnets, and Hymenaea. Eire Answer opens the book. O Eire, Eire, what of the morrow, the poem asks. Speak to us who are thinking long, mother of sorrow, mother of song, it pleads.

We that cling to thy knees for ever, true to thy hills and glens and streams, the voices say. We have laid our hearts on thy high green altar, they add. Children dear, I have wandered, wandered, Eire answers. For you I have laboured, for you have pondered, have wept for you, she says. Tír na nóg, The Sidhe, and The Exile follow. The Hedge Schoolmaster to His Love fills the set. Poetry readers get Flower Irish lyrics in a Celtic twilight key.
77442-the-black-christ-other-poems:
Countee Cullen published The Black Christ and Other Poems with Harper and Brothers of New York in 1929, with decorations by Charles Cullen. Many of the poems had first appeared in magazines, and a Guggenheim grant had helped Cullen write them.

The book falls into three parts. Varia gathers short lyrics, epitaphs, and sonnets to friends, including a poem for Helen Keller and one headed Not Sacco and Vanzetti. Interlude holds love poems and partings. The third part, Color, turns to race and faith: To Certain Critics, Black Majesty, a song of praise, and the title poem, The Black Christ. Cullen's earlier books, Color and Copper Sun among them, had already made him a leading voice of his generation of poets.
77514-shakespeare-s-legal-maxims:
William Rushton wrote this study of Shakespeare legal maxims and obscure lines. Young printed it at Liverpool in 1907, by a Gray's Inn barrister. Rushton also wrote Shakespeare a Lawyer and kindred studies before. A notice says a first edition came when he was a student.

London papers mistook that pamphlet for a second edition of the earlier work. Elze German book cites Rushton 1858 work beside Lord Campbell 1859. The Examiner held Campbell used Rushton labour without credit, the notice says. The brochure shows the author deeply read in law, papers agreed.
77721-a-dictionary-of-scientific-terms:
Dictionary of Scientific Terms, by Leo Markun, is a small plain language glossary. Haldeman Julius issued it in nineteen twenty seven as Little Blue Book number four hundred fifty two. The book comes from Girard, Kansas, in a cheap pocket format. Terms run in letter order from the start of the alphabet.

Early entries define abasia, abdomen, aberrant, and aberration in short plain lines. Abiogenesis is glossed as spontaneous generation in a few words flat. Absolute is given both a plain sense and a thought sense. The aim is quick help for lay readers who meet science words. Breadth, not depth, marks the book, with one or two lines per term.
77736-color-problems:
Color Problems is a practical manual for the lay student of colour by Emily Noyes Vanderpoel. Longmans published it in New York in 1902, with one hundred and seventeen coloured plates. Vanderpoel dedicates the book to her father. Chapters open with colour-blindness, then take up colour theories and colour qualities.

Contrasts and complements, colour harmonies, and the colour of history and nature follow. The first plate shows wools as sorted by a colour-blind man. Others give the solar spectrum and tables of spectral colours in their order of brightness. Appendixes define terms and list books for reference. The manual taught artists and decorators to handle colour with system.
7796-poems:
Madison Cawein's Poems, selected by the author with a foreword by William Dean Howells, gathers verse from a five-volume collected edition of 1907 plus later books. Newer sources include Nature Notes and Impressions, The Giant and the Star, an ode for the Massachusetts Bay Colony, New Poems of 1909, and Kentucky Poems.

Howells introduces a Kentucky poet of nature, myth, and music, whose work ranges from Arcady to modern scenes. The volume offers a chosen path through a large output, letting readers meet Cawein's best-known lyrics without wading through five volumes of collected verse.
78243-the-silver-cat-and-other-poems:
The Silver Cat and Other Poems is a verse book by Wolfe, made as a gift book for a book crafts feat of the proof hands guild. Its rights were held in the late nineteen twenties by a press of that guild. It was printed in America.

Its parts run short: a call, the title piece, a turn on a child song, and a piece on how free days and peace come. A spring and death piece and a piece on the hour that can not die close the set. Its call tells its faith in a few lines. If in a fell petal shows the out line of the full rose, it says, no less on these may a hint fall of the first form from on high.
78763-modern-thinkers-and-present-proble:
Modern Thinkers and Present Problems approaches modern thought through its history, written by Edgar Singer of the University of Pennsylvania. Holt published the book at New York in 1923. Eleven chapters run from Giordano Bruno to a closing look backward and forward. Singer writes for students meeting the great systems for the first time.

The first chapter opens with a letter of denunciation from Venice in 1592. Bruno's host reports his guest's talk against the mass and the faith. From that vivid start Singer traces the line of modern thought. Spinoza, Hume, Kant, Schopenhauer, and Nietzsche each take a chapter. Pragmatism and progress get chapters of their own. Royce on love and loyalty closes the survey. Singer links each thinker to the problems of the present day.
78789-the-book-of-talismans-amulets-and-:
The Book of Talismans, Amulets and Zodiacal Gems, by William Thomas and Kate Pavitt, first came out in 1914. The hosted copy is the second and revised edition of 1922, from William Rider of London. A colored frontispiece shows the gems, symbols, and glyphs of the zodiac, and ten plates back the text.

Early chapters move from the lucky signs of early races, the axe, the swastika, and the serpent, through Indian, Chinese, Japanese, and Egyptian charms to the scarab and the Eye of Osiris. Later parts take up birthstones and the gems of each sign. It is a full, friendly handbook of lucky things.
78927-strange-marriage-customs:
Leo Markun wrote Strange Marriage Customs, issued as Little Blue Book number 1436 by Haldeman-Julius Publications of Girard, Kansas in 1929. The Little Blue Books were cheap pocket volumes meant to carry plain knowledge to working readers. Markun opens with the matchmaker and the power of parents over marriage.

He notes that young Americans now choose their own mates and resent interference. That has not always been so, and is not so everywhere. In China, he writes, the worship of parents and ancestors still rules. In old New England, rebellion against authority could be a capital offense. Under the Roman paterfamilias, a father's power over his children could last until his death. The book surveys such customs to show how widely marriage rules differ across peoples and ages.
7925-expositions-of-holy-scripture-psalm:
Alexander MacLaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture: Psalms, volume one covering Psalms 1 to 49, opens with blessedness and praise, a staircase of three steps, and one saying from three men. Man's true treasure in God, God with us, two wakings, secret faults, and open sins follow in order.

Later sermons feast on sacrifice, hail the shepherd king of Israel, ask a great question and answer it, and seek pardon, guidance, and God's guests. Through close, plain exposition, MacLaren turns each psalm into counsel for prayer, trust, and daily conduct, for readers and preachers alike.
79344-the-eternal-laughter-and-other-poe:
The Eternal Laughter and Other Poems is a volume of verse by Burgess, published at Boston in 1903 with an introduction by Julian Hawthorne and drawings by Edward Lyne and Edmund Garrett. Some fifty short poems follow the title piece, most of them addressed to a beloved woman or to God, under titles like Waiting, The Wish, A Prayer and The Sleep of Death.

The title poem is a dream vision. The speaker speeds beyond the calling wind into lightless space, until the eternal King calls to him over paths of sun and star. God's thought grows clear, and the dreamer laughs with him, knowing the Father well. The poems that follow keep that mystical key: night, sleep, flowers and parting all become occasions for addressing the divine through the human beloved. The manner is the high romantic lyric of 1903, earnest and unembarrassed.
795-ballads-and-lyrics-of-old-france-wit:
Andrew Lang translated ballads and lyrics of old France in this 1872 volume, with other poems of his own. Charles d'Orléans opens the set with spring songs and rondels, and François Villon and other medieval poets follow. Lang renders their grace and melancholy into English verse that keeps the old music.

The book introduced many English readers to French medieval lyric, from courtly love to thieves' slang. Lang's versions are light, faithful, and musical, and his notes name each poet in turn. The volume stands as a charming bridge between France and Britain, and as a model of how translation can keep a distant age alive.
79742-essays-on-museums:
Essays on Museums and Other Subjects Connected with Natural History is a set of essays by Sir William Henry Flower, printed in London in 1898. Flower, a leading zoologist, directed the natural history museum in London. The book is dedicated to his wife, his counsellor through forty years of their shared life's work.

The first essay is his 1889 presidential address to the British Association, on museum organisation. It defines a natural history museum, tells the history of museums from ancient times, and sets out their aims of research and teaching. It also treats ways of arranging specimens for study and for the public. The other essays gather his occasional writings on kindred themes.
8019-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
One hundred and fifty songs and prayers make up the book of Psalms, the Bible's hymnbook. Many are linked to David, others to temple singers, and they cover every human mood: praise for creation, thanks for deliverance, laments in trouble, confessions of sin, and trust in dark times. Some psalms were sung in worship, others prayed alone, and their poetry ranges from the shepherd's calm of the twenty-third to the anguish of exile.

No other biblical book has been used so widely, in Jewish and Christian worship alike, for three thousand years. Its language has entered everyday speech, and its pattern of honest complaint turning to trust has comforted countless readers. In the King James Version, the psalms' rhythm and imagery remain unmatched in English, which is why they are still read aloud and sung today.
8192-the-bakchesarian-fountain-and-other:
Alexander Pushkin's The Bakchesarian Fountain, a tale of the Tauride, appears here in William D. Lewis's translation, with other poems by various Russian authors translated from the original Russian. Lewis dedicated the volume, from Philadelphia in July 1849, to his Russian friends, thanking them for kindnesses received in their hospitable country in early life. The fountain poem opens with Giray, mute, with downcast eye, as though bound by a spell of sorrow, among slavish courtiers.

Pushkin's tale of a khan, his captive, and a fountain built for grief is one of Russian poetry's best-loved narratives. Lewis's early translation, though old-fashioned, brings its music to English readers. For students of Pushkin, the volume is a historic curiosity, and a reminder of how Russian literature first reached America.
8212-poems:
Robert Southey published these poems in 1797, opening with an epigraph from Akenside: with the goddess of the lyre comes majestic truth. And where truth deigns to come, her sister liberty will not be far. The first sonnet presents a pilgrim, wayworn and woe-begone, journeying life's upward road for many a day, hymning sad yet soothing lays. Plucking wild and simple flowers of poesy as he passes, and weaving them into a rude wreath for his beloved.

Southey, later poet laureate, was here a young radical Romantic, writing sonnets of travel, sorrow, and liberty. The volume shows his early voice before fame and office softened it. For students of Romantic poetry, it is a valuable first collection, and a reminder of the movement's youthful idealism.
8246-the-world-english-bible-web-psalms:
Psalms, in the World English Bible, opens with a blessing on the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked. Nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers, but delights in Yahweh's law, meditating day and night. He will be like a tree planted by streams of water, bearing fruit in season, its leaf never withering. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book gathers one hundred and fifty songs and prayers.

The modern rendering keeps the psalms' images vivid while easing their older grammar, so praise, lament, and trust read naturally aloud. The second psalm already asks why the nations rage, showing the collection's range. For worship and private reading, this version offers the Bible's hymnbook in today's English, ready for singing and prayer.
8402-east-and-west-poems:
Bret Harte gathers poems of East and West in this volume, moving between New England and California. Contents include A Greyport Legend, A Newport Romance, The Hawk's Nest, In the Mission Garden, and Truthful James's answers. California subjects, big trees, gold country, and San Joaquin springs, beside eastern scenes. Harte, famed for his California stories, writes verse in the same vein.

The poems mix humor, sentiment, and local color, and the California pieces carry his best-known voice: the rough mining camps softened by feeling. Readers of Harte's stories will find the same world in shorter form. The volume suits anyone tracing how the West entered American poetry, through a writer who helped invent its image.
856-dreams:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short comic piece on dreams, opening with the strangest he ever had. Going into a theatre, he fancies the cloak-room attendant stops him and insists he leave his legs behind. He is not surprised, he notes, for his knowledge of theatre folk would bar surprise at any demand, even in a dream.

Jerome spins the fancy into a meditation on how dreams mix sense and nonsense, fear and farce. His tone is light, wry, and confessional, the idle fellow at his best. The piece is brief, but it shows Jerome's gift for turning a small absurdity into a pleasant essay on the mind at play.
8775-poems:
Victor Hugo's poems appear here in an 1888 English selection, opening with a memoir of Victor Marie Hugo and ranging across his long career. Early poems include Moses on the Nile and Envy and Avarice, followed by odes from 1818 to 1828: King Louis XVII. The Feast of Freedom, Genius, The Girl of Otaheite, Nero's incendiary song, and Regret. Ballades from 1823 to 1828, including The Grandmother, continue the gathering.

Translators from the Dublin University Magazine, Fraser's Magazine, and other periodicals give the volume a Victorian anthology feel, with notes on where each piece first appeared in English. Hugo's range, from royalist youth to republican prophet, shows in miniature. Readers new to Hugo the poet, as opposed to Hugo the novelist, get a useful sampler, while specialists can trace how English readers first met his verse.
8930-counter-attack-and-other-poems:
Siegfried Sassoon, a British officer in the First World War, published these poems in 1918, with an introduction by Robert Nichols. Sassoon had fought in France and come home angry at the war's waste, and these short, biting poems say so without flinching. They speak in the voice of men in trenches, not of generals at home.

Blast, mud, gas, and the deaths of friends fill the lines, often with bitter irony aimed at those who cheered the war on from afar. The book made Sassoon a leading war poet, and it still hits hard as a first-hand protest against a war that ate a whole generation of young men.
9105-reflections-or-sentences-and-moral-:
François, Duc de La Rochefoucauld, wrote these maxims in seventeenth-century France, and translators J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell bring them into English here. The maxims are short, sharp sentences on self-love, pride, and the masks men wear. Swift praised them as drawn from nature and true.

Each maxim bites in a line or two, arguing that much virtue hides a love of self. Readers have quoted them for centuries, in praise and in protest. The book remains a classic of moral wit, best read slowly, one sting at a time.
9111-the-bride-of-dreams:
Frederik van Eeden wrote this Dutch tale, here in an authorized translation by Mellie von Auw. It opens in a dreamy little Dutch city seen from the sea, with tall trees on the ramparts and an old bell tower in deep cobalt blue. In Holland's prime, ships filled its harbor and fine houses rose with crow-stepped gables.

The story moves between waking life and dream, as its hero seeks love and meaning beyond the town's faded grandeur. Van Eeden writes with a poet's eye for light on water. The book remains a lovely, strange work of Dutch symbolism, half tale and half vision.
9263-in-the-midst-of-alarms:
Robert Barr wrote this novel in 1894, opening in the marble vestibule of Buffalo's Metropolitan Grand Hotel. Professor Stillson Renmark stands anxious amid gaudy splendor, unused to such a house. He pauses halfway to the counter, fearing an inopportune hour, as hurry and bustle bewilder him. An omnibus waits at the door, and porters heave iron-bound trunks.

Saratogas of lady travelers join the commercial men's luggage, and alarms multiply from there. Barr, master of brisk romance, spins a tale of mistaken identity and Canadian-American intrigue. The novel remains a lively period thriller, humorous and fast.
9323-foliage-various-poems:
William Davies published these various poems in 1913 under the title Foliage. Contents range from Thunderstorms and Strong Moments to A May Morning, The Lonely Dreamer, and Christmas. Laughing Rose, Seeking Joy, and The Old Oak Tree follow, with Poor Kings, Love and the Muse, and My Youth. The Bird-Man and Winter's Beauty close the set.

Davies opens with thunderstorms brooding in his mind till they rain him words, while thoughts droop like flowers. His verse is plain, musical, and close to nature. The book remains a fine sample of the tramp poet's art, simple, observant, and full of life.
9559-the-ride-to-the-lady-and-other-poem:
Helen Gray Cone wrote The Ride to the Lady and Other Poems in 1891, a book of lyric and narrative verse. The title poem tells of a dying knight who rides to his lady, his life ebbing fast from wounds of steel. Other poems include The First Guest, Silence, King Raedwald, Ivo of Chartres, and Madonna Pia. Sonnets on sleep, snow, and the torch race close the set.

Cone's verse favors romance, history, and quiet feeling, with a scholar's care for form. Tales of knights, saints, and singers sit beside lyrics of love and loss. A reader gets a refined, late Victorian poetry book, rich in chivalry, legend, and the music of well-made verse.
980-alice-adams:
Booth Tarkington wrote this novel about Alice Adams, a young woman of a middling family in an American town, who longs for a place in society. Her father, an old-fashioned man ill at home, thinks the nurse mistaken to keep both windows open, while Alice dreams of dances, beaux, and a life beyond her station.

Tarkington tells Alice's story with sympathy and irony, as she schemes, hopes, and learns the price of pretence. Her father's quiet heroism and her own growth give the novel its heart. Alice Adams, which won the Pulitzer Prize, remains a classic American novel of class, ambition, and a young woman's coming of age.
9801-the-habitant-and-other-french-canad:
William Henry Drummond, a Canadian doctor, wrote The Habitant and Other French-Canadian Poems, with an introduction by Louis Fréchette. Drummond dedicates the verses to his teacher George Murray. Poems include The Wreck of the Julie Plante, Le Vieux Temps, and How Bateese Came Home, with De Nice Leetle Canadienne and Maxime Labelle beside. Frederick Simpson Coburn drew the pictures.

Drummond writes in habitant dialect, warm and comic, of rivers, rapids, and parish life. The Habitant himself opens the set, born by the Cheval Blanc rapids. A reader gets a beloved Canadian classic, rich in French-Canadian speech, humor, and home feeling.
9998-poems:
Matilda Betham's Poems, published in 1808 and inscribed to Lady Rouse Boughton in February 1809, gather the verse of a poet and portrait painter. Betham declined a preface, saying she saw no particular purpose it would answer, and let the poems speak.

Among them is The Old Fisherman, whose speaker rests on the beach, reflects on days past, and hurries home with his spoil to welcome and caress. Betham's verse is gentle, domestic, and musical. Readers interested in women poets of the Romantic age get a modest, pleasing volume, long overlooked. Betham later became known as a portrait painter as well.
a-collection-of-college-words-and-custom: Benjamin Homer Hall collects the words and customs of American college life. Compiled during his senior year and enlarged in a second edition, the book defines student slang and describes commencement, societies, and campus habits. Notes from Professor Sidney Willard and others enrich its picture of college manners. Hall's collection preserves a vanished student world for later readers.
a-defence-of-poesie-and-poems:
Sir Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesie stands here in the 1891 Cassell edition, with a long introduction giving his life from his birth at Penshurst in 1554. Sidney wrote the essay to answer attacks on poetry in a puritan age. He argues that the poet teaches and delights better than the historian or the philosopher.

The essay ranges over epic, tragedy, comedy, and lyric, weighs the poets of Greece and Rome, and closes by cursing those who scorn the craft. Sidney's own poems follow, including sonnets that made him the model courtier-poet of Elizabeth's England. The pairing shows the critic and the poet in one short, brilliant career.
a-further-contribution-to-the-study-of-t: Harry Creecy Yarrow contributes further to the study of mortuary customs of North American Indians. The work classifies burial into inhumation, pit burial, grave burial, stone graves, mounds, cabins, and cave burial. Illustrations and a careful introduction support the survey. Yarrow's study preserves a record of Native funeral practices for scholars.
a-hidden-life-and-other-poems: George MacDonald gathers a hidden life and other poems in this volume. The title poem stands beside the homeless ghost, Abu Midjan, an old story, and a book of dreams. Sonnets, prayers, and memorials complete a collection of faith and feeling. MacDonald dedicates the book to his father in verse of gratitude.
a-midsummer-holiday-and-other-poems: Algernon Charles Swinburne gathers a midsummer holiday and other poems. The title sequence visits the seaboard, a haven, a country road, a mill garden, and a sea mark. A new year ode, lines on Mazzini, Les Casquets, and a ballad of Sark follow. Swinburne's summer verse closes this slice with sea, cliff, and light.
a-reading-of-life-with-other-poems:
George Meredith's verse volume, printed in London in 1901, takes its name from the long opening group of poems, A Reading of Life. The contents list pieces such as The Vital Choice, With the Huntress, With the Persuader, and The Test of Manhood. Meredith was better known as a novelist, but he prized his poems highly.

The poems weigh love, strength, regret, and man's place in nature, often in tight, demanding stanzas. Later pages hold Forest History, A Garden Idyl, and hexameter fragments retelling scenes from the Iliad, plus a piece drawn from the Provençal poem Mireio. The book rewards slow reading and a taste for thoughtful verse.
across-the-sea-and-other-poems: Thomas Chard writes poems across the sea, published at Chicago in 1875. Under a Pilgrim's Progress epigraph of a city shining like the sun, with streets paved with gold, the saints bear crowns, palms, and harps. The preface notes that the title poem first appeared in sketched form in the winter of 1869 and is now completed for the first time. The sea, the author says, is a picture of life celebrated by poetic thought in all ages, and he hardly hopes to say much new.
alice-adams:
Booth Tarkington's novel opens in the Adams home, where old Virgil Adams lies sick and quarrels with his nurse about night air. The story then turns to his daughter Alice. She is a young woman in a midwestern town. She longs for finer rooms, finer clothes, and a finer place in society than her family's money allows.

Alice and her mother scheme, pretend, and spend beyond their means to win the notice of a wealthy young man. A disastrous dinner party exposes the gap between the family's show and its truth. Tarkington treats Alice with both satire and pity, and the novel became one of his best known works.
among-the-millet-and-other-poems: Archibald Lampman gathers poems among the millet and other verses, dedicated to his wife, in a book of Canadian nature poetry. The poems dwell on fields, seasons, and quiet hours, with a careful ear for landscape and mood. Lampman's work helped give Canadian poetry a voice rooted in its own woods and farms.
andromeda-and-other-poems: Charles Kingsley gathers Andromeda and other poems, including pieces on Trehill Well, an illuminated missal, and the weird lady. The title poem retells the Greek myth in flowing verse, while the shorter pieces range over nature and fancy. Kingsley's poems show a clergyman-poet's love of legend and landscape. Music and myth carry the whole book along.
anne-s-house-of-dreams:
Lucy Maud Montgomery opens this Anne novel in the garret of Green Gables, with Anne Shirley finishing with geometry for good and her wedding to Gilbert Blythe ahead. The contents list forty chapters. The couple's first home is a small house at Four Winds harbor, which Anne had dreamed of, and the book follows their first year of marriage there.

New neighbors fill the story. Captain Jim is the lighthouse keeper, with a life-book of sea tales to write down. Miss Cornelia Bryant is tart and kind. Leslie Moore is beautiful and trapped in a loveless marriage to a man lost in his mind. Joy and grief both visit the little house, including the loss of a first baby. The final chapters free Leslie, finish Captain Jim's book, and take Anne to a larger house.
aretaeus-extant-works-adams:
Francis Adams translated the Extant Works of Aretaeus the Cappadocian in 1856. Aretaeus practiced medicine around 150 CE in the Roman Empire. Posterity ranks him the finest clinical observer of antiquity.

His descriptions of diabetes, asthma, epilepsy, and tetanus remain classics. He watches symptoms closely and writes them down with literary power. Diabetes receives its classic portrait here, thirst and wasting included. Adams kept the exact Greek sense in careful English prose. Little is known of Aretaeus's life beyond these surviving books. Clinical medicine before the name existed is what his pages show. Physicians still quote his disease portraits with respect. His eye was sharp and his pen was just as sharp.
ballads-and-lyrics-of-old-france-with-ot:
Andrew Lang published Ballads and Lyrics of Old France in 1872, his first book, built largely on translations from French poets of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Charles d'Orleans opens the volume with spring songs and rondels. Francois Villon's Ballad of the Gibbet follows, then du Bellay, Remy Belleau, and Ronsard.

Lang renders roses, moons, dead ladies, and waking mistresses in the old fixed forms: ballade, rondel, and sonnet. His own poems close the collection, including a singer by the waterside drying her hands with willow leaves. The book helped revive English interest in the French lyric forms, and Lang's light, exact touch became his signature across a huge body of work.
britannica-1911-adams:
Adams is a township in north-western Massachusetts. It sits in the extreme north of Berkshire county. The Hoosac river valley runs through it. Greylock Mountain rises partly within its bounds. Greylock is the highest point in the state. The valley floor is level and settled. Its largest village is a busy industrial centre. Cotton and paper manufactures employ its people. A railroad branch serves the village directly.

Specialization is the township's economic story. Cotton goods formed eighty-four percent of factory value in 1905. No other American place matched that degree, the entry says. Population passed thirteen thousand by 1910. The township was incorporated in 1778. It was named for Samuel Adams, the revolutionary. North Adams split off a century later.
britannica-1911-alms:
Alms means both the giving of relief and the relief itself, in goods or money, to the poor. The word is applied particularly to charity given under a sense of religious obligation. Its Old English form was aelmysse, descending through a Teutonic adaptation of a Latinised Greek word, eleēmosynē, which meant compassion or mercy and came from eleos, pity.

From that same Greek root English takes eleemosynary, meaning anything given in the way of alms, charitable, or gratuitous. The entry adds a small grammatical caution: alms is often wrongly taken as a plural word, like riches, though its history and use differ. Readers are pointed onward to the fuller treatment under the heading Charity and Charities for how such relief was organised and given.
britannica-1911-angiosperms:
Angiosperms are the flowering plants whose seeds sit enclosed in a receptacle, in contrast with gymnosperms, whose seeds are naked. Paul Hermann coined the term in 1690 for one of his primary divisions of the plant kingdom, and Linnaeus kept it with a narrower application. Its modern scope became possible only after Robert Brown established in 1827 that cycads and conifers bear truly naked seeds.

Hofmeister's 1851 discovery of the changes inside the embryo-sac of flowering plants reshaped the group's classification, and the long entry builds on that foundation. Sections treat the flower, fertilisation, and embryology, then fruit and seed, including the storage tissues called endosperm and perisperm that divide seeds into albuminous and exalbuminous kinds. A full bibliography of botanical authorities closes this major survey article, signed by two named contributors.
britannica-1911-blakesley-joseph-william:
Joseph Williams Blakesley (1808–1885) was an English churchman and scholar who wrote widely for The Times. Born in London, he studied at St Paul's School and at Corpus Christi and Trinity Colleges, Cambridge, became a fellow of Trinity in 1831, and later its tutor. He held the college living of Ware from 1845 to 1872.

Writing as the Hertfordshire Incumbent, he sent The Times many letters on the social and political questions of the day and reviewed books for it as well. He became a canon of Canterbury in 1863 and dean of Lincoln in 1872. His books include the first English Life of Aristotle (1839), an edition of Herodotus, and Four Months in Algeria (1859).
britannica-1911-buchanan-robert-williams:
Robert Williams Buchanan (1841–1901) was a British poet, novelist and dramatist. This 1911 Britannica entry reviews his life and books. He was born at Caverswall, Staffordshire, on 18 August 1841. His father was an Owenite lecturer and journalist. The family moved to Glasgow, where Buchanan was schooled. He went to London in 1860 with his friend David Gray. Both young men were seeking fame.

His first book, Undertones, came out in 1863. London Poems followed in 1866. His strength lay in narrative verse about humble life. In 1871 he attacked Rossetti's circle in print. The article “The Fleshly School of Poetry” caused a famous quarrel. Buchanan later withdrew his charges and regretted them. The Shadow of the Sword, in 1876, began a long run of novels. The entry lists his later fiction and essays. It also praises The Land of Lorne, his record of yachting in Scotland.
britannica-1911-homs:
Homs, known in ancient times as Emesa, is a town of Syria, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out why the place has mattered for ages. It stands on the right bank of the Orontes, with about 30,000 people, and commands the great north road from Egypt, Palestine, and Damascus up the Orontes valley.

The entry traces battles near the town from Rameses II at Kadesh to Ibrahim Pasha in 1831. Ancient Emesa was devoted to Baal, the sun god, whose priest the emperor Heliogabalus had been. Aurelian crushed Zenobia's rising there in 272, Caracalla made it a Roman colony, and Muslim forces took it about 630.
britannica-1911-leader-benjamin-williams:
Benjamin Williams Leader was an English painter who was born in eighteen thirty-one. He was the son of an engineer. He learned art first at a school in Worcester and then at the schools of the Royal group in London. He first showed work there in eighteen fifty-four.

He rose step by step in that group, to full rank in eighteen ninety-eight. His views of the land won wide love for their charm and skilled lay out. A gold prize came at the Paris show of eighteen eighty-nine. He was made a knight of a French order of honour as well. One named work hangs in a state hall.
britannica-1911-oerlams: Oerlams is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a tribal group in Africa. The name is said to be a worn form of a Dutch word. That word, Oberlanders, points to folk from the uplands in the north. The Oerlams live in Great Namaqualand as their home ground. They came there first from Little Namaqualand in Cape Colony. Their blood is of mixed stock, the entry states in brief. It blends Hottentot and Bantu lines in one people.
britannica-1911-reeves-john-sims:
John Sims Reeves, an English singer who lived from 1818 to 1900, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Woolwich, son of a musician in the Royal Artillery. His father gave him his first music training. At fourteen he was organist of a church and could play several instruments.

Reeves sang first as a baritone, making his debut at Newcastle in 1839. His voice settled as a tenor, and he sang small tenor parts at Drury Lane. Four years of study in Paris and Milan followed. He made his Italian opera debut at La Scala as Edgardo in Lucia. Back in London he sang the same part under Berlioz in 1847. The article also marks his triumph at the Norwich Festival of 1848.
britannica-1911-tapeworms:
Tapeworms are the subject of a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry places them as a class of flatworms that live only inside other animals. They are marked by long shape, bodies made of segments, and the lack of any digestive system. That lack sets them apart at once.

The article breaks the body into three parts for the reader. First comes a tiny organ that fixes the worm in place at its front end. Next is a narrow neck, and from it segments are budded off toward the rear. Those segments can number from three to several thousand. Groups of them break away and, if kept moist, can move and stay alive for some time. That fact once fed a false idea about how tapeworms begin.
britannica-1911-turpin-of-rheims:
Turpin was archbishop of Reims who died in about the year eight hundred. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. For many years men thought he wrote a famed life of Charlemagne and Roland. He also appears as one of twelve peers in old French songs.

The entry links Turpin with Tilpin, archbishop of Reims in the eighth century. Flodoard tells how Charles Martel drove out Rigobert and set Milo in his place. Tilpin was first a monk at Saint Denis, then rose to Reims. He worked to restore the rights and wealth of his church. Those rights had shrunk under Milo, who held the post before him.
britannica-1911-ward-john-quincy-adams:
John Quincy Adams Ward was an American sculptor born in a small town in Ohio. He was born in the early eighteen hundreds. His schooling came from village schools. He trained for seven years under a New York master. By the time he opened his own New York studio, he had made busts of famed men of the day.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his best known works in bronze and stone. They include a hunter figure in a great park. They include a heroic Washington on the steps of a state vault in Wall Street. They also include statues of a preacher, generals, and a famed news man. He led the chief art body of his city. Later he led the new guild of sculptors for the whole land.
browning-s-shorter-poems:
Franklin T. Baker chose and edited a school set of Robert Browning's shorter poems, in a fourth revised print of 1917. Baker taught English at Teachers College, Columbia. First print came in 1899, and runs of the book came near each year since. Life of the poet, views of him as poet, and praise from critics front the verse.

A dated list of Browning's works and a book list aid the student. The Pied Piper of Hamelin leads the poems. Tray, Incident of the French Camp, and How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix follow. Hervé Riel, Pheidippides, and My Star stand in the run. Evelyn Hope, Love among the Ruins, and Natural Magic show the love and thought side. Macmillan of New York and London put out the book for class use.
canada-and-other-poems:
T. F. Young's Canada and Other Poems introduces its author's poetical attempts with great diffidence, and with a patriotic purpose. Young writes that, like Burns, he wished to do something for his country, and chose poetry as his method.

Canadian literature was in its infancy, Young argues, and must not remain so if Canada is to become a great nation. Literature, in his image, holds up a mirror to a nation's life and thought, one that heartens and ennobles its students. Young expects pedantic critics to fault his grammar and mechanics, and answers them with purpose rather than polish. Readers of early Canadian verse will find his ambition larger, and more interesting, than his finish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphabetic-ps:
Alphabetic psalms are so called because their verses, or parallel series, start with successive alphabet letters. Some formations are perfectly regular, others more or less defective. Among the regular ones are Psalms 110, 111, and 118. The praise of the strong woman in Proverbs 31:10-31 and Lamentations' first four chapters show a similar regular formation. Psalms 110 and 111 have twenty-two verses each, each verse beginning with the corresponding letter. Psalm 118 has twenty-two strophes of eight distichs each, each strophe built on one letter.

Proverbs 31:10 has twenty-two distichs, each beginning with the successive letter, and Lamentations 1, 2, and 4 each have twenty-two short strophes beginning with successive letters. In Lamentations 3, each letter begins three lines, making sixty-six lines in which each letter occurs three times as a line's initial. Defectively alphabetic psalms appear in Psalms 9, 24, 36, and 145, and the device also appears in other poetical portions of the Old Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burchard-of-w:
Burchard of Worms, bishop from 1000 to 1025, rebuilt his city, codified its laws, and gave clergy a canon-law manual used for over a century. Born of noble Hessian parents after mid-century, he studied at Coblenz, served Archbishop Willigis of Mainz as deacon, chamberlain, and city judge, and won Otto III's notice for discretion and fairness. Willigis made him Bishop of Worms in 1000 and raised him to priesthood and episcopate at Heiligenstadt.

He rebuilt Worms's walls, tore down Duke Otto's criminal refuge with Henry II's approval, and raised Saint Paul's monastery on its site. His sister Mathilda led a rebuilt women's community, and Saint Peter's cathedral rose again and was dedicated in 1016. Between 1023 and 1025 he issued the Leges et Statuta for Saint Peter's household to secure fair justice. His twenty-book Decretum, called Brocardus, gathered councils, popes, fathers, penitentials, and Scripture, and ruled clerical practice until Gratian about 1150.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-mus:
An entry on Christian museums, a term usually kept for collections rich in Christian objects from before the Middle Ages: sarcophagi, inscriptions, and minor arts. Such objects appear in many museums, but few houses devote themselves chiefly to them. Early humanist collections, such as the Medici at Florence, held medieval works for their art rather than their faith. Renaissance inscription collections ignored Christian texts until Bosio's discovery of the Roman catacombs drew collectors.

The Vatican's was the first Christian museum properly so called, founded by Benedict the Fourteenth as the Museum Christianum. With Marchi and De Rossi behind it, part of its holdings formed the Lateran Museum of 1854, which no other museum equals for Christian antiquities. Italy remains richest in such collections, from the Kircheriano and Saint Paul's to church atria and catacomb sites at Saint Domitilla and Saint Agnes, where inscriptions and sculptures still stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communicatio-:
Anthony Maas's entry explains communicatio idiomatum, a technical term of Incarnation theology, seeking its source and setting rules for its use. It means that properties of the Divine Word may be ascribed to the man Christ, and properties of the man Christ to the Word, an exchange Scripture and the Fathers allow. Its source is not a moral union, as Nestorians held, nor Christ's fullness of grace, nor the Word's right by creation.

Its base is one person subsisting in Christ's two natures. Three rules follow. Concrete terms stand for the person, so divine and human properties generally exchange. Abstract terms stand for their own nature and do not exchange. Care must guard both natures intact, even in negative sentences. By his divine nature Christ did not die, yet none may flatly say Christ did not die. A wider use in Eucharist theology closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congress-of-e:
Michael Ott's entry follows the Congress of Ems, a meeting at Bad-Ems near Coblenz in August 1786. Representatives of four German archbishops gathered: Erthal of Mainz, Maximilian Franz of Cologne, Clemens Wenceslaus of Trier, and Colloredo of Salzburg. Their purpose joined protest against papal interference in episcopal powers with fixing future archbishop-pontiff relations. Gallican principles on bishops and pope, spread in Germany by Hontheim, Trier's auxiliary, shaped their stance. His 1763 treatise, published as Febronius, argued episcopal rights against Roman claims.

Nuncio shifts framed the dispute, Bellisomi moving from Cologne to Lisbon while Pacca succeeded him at Cologne. The archbishops' Punctation assumed Christ gave apostles and successors unlimited binding and loosing power, treating papal prerogatives and reservations as concessions. Its articles reduced papal primacy toward the merely honorary and claimed independence from Rome. Archbishops insisted on their demands despite papal reply, though the reply still carried effect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foundling-asy:
Foundling asylums were institutions that took in infants whose parents could not or would not care for them, above all foundlings in the strict sense, babies deliberately abandoned. In pagan Greece and Rome, exposure of unwanted infants and direct infanticide had the sanction of law and opinion. Lycurgus and the Decemviri ordered deformed children killed, Aristotle defended exposure in his ideal state. Rome set aside two places for abandoning infants, most of whom were rescued only to become slaves.

Christian teaching that a child is sacred in itself, not a mere means to the state's ends, brought the first condemnation and the first organised rescue. Writers, priests, and bishops such as Lactantius, Tertullian, and Cyprian led it. The first recorded asylum was founded at Milan by Archpriest Datheus in 787, and Innocent III built one at Rome in 1198.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gradual-psalm:
The Gradual Psalms are fifteen psalms, Psalms 119 to 133 in the Vulgate numbering, 120 to 134 in Hebrew, bearing a Hebrew inscription rendered canticum graduum, a gradual canticle. The Authorized Version calls them songs of degrees and the Revised Version songs of ascents. A Catholic Encyclopedia article favors the pilgrim-song explanation.

Of the various conjectural explanations, the most probable treats them as psalms sung on the way up to the annual festivals in Jerusalem. The days on which they were formerly recited are still indicated in the Roman Breviary, but Saint Pius V removed the obligation of reciting them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hincmar-archb:
Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, was born in 806 and died at Épernay in 882. Descended from a distinguished West Frankish family, he was educated at St-Denis under Abbot Hilduin. He followed Hilduin to the court of Louis the Pious in 822, learned political and church administration at first hand, shared his master's banishment at Corvey, and returned with him to St-Denis.

King Charles the Bald took Hincmar into permanent service in 840, and he became the king's skilful counsellor in all matters. Raised to Reims in 845 at the Synod of Beauvais, he succeeded the deposed Ebbo in one of the great sees of the Frankish realm. The entry follows a statesman-prelate whose learning, loyalty, and long career shaped church and kingdom alike through decades of turmoil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-interims:
Temporary religious settlements imposed by Emperor Charles V on German Protestants are the subject here, from a Latin word meaning meanwhile. The first, the Interim of Ratisbon, closed the imperial diet on 29 July 1541 and built on a Catholic-Protestant conference that had agreed on justification and other points of doctrine. Its recess postponed a final settlement to the next council or diet.

Meanwhile Protestants were to hold to the agreed articles and go no further, church reform was to start under the bishops, the Peace of Nuremberg of 1532 was to stand. Monasteries, chapter houses, and church property were to stay intact. Protestants were also barred from winning new adherents. The entry shows an emperor buying time with a truce that settled nothing for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-interpretatio:
Sleep and dreaming have puzzled people since the earliest times, and this entry traces how that puzzlement became a theory of dreams. Waking minds can steer their thoughts. Sleepers can neither summon the dreams they want nor rule the dreams that come. That helplessness led early peoples to treat sleep as divine power's work and as something sacred. Arab reverence for a sleeping man may preserve a trace of that old view.

From that mystery grew the art of reading dreams as messages, and the entry follows dream lore through ancient and Christian sources, weighing what dreams can and cannot reveal. It treats dreaming as a human riddle rather than a settled science, inviting readers to see how theology, folk belief, and early psychology each tried to explain the night mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-adams:
James Adams was professor of humanities at St Omers. He was born in England in 1737 and died at Dublin on 6 December 1802. He became a Jesuit at Watten on 7 September 1756. He worked on the mission in England. He translated from French an early work on taking likenesses, titled Early Rules for Taking a Likeness, by Bonomaci.

The Royal Society of London thanked him for a treatise on English pronunciation. That work added appendices on dialects and a discussion defending Scots speech. He also composed a volume of Roman history. He planned a book on a tour through the Hebrides, which was never printed. The entry presents a Jesuit schoolman of letters, modest in output but noticed by London's learned society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-willem:
Pierre Willems was a Belgian scholar of Latin and Roman public law who taught at Louvain for more than thirty years. He was born at Maastricht in 1840 and studied at Louvain, Paris, Berlin, Utrecht, and Leyden. In 1865 he became professor of Latin philology, the study of language and literature, at Louvain.

His handbook of Roman public law, first issued in 1870 and running to seven editions, traces Roman institutions through monarchy, republic, and empire in clear, compact form. His three-volume study of the Roman Senate argued, against older views, that plebeians entered the Senate as former magistrates. Later scholars accepted that doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pius-bonifaci:
Pius Bonifacius Gams was a German Benedictine historian of the church, best known for two vast reference works. He was born at Mittelbuch in Württemberg in 1816 and studied at Tübingen. He was ordained in 1839 and taught philosophy and history at Hildesheim. In 1856 he took Benedictine vows at Saint Boniface's Abbey in Munich, adding Pius to his name.

His three-volume Church History of Spain of 1862 to 1879 is praised as conscientious and methodical, if too trusting of weak sources for the earliest period. More lasting is his Series of Bishops of the Catholic Church of 1873 to 1886, gathering the lists of bishops for every known see, ancient and modern, gaps and uncertain dates notwithstanding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalms:
The Book of Psalms, the first book of the Writings in the Hebrew Bible, receives a vast survey here. Its place in the canon varied across traditions. The Talmud puts Ruth before Psalms. Saint Jerome heads the Writings with Psalms in one letter, and with Job in another. Spanish Masoretic manuscripts begin with Chronicles. The Septuagint places Psalms first among the wisdom books. These shifting orders open a study of authorship, grouping and use.

Collections within the Psalter get close attention, including the hymns of the sons of Korah. Those psalms share a love of the Holy City, a yearning for public worship, a deep trust in God, and a simple, balanced poetic form. Their Messianic ideas and historical hints place them between Isaiah's days and the return from exile.
